sources.title: How Alexandr Wang built Meta's Muse agent: small teams, flat labs, and meme-led distribution
sources.originalTitle: Building Muse, Working with Mark Zuckerberg & The Future of AI | Alexandr Wang, Meta
sources.summary: Wang explains how Meta Superintelligence Labs went from a personal-superintelligence vision to shipping Muse, a consumer AI agent, in 7 months with under 200 people. He covers launch-blocking evals, single-point-of-view product building, self-interest marketing, meme-driven growth, and running a flat, talent-dense lab.

principles.text: Build a consumer agent by listing 100+ specific behaviors, setting launch-blocking thresholds, and shipping only when all are green.
principles.quote: We had set for each of those rows what threshold is launch blocking and above what threshold is good. We had many checkpoints that like were like green on 80 of the rows but red on 20 of the rows. We knew that wasn't good enough.

principles.text: Keep the team small and focused on a flagship product; one strong point of view beats a committee smoothie.
principles.quote: it was a really small focused team working on it and that it didn't balloon to this like oh you have like you know huge swasts of the company working on because we knew it was a single work of art.

principles.text: Reliability is the product: unreliable agent experiences make users churn, so sand out every edge before scaling.
principles.quote: personal agents was one of these product areas that kind of rested on a knife's edge, which is if it can reliably deliver these magical experiences, it has the potential to be one of the greatest consumer products ever.

principles.text: Market on what the product does for the user, not on you; people are self-interested.
principles.quote: most people in the world, they don't give a [ __ ] about like OpenAI or the research or you know these other companies or the research or even us or our research or whatever. They care about like what it can do for them.

principles.text: Distribution alone doesn't break through; use surprising, risky content and a recognizable mascot to make screenshots travel.
principles.quote: the internet rewards risk and it rewards like surprise and like things that like people don't expect.

principles.text: For research-driven work, hire top talent, keep the org flat and anti-bureaucratic, and act as steward of the environment, not a micromanager.
principles.quote: they don't need managers, they need a great environment. They are all brilliant. They're all extremely capable. They just need the room to cook.

sources.title: How Alexandr Wang launched Muse: agents for non-coders, trust over raw capability
sources.originalTitle: The Biggest Launch Since ChatGPT (Muse)
sources.summary: Wang explains why Muse took off: it brought the agent experience engineers had to everyone else, pitched as saving money and time. He stresses polish, hard security work before launch, and that consumer trust will matter more than raw model intelligence.

principles.text: Find the gap: bring what power users already enjoy to everyone else
principles.quote: most people in the world they don't know how to code. They probably never even want to code. Um but they still want to feel the experience of agents

sources.title: How Meta Superintelligence Labs built Muse Wonder: talent density, big bets, product-shaped models
sources.originalTitle: Zuckerberg’s $100 Billion Bet
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang and Mark Zuckerberg describe how Meta rebooted its AI effort into a small, elite lab and shipped the Muse agent and the Muse Wonder model. Wang covers making huge compute bets with no feedback loop, treating the model as the product, why internal evals beat public benchmarks, and why leaders must stay technical.

principles.text: In AI, product decisions are really model-design decisions: behavior and personality get specified through training, data and evals.
principles.quote: how do you specify these product decisions well it's ultimately in model design decisions which ultimately boil down to like training methods or data or vals or you know all these things.

principles.text: Frontier AI is entrepreneurship on hard mode: you commit huge sums years ahead, before any proof points exist.
principles.quote: this is like entrepreneurship on hard mode it's like the opposite of lean startup like lean startup is like yeah you like see if you get something working and then you double down

principles.text: Don't outsource product thinking to public benchmarks; build your own evals for the capabilities users value.
principles.quote: you're kind of outsourcing all of your product thinking to that PhD student who happened to make a viral benchmark. Um so clearly like that's wrong.

principles.text: Many small improvements, each worth about 2% to the user, add up to a product that feels magical.
principles.quote: Maybe each of them matters like 2% to the user, but in aggregate that's like the obsession that will ultimately result in these models that feel magical.

principles.text: Stay technical as a leader; in a fast-moving domain, leaders who stop using the tools lose touch quickly.
principles.quote: you go from being very technical to you go to a role where you're not like in the details anymore and then you very quickly become not technical or don't kind of understand it much faster than you probably realize

principles.text: Early in RL post-training, less data of higher quality often beats more, the opposite of pre-training.
principles.quote: you notice very funny things like if you uh you know in a lot of cases less is actually more when it comes to data in RL.

sources.title: How Alexandr Wang built Meta's frontier AI lab from scratch in 9 months
sources.originalTitle: The Most Expensive Hire In AI History Finally Talks
sources.outlet: Core Memory Podcast and Core Memory
sources.summary: Wang explains how Meta Superintelligence Labs was structured after Llama 4 fell behind: small, talent-dense teams, high compute per researcher, and a clean rebuilt stack designed for predictable scaling. He also covers recruiting, why compute splits tech companies into two classes, and why AI sentiment stays low until it empowers ordinary people.

principles.text: Build the whole organization around the belief that superintelligence is near, then reset every other assumption around it.
principles.quote: they build the entire organizations around the premise that superintelligence is coming and it is very close and this is a very realistic thing to believe

principles.text: Concentrate compute on fewer researchers; higher compute per researcher speeds up research more than spreading it widely.
principles.quote: if you build a more focused effort with a smaller team that has higher compute per researcher, you can actually make faster research progress.

principles.text: Hire brilliant people and give them the environment to do their best work instead of bossing them around.
principles.quote: most companies hire people and tell them what to do, but we hire people for them to tell us what to do.

principles.text: Recruit top talent by personally explaining your mission and proving you are serious, especially if your reputation is weak.
principles.quote: it took a lot of like going to people, talking to them, explaining what we were building, explaining what we were focused on, explaining what we why we cared about the technology

principles.text: Compute splits tech companies into two classes; those with it can build and bet in ways others cannot.
principles.quote: so much of this next phase of technology really boils down to compute.

principles.text: A rebuilt, clean stack from scratch can beat messy incumbents on both speed and efficiency.
principles.quote: a lot of it comes down to just having built a very very clean stack from scratch

sources.title: Alexandr Wang at YC: conviction, AI-era building, and agentic loops
sources.originalTitle: Alexandr Wang: “This is a Once-in-a-Civilization Opportunity”
sources.summary: Wang recounts how Scale AI started after a failed medical-agent idea, and why early conviction in unpopular beliefs matters. He argues AI makes startups "Goliath vs Goliath," that vision and ambition become the scarce resources, and that agentic feedback loops with the right metric are the biggest near-term opportunity.

principles.text: Build conviction in beliefs nobody else shares; the herd will confuse you.
principles.quote: you need to develop conviction in a set of beliefs that nobody else um agrees with.

principles.text: Winning companies toil in obscurity before their idea becomes consensus; don't base decisions on what others say.
principles.quote: you can't base your business decisions based on what everyone else is saying around you. Like if you go too much with the herd, you will get immensely confused

principles.text: Founders start out bad at everything; the game is learning and improving fast.
principles.quote: for all entrepreneurs, you start out pretty shitty at everything. And um the whole game is how do you develop yourself to continuously improve to get better and learn quickly?

principles.text: Spot the bottleneck from your own experience: Scale came from needing data to train models.
principles.quote: for two out of these three things, you could just press a button online and get them. And then for the last one for data, there was like no effective way to get data

principles.text: With AI agents, startups can compete with incumbents as equals, not underdogs.
principles.quote: I actually think with the power of agents um and AI broadly speaking it's much closer to Goliath versus Goliath

principles.text: Pick the steepest, longest-lasting exponential, even if its starting point looks boring.
principles.quote: try to identify what is the what is the exponential in the world that has both the steepest curve and will go the longest

sources.title: How Scale AI grew: narrow wedge, infinite markets, and hiring people who care
sources.originalTitle: Alexandr Wang: Building Scale AI, Transforming Work With Agents & Competing With China
sources.summary: Wang recounts how Scale started at YC as an API for human labor, won by focusing on self-driving data, then repeatedly built ahead of AI waves (OpenAI, defense, enterprise agents). He explains when to move from narrow markets to infinite ones, why specialized data and models will be a company's IP, and why caring deeply is the trait he hires for.

principles.text: If an incumbent product is widely mentioned but awful in practice, that's a good sign there's room to win.
principles.quote: whenever you're in a space and that's kind of the like that's like the thing. It's like people mention a thing, but it sucks, that's usually like a pretty good sign.

principles.text: Focus on one seemingly narrow, fast-growing vertical to build momentum quickly, even if it can't sustain the final business.
principles.quote: it is both true that it enabled us to build the business to be to get to scale pretty very quickly and it is also true that that was not a big enough market to sustain a gigantic business.

principles.text: Start in the narrowest market, then switch gears toward infinite markets if you want a $100B company.
principles.quote: early on you're trying to go for very very narrow markets like almost the narrowest markets you can and then you're just trying to like gain momentum and then sort of like slowly grow out from those hyper narrow markets

principles.text: Serve the layer every wave of a technology depends on, so you end up building ahead of the trend.
principles.quote: for AI to be successful in any vertical area it needed data and so like our demand for our our products would preede a lot of times the actual sort of like evolution of AI into those industries.

principles.text: Differentiation comes from encoding your unique business problems into data and environments for specialized models.
principles.quote: alpha in the modern world will be determined by you know to what degree you're able to sort of like encapsulate your business problems into data sets or environments

principles.text: Hire people who deeply care about their work; the magnitude of care is the strongest signal of success.
principles.quote: I wrote this post many years ago called hire people who give a and it really is pretty simple.

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on rebuilding Meta's AI lab: predictable scaling, safety-gated open source, personal agents
sources.originalTitle: Meta AI Chief Wang on Winning the Race in AI
sources.summary: Wang explains how Meta Superintelligence Labs spent a year rebuilding its model stack around "predictable scaling" after Llama 4 fell short, shipping Muse Spark as an early data point. He covers why risk testing pushed Meta away from open-sourcing it, his view of agents as deeply personal tools, and why AI is also creating more small businesses.

principles.text: Build the research effort around predictable scaling: more data and compute yield predictable capability gains.
principles.quote: overall we built the entire research effort around predictable scaling. So the so the entire belief of our overall research effort was, you know, that in many ways the central belief behind the current modern AI boom is that as you scale these models

principles.text: Treat an early release as a data point on a scaling ladder, not the finished product.
principles.quote: new Spark it was an early data point on that scaling ladder for us. The next models we release will be an even greater point on that on the scaling curves

principles.text: Frontier progress needs scaling data, compute, research and infrastructure together.
principles.quote: it's about continuing to scale the data, the compute going into the models, as well as continuing scale with research.

principles.text: Gate open-sourcing on risk testing, because mitigations are harder once a model is released openly.
principles.quote: when we launch a model like New Spark in a product, we have a lot of ways to mitigate some of these risks and ensure that we're able to launch it in a safe and responsible way. Um it's much harder to do that when you open source a model

principles.text: Double down on the strengths you observe in early models, such as multimodality, health and agentic ability.
principles.quote: So, we are doubling down on some of these and and continuing to invest into the agentic capabilities of the model.

principles.text: AI tools are enabling more new businesses and entrepreneurs, which offsets some job-loss worries.
principles.quote: AI is enabling the creation of more businesses than ever before in the world and, you know, we see this in our data.

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on building Meta Superintelligence Labs: research-led flywheel, durable foundations, personal agents
sources.originalTitle: Zuckerberg's Secret Plan To WIN The AI Race | Meta AI Chief Reveals Future
sources.summary: Wang explains how he designed Meta Superintelligence Labs from a blank slate: research-led, high talent density, no artificial deadlines. He describes a flywheel of models, products and infrastructure, and reflects on trading youthful impatience for long-term foundations.

principles.text: Run models, products and infrastructure as one flywheel: frontier models enable products, products fund infrastructure, infrastructure enables better models.
principles.quote: by building frontier models... that enables to build incredible products. Those products, as they gain scale, then give us the ability to grow our infrastructure footprint... And then that will enable us to build even greater models

principles.text: Best AI products come from researchers thinking about product and product people thinking about research, working together, not handoffs.
principles.quote: we're I think past the phase where it's just about research in, you know, a corner and then that hands off to product people and then they deploy that.

principles.text: Design the organization from a blank slate around scientific foundations and talent density, and remove artificial deadlines.
principles.quote: We're going to set up with the incredible talent density and the focus on the long-term science. We're going to remove artificial deadlines so that we're actually building the technology at the best pace.

principles.text: Don't cut corners for short-term outcomes that mortgage the long-term opportunity.
principles.quote: we're not just setting ourselves up to cut a corner here or to opt in for some short-term outcome, but but mortgage the long-term opportunity.

principles.text: Businesses with staying power build a foundation that is hard to replicate; don't let impatience drive you too far.
principles.quote: the ones with true staying power have built some sort of foundation that is actually very difficult to replicate. And it's something that is it's almost like a seed that is planted and grows

principles.text: Distribution is a core AI advantage: reach to billions of users lets you deploy personal agents in ways other labs cannot.
principles.quote: It has the distribution, it has the billions and billions of users, it has the scale, it has the business model, it has um the incredible talent, it has the infrastructure.

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on Scale AI, data as the AI bottleneck, and why AI creates jobs (Theo Von #563)
sources.originalTitle: AI CEO Alexandr Wang | This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von #563
sources.summary: Wang tells how AlphaGo's 2016 win pushed him to drop out of MIT and found Scale AI. He frames AI as chips, data and algorithms, with data quality as the real bottleneck. He argues AI will create jobs, turn workers into managers of agents, and should stay a helpful tool rather than an ad platform.

principles.text: Act when you see a technology inflection point, even if it means leaving school early.
principles.quote: I remember feeling like oh wow AI it's happening

principles.text: Data is the scarce input that powers AI, so owning high-quality data is a durable advantage.
principles.quote: data is the new oil or data is the new gold like data is really really valuable because it's it's how the algorithms are learning everything that they're learning

principles.text: Build a marketplace that turns a bottleneck into an opportunity: pair AI labs needing data with a network of contributors.
principles.quote: we're kind of like the Uber for AI so just like how Uber you have you know Riders and drivers for us we have uh you know we have the AI systems you know the algorithms that need data

principles.text: Keep AI trustworthy by constantly testing it and keeping its data clean.
principles.quote: we have to constantly be testing the AI system

principles.text: AI turns knowledge workers into managers of AI agents rather than replacing them.
principles.quote: it'll almost be like everybody gets um promoted to being a manager like because I'm going to be managing like a a little pod of 10 AI agents that are doing the work that I used to do

principles.text: Keep AI a tool that helps people first, not an advertising platform.
principles.quote: I wanted to make sure it's a tool that helps people first and foremost

sources.title: How Alexandr Wang built Scale AI: focus, overdoing it, and finding the neglected bottleneck
sources.originalTitle: Alexandr Wang - CEO, Scale AI | SRS #208
sources.summary: Wang spends most of this Shawn Ryan interview on AI, national security and China, but the founder lessons are clear. He found data as the ignored bottleneck in AI, focused on a few big customers, outworked peers, and traded perfectionism for speed. He also shares how he got early hires and traction with no credibility.

principles.text: Spot the neglected bottleneck: everyone built algorithms and chips, so he built the data layer.
principles.quote: You have plenty of people working on building the chips and the computational capacity and and um and all that. Nobody working on data.

principles.text: Focus on a small number of top customers where you can have outsized impact.
principles.quote: how do we focus on a small number of customers who where we can have like a really big impact.

principles.text: Outwork peers by overdoing it; hyperfocus and extra effort compound into much faster progress.
principles.quote: if you overdo things, like you like really like invest lots of time, lots of effort, you go the extra mile, you go the extra 10 miles, and you're like constantly overdoing things, then you will improve faster than anybody else by many times.

principles.text: Ship at 80% for 20% of the effort, repeatedly; speed usually beats perfection.
principles.quote: you got to just do the 8020 lots of times. Like you got to do 20% of the effort. That's 80% as good and you just have to be okay with that.

principles.text: With no credibility, hire from your existing trusted network first.
principles.quote: I mostly hired people I knew from school.

principles.text: Early on, ship fast and launch publicly on startup sites, then push friends for traction.
principles.quote: I just coded it all up and then there like I like put it out on one of these there's all these like websites where you can launch startups

sources.title: How Alexandr Wang built Scale AI: data infrastructure, reinvention and hiring for internal locus of control
sources.originalTitle: Alexandr Wang: 26-Year-Old Billionaire Powering the AI Industry
sources.summary: Wang explains why data is the building block of the AI era and how Scale positioned itself as infrastructure, taking cues from Stripe and Amazon. He also covers hiring for internal locus of control, a merit-based culture, anchoring on big problems, and holding a strong point of view.

principles.text: Build infrastructure that makes a universal pain point simple and scalable, so it becomes the industry default.
principles.quote: لقد أخذوا تلك المشاكل وبنوا تجارب سهلة للمطورين، ووصلوا بها إلى مستوى من البساطة ووضوح وفورات الحجم، مما جعلها الخيار الافتراضي في الصناعة.

principles.text: The real bet on a great company is its ability to keep reinventing itself, not its near-term revenue forecast.
principles.quote: هم يراهنون في أفضل الشركات على إعادة الابتكار المستمرة.

principles.text: Run a merit-based culture where anyone with a good idea owns turning it into something big.
principles.quote: إذا كانت لديك فكرة رائعة- بدايةً يمكن لأي شخص أن يطرح فكرة رائعة- فلديك كامل المسؤولية لتحقيقها وجعلها واقعًا ملموسًا.

principles.text: Anchor the company on the industry's biggest problems; opportunities keep growing as you solve them.
principles.quote: فهي بالنسبة لنا التفكير في المشكلات الكبيرة في هذا القطاع، عندها ستجد دائماً فرصاً تستمر في النمو لتصبح أكبر وأكبر.

principles.text: Hire people with an internal locus of control who own outcomes on what they care about.
principles.quote: وأجد أنني أرغب فقط في العمل مع الأشخاص الذين لديهم مركز تحكم داخلي.

principles.text: Take a strong, public point of view; it attracts aligned talent, builds culture and keeps the company authentic.
principles.quote: أصبح من الصواب امتلاك وجهة نظر قوية والجهر بها، لأن ذلك يسمح لك بجذب المواهب التي تتفق معك

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on Scale AI: irrational self-belief, unsexy problems, and independent thinking
sources.originalTitle: Scale AI & the Startup Hunger Games with Alexandr Wang
sources.summary: Wang recounts Scale's year of "wandering" after YC, then explains how he thinks about competition, enterprise sales, culture, and AI startups. Core themes: blustery self-belief, treating unglamorous problems with respect, optimizing for net economic impact, thinking independently of trends, and focusing instead of out-spending giants.

principles.text: Competing requires irrational self-belief that you'll out-recruit, out-build and out-work others; it compounds over time.
principles.quote: I think you need some kind kind of you know irrational self-belief to be to believe that you will be able to compete in the marketplace

principles.text: In enterprise, perception often outweighs reality, so shape perception as well as improving the product.
principles.quote: just as much as your job is to improve the reality it is to shape the perception

principles.text: Treat the least sexy problems with the same respect as elite ones; pair strong problem solving with humility.
principles.quote: we treat that problem with the same level of respect that we would you know let's say a math Olympiad problem

principles.text: Motivate people by net economic impact, not technical difficulty; much value sits in messy, unglamorous problems.
principles.quote: you just think about like net economic impact of problems that you're solving relative to just technical difficulty um that's the ladder you want to be climbing

principles.text: In hyped markets, work out what you actually believe and keep learning, rather than following trends.
principles.quote: the biggest challenge I think for Founders is to develop a sense of what you actually believe and then also having a mechanism by which you're constantly learning from the ecosystem

principles.text: Don't compete with infinite balance sheets; pick one problem and stay focused on it for a long time.
principles.quote: the premium is actually just picking a certain problem to care about for a really long time

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on why data, not compute, is the AI bottleneck, plus hiring and PR principles
sources.originalTitle: Alex Wang: Why Data Not Compute is the Bottleneck to Foundation Model Performance | E1164
sources.summary: Wang argues AI progress has hit a "data wall": compute spend has exploded since GPT-4, but the easy internet data is used up. The next gains need frontier data (reasoning chains, agent traces) produced by human experts working with models. He also covers data as the one durable moat, consumption pricing, going direct instead of traditional PR, and keeping a very high hiring bar.

principles.text: Progress needs algorithms, compute and data together; scaling only compute hits a data wall.
principles.quote: a lot of the plateau that we've recently seen can almost be explained at a very high level from um hitting kind of a data wall

principles.text: Internet data can't teach agents, because the reasoning behind real work never gets written down.
principles.quote: all of the reasoning and thinking that is powering the economy today none of that gets written down on the internet

principles.text: Build the means of production for data the way the industry builds fabs for chips: a human-plus-synthetic process.
principles.quote: it's sort of a hybrid uh human synthetic process and that's really how we think about it which is you need you need algorithms that can do a lot of the heavy lifting in producing uh synthetic data but you need human experts

principles.text: Data is the one pillar where a lasting competitive advantage can form, since algorithms leak and compute can be bought.
principles.quote: data is one of the few areas where you can produce a a long-term sustainable competive Advantage

principles.text: Founders should own their distribution and tell their story directly instead of relying on traditional press.
principles.quote: the imperative is on the companies themselves to properly tell their story through direct channels and through podcasts

principles.text: Hypergrowth in headcount erodes the hiring bar. Keep the team small and approve every hire yourself.
principles.quote: when you hire that quickly it is impossible to to do what we've just been talking about which is maintain M this High bar

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on frontier data, model economics, and keeping headcount flat at Scale AI
sources.originalTitle: Why Human Data is Key to AI: Alexandr Wang from Scale AI
sources.summary: Wang explains why data is the next bottleneck for AI after compute and algorithms, and why renting out models is a weaker business than the layers above and below it. He also shares hiring lessons: keep high-performing teams small, onboard outside executives slowly, and stay in the key decisions as founder-CEO.

principles.text: Public data is exhausted, so the next AI advances depend on producing new, harder data.
principles.quote: we've kind of run out of all the easily accessible and easily available data out there

principles.text: Capabilities like agents are blocked by missing data, so you must produce data that doesn't exist yet.
principles.quote: it turns out there's just no agent data on the internet

principles.text: Pure model rental has weak pricing power; better businesses sit below (compute) and above (applications).
principles.quote: it turns out intelligence might be a commodity

principles.text: Scaling headcount erodes a high-performing team, so hold it flat while the business grows.
principles.quote: if you have a very high performing team and a very high performing org it's in near impossible to grow it dramatically without losing all that high performance

principles.text: Bring outside executives in slowly: small steps first, trust and verify, larger changes only after a track record.
principles.quote: they take small steps and you sort of like you trust and verify each of these small steps

principles.text: A founder-CEO should not outsource key decisions; making them well is the job.
principles.quote: the reason that you are a good founder CEO is because you make very good decisions over and over and over again

sources.title: How Scale AI became the data foundry for AI: Alexandr Wang on data abundance, evals and human+model teaming
sources.originalTitle: No Priors Ep. 65 | With Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang
sources.outlet: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang explains why he started Scale AI around the data pillar of AI, how the company moved through self-driving, government and generative AI, and why frontier data, hybrid human-AI synthetic data and rigorous evals are the bottlenecks to better models. He also argues AGI will come by solving many small problems, each with its own data flywheel.

principles.text: Find the neglected pillar: AI rests on algorithms, compute and data, and in 2016 nobody was focused on data.
principles.quote: there were companies working on the algorithms ... Nvidia was already a very clear leader in building compute for these AI systems um but there was nobody focused on data

principles.text: As infrastructure, lay the tracks before the freight train arrives: anticipate where breakthrough use cases will land.
principles.quote: our burden is to be thinking ahead as to where are the Breakthrough use cases in AI going to be and how do we basically lay down the tracks before the sort of you know freight train of AI comes rolling through

principles.text: Focus early: build for one use case first (sensor-fused data for AVs) and let it become the industry standard.
principles.quote: we followed the early startup advice you have to focus uh early on as a company and so we we built the very first data engine that supported um sensor fuse data

principles.text: Not all data is equal; frontier, high-supervisory-signal data can be vastly more valuable than run-of-the-mill data.
principles.quote: not all data is created equal and high quality data or Frontier data is is can be you know 10,000 times more valuable than just any run-of-the-mill data uh within an Enterprise

principles.text: The question is whether human plus model beats the model alone, and Wang expects that to hold for a very long time.
principles.quote: the question is is a human plus a model together when people produce better output than a model alone and I think that'll be the case for a very very very long time

principles.text: Build self-improvement into products via data flywheels: constantly collect new data and evaluate where the system is weak.
principles.quote: self-improvement comes from data fly wheels so how do you have a flywheel by which you're constantly you know getting new data that improves the your model you're constantly evaluating that system to understand where there's weaknesses

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on building Scale AI: data as AI infrastructure and picking uncrowded ideas
sources.originalTitle: Scale AI’s Alexandr Wang | Our Most Powerful Tech | Spotlight On: AI | S1E5 | AccelVC
sources.summary: Wang explains how Scale became the data infrastructure layer for AI by focusing on a base primitive (data) that must scale as the industry scales. He gives founder advice: start before a trend is cool, avoid crowded categories, don't build ahead of the technology, and ignore small-TAM objections. He also shares his outlook on multimodality, proprietary data and enterprise AI.

principles.text: Build infrastructure around base primitives that can't be bypassed and must scale exponentially with the industry.
principles.quote: you can't build AI without data fundamentally and then it's something that um has to scale exponentially as the entire field develops

principles.text: Start in an area before it gets cool, so you have a head start when the opportunity arrives.
principles.quote: the thing that allows you to actually win is that by the time the thing becomes cool or interesting you've had this like head running Head Start

principles.text: Avoid crowded categories; pick unpopular areas where AI can still have a large impact.
principles.quote: I would pick I would pick areas uh which are not very popular

principles.text: Don't bet the company on technical limitations disappearing; stay within what the technology can do today.
principles.quote: don't try to start something that's too far ahead of where the capability of the technology is

principles.text: A blank-slate, naive approach lets you accomplish what incumbents stuck in ruts cannot.
principles.quote: approaching Industries with a totally blank slate and and no with Without A fine grain understanding of what makes things hard is actually part of what allows you to accomplish things

principles.text: Small TAM objections are normal for important companies in fast-growing markets; have conviction early.
principles.quote: the T was small of every important company when they were getting started basically

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on building Scale AI: hiring missionaries, thinking big, and practical AI
sources.originalTitle: MOST INNOVATIVE COMPANIES PODCAST: This CEO is betting on AI to solve the world’s biggest problems
sources.summary: Wang explains how Scale AI grew from solving AI's data bottleneck into a 700-person company. He covers keeping startup energy while growing, hiring people who care, and why ambition shapes outcomes. He also argues AI should be applied through concrete, near-term use cases.

principles.text: Find the unglamorous bottleneck between a big vision and real impact, and build the company there.
principles.quote: there need to be people who are focused on what are the foot by footstep interactions that are required to actually get artificial intelligence to actually have an impact on the world

principles.text: Hire people who truly care about the mission; don't let recruiting turn into a college admissions office.
principles.quote: how do you bring on sort of missionaries versus mercenaries is a really really important thing for for companies to get right

principles.text: As a company grows, recruiting drifts from finding people who care to selecting impressive applicants. Resist it.
principles.quote: the recruiting team turns into almost like a college admissions office and it turns into sort of this you know we have all these applicants coming in let's select the most impressive diverse and and sort of like interesting group of people

principles.text: Ambition caps outcomes, so build a culture where people dream big; thinking small is self-fulfilling.
principles.quote: thinking small is a self-fulfilling prophecy right if you think small then maybe you accomplish those small things but you're never going to accomplish the big things

principles.text: Growing companies drift into maintaining the core; keep deliberately building new upside.
principles.quote: there's a massive temptation to just think about incrementally maintaining or incrementally improving that core instead of also thinking big about what are other ideas that you could do

principles.text: Invite people to think bigger by framing their work against a large global problem.
principles.quote: there's nothing more seductive than the invitation to think bigger

sources.title: How Alexandr Wang built Scale AI: data-centric AI, people, and bias for action
sources.originalTitle: ETL Speaker Series: Alexandr Wang, Scale AI
sources.summary: Wang explains how he spotted data as the missing pillar of AI after seeing AWS and Stripe become platforms for their eras. He shares lessons on ambition, hiring and people, acting under uncertainty, and a costly early mistake of neglecting a key customer.

principles.text: Find the missing infrastructure pillar of a new technology by pattern-matching to past platforms like AWS and Stripe.
principles.quote: what aws has done for the cloud or what stripe has done for payments you know there's an opportunity for a company to do that for ai and unlock this huge amount of potential for the technology

principles.text: Ambitious and unambitious goals take the same work, so dream big and then build.
principles.quote: doing something that's ambitious versus not ambitious you know they might take literally the same amount of work

principles.text: Invest in people; their importance is vastly underestimated early on.
principles.quote: however much i thought that people mattered at the start they matter like 10 it's like obviously they matter 10x more now

principles.text: Self-doubt is normal; never be paralyzed. Any action beats none because you can course correct.
principles.quote: it is totally okay for that to happen to you um it is not okay to be paralyzed when that happens

principles.text: Don't treat starting a company as a big sacrifice decision; put yourself in situations with freedom and let momentum build.
principles.quote: just put yourself in situations where you have sort of freedom and flexibility to explore and then and then like see how you gain momentum

principles.text: Never neglect an early anchor customer; stay customer-centric and aim to exceed expectations.
principles.quote: it's just so so important to be customer-centric and it's so important to to always be focused on your customers

sources.title: How Scale AI's Alexandr Wang frames data infrastructure, hiring and daily improvement
sources.originalTitle: E1005 ScaleAI CEO Alexandr Wang: future of self-driving, China’s ML advantages, next major AI trends
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang explains Scale AI as a data refinery for machine learning, where machines do the bulk of labeling and humans correct errors. He argues infrastructure providers must be reliable like AWS, that great people differ exponentially from good ones, and that products must improve every day or decay. Much of the episode is AI-future opinion rather than business playbook.

principles.text: Find the bottleneck everyone shares and become the infrastructure for it; for ML that bottleneck was labeled data.
principles.quote: one of the the huge bottlenecks for machine learning is is data ends up being like data that tells these algorithms tell these models what they're supposed to be doing and and that's where that's where scale comes in

principles.text: Automate most of the work with machines, then use humans to catch errors so output quality stays extremely high.
principles.quote: a lot of work is done behind the scenes by machines and our own our own AI models originally and then humans basically give input and correct mistakes to make sure that that the end data is extremely accurate

principles.text: If you are infrastructure, reliability is the product. Customers build on you and must be able to depend on you.
principles.quote: as a general rule as an infrastructure provider you are you need to give infrastructure that's very reliable that people can depend on

principles.text: Improve the product every single day. Standing still means decay while competitors improve.
principles.quote: your products either getting better or getting worse right because if you are not improving it it's deprecating and a competitor is improving and your users are getting used to this average product

principles.text: A simple founder loop: build something you care about, find users and listen, then improve it daily.
principles.quote: build something you care about number two find users listen to them three improve it every single day

principles.text: Great people are not just slightly better than good ones. There is a huge gap, so hire for greatness.
principles.quote: many folks believe there's a smooth continuum between good people and great people in my experience is a huge band gap between good and great

sources.title: Why AI will never replace humans: Wang on data, human judgment and building Scale AI
sources.originalTitle: Why AI will never replace humans | Alexandr Wang | TEDxBerkeley
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang argues AI depends on humans because algorithms need data and good data needs human judgment and values. He explains how he saw the data bottleneck at MIT and founded Scale AI around it. He frames AI as a tool that automates repetitive work so people can focus on creative problems.

principles.text: Data quality is the core bottleneck of AI. Bad or missing data means bad AI, so never treat data as an afterthought.
principles.quote: لا يمكنك التعامل مع البيانات كفكرة متأخرة. البيانات السيئة أو نقص البيانات تؤدي إلى ذكاء اصطناعي سيئ.

principles.text: AI's basic setup is algorithms that need data, and data that needs humans. That keeps humans in the loop.
principles.quote: إذا فكرت في الإعداد الأساسي للذكاء الاصطناعي، فإن الخوارزميات تحتاج إلى بيانات، والبيانات بحاجة إلى بشر.

principles.text: Build a company around a core problem that every application shares. Scale started from the need for large, high-quality datasets.
principles.quote: بناء مجموعات بيانات كبيرة الحجم وعالية الجودة لتشغيل كل تطبيق بدون إستثناء. كان هذا هو الدافع خلف اطلاق سكايل

principles.text: Aligning AI with human intent and values is ongoing work that will always require people.
principles.quote: إن المواءمة المستمرة للذكاء الاصطناعي مع النوايا البشرية ستتطلب دائمًا البشر.

principles.text: AI automates first where there is the most data, not where tasks seem simplest to humans.
principles.quote: لذلك، هذا ليس ما يعتبره البشر أبسط مهمة سوف يقوم الذكاء الاصطناعي بأتمتتها أولاً، ولكن بدلاً من ذلك حيث لدينا معظم البيانات.

principles.text: Use AI to automate repetitive tasks so people have time for new ideas and creative work.
principles.quote: سيقوم الذكاء الاصطناعي بأتمتة المهام المتكررة التي لا تتطلب قرار أو إبداع بشري مستمر، مما سيعطينا الوقت لاستكشاف أفكار جديدة والتركيز عليها.

sources.title: Hire people who give a shit: Alexandr Wang's hiring screen at Scale
sources.originalTitle: hire
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang explains that after interviewing every Scale offer, he screens for two things: caring about the company's mission and caring about work in general. He warns against becoming a credential brand, argues recruiting should feel like courtship, and shares his interview questions for spotting obsession.

principles.text: Screen for two things: they care about the company, and they care about their work in general.
principles.quote: I mainly screen for one key thing: giving a shit. To be more specific, there’s actually two things to screen for:

principles.text: Caring doesn't guarantee great work, but not caring guarantees bad work, so mission fit is non-negotiable.
principles.quote: While it is not guaranteed that someone who gives shit will do great work, it is guaranteed that they will not do good work if they do not give a shit.

principles.text: As a company grows, more candidates come for the brand; more top-of-funnel hides a sharp drop in hire ROI.
principles.quote: it will be more common for people to interview for the brand rather than the substance. In fact, most growing companies often miss this effect entirely, and simply observe the fact they’re getting far more top-of-funnel.

principles.text: Recruit like courtship, not a college admissions office; look for people you'd want beside you through long nights.
principles.quote: A recruiting team that looks like a college admissions office is certain death for a startup. If you’re built to simply sift through a swarm of homogeneous candidates, then on the other side you will simply get a higher credentialed homogeneous soup.

principles.text: Past obsession predicts future obsession; probe how hard they've worked and why they cared.
principles.quote: If someone is applying to Scale and has never been deeply obsessed about something before, then it’s a bad bet to think Scale will be the first.

principles.text: Culture is the people and their effort, not perks or office cosmetics.
principles.quote: No perk tells me anything meaningful about the company, other than how comfortable with spending money they are. The company _is_ the culture.

sources.title: Why we're building Muse: an AI second mind that turns stated wants into reality
sources.originalTitle: why were building muse
sources.summary: A short vision essay arguing that most human wants go unexpressed and unrealized because the world is a maze of obstacles. Muse is pitched as a general-manager-like AI that draws out what you want and handles the execution. The thesis is that no one knows what people will want once everyone's agency is switched on.

principles.text: Unexpressed wants are the core problem: people can't reach goals they can't name.
principles.quote: When we can’t name our dreams, we mostly can’t reach them.

principles.text: Friction (forms, gatekeepers, not knowing where to start) kills more ambitions than lack of desire.
principles.quote: They die in the not-knowing-where-to-start and in the phone calls never made.

principles.text: Build AI as an agent that handles execution so the human only has to want and dream.
principles.quote: Clears the way and solves all the problems it can until the human part, the wanting and the dreaming, is all that’s left.

principles.text: A good AI assistant should help elicit vague intent, not just execute precise commands.
principles.quote: Someone that hears the half-sentence, “I feel like there’s something more I could be doing,” and helps fill in the blanks.

principles.text: Lowering the barrier to action unlocks unpredictable demand; don't assume you know what people will want.
principles.quote: we have no idea what people will want.

principles.text: Historically only a few fanatics made their wants real; the opportunity is giving everyone that agency.
principles.quote: The world until now has been shaped by the small number of fanatics who have somehow found a way to make their wants real.

sources.title: What I learned in 2016: risk-seeking, hard work, and speed at Scale's founding
sources.originalTitle: What I learned in 2016 - Medium
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang reflects on founding Scale in 2016. He argues for taking risks while you are most risk-seeking, minimizing regret, and working extremely hard because learning compounds super-linearly. Since startup idea returns follow a power law, he says to compress ideas to MVPs and move fast.

principles.text: Take the big risk now: you're the most risk-seeking you'll ever be, and the risk you skip today may never get taken.
principles.quote: That means today, you’re the most risk-seeking you’ll ever be. So, if there’s a risk today that you aren’t willing to take, then you might never end up taking that risk.

principles.text: Minimize regret by chasing many opportunities; having no regrets means you aren't chasing enough.
principles.quote: I believe that if you don’t have opportunities you regret not taking, you aren’t chasing after enough opportunities.

principles.text: Learning compounds super-linearly with effort, so working harder yields outsized growth.
principles.quote: the amount I learned grew super-linearly with how hard I worked. That is, there’s an economies of scale effect with how hard I worked.

principles.text: When good ideas outnumber your build capacity, time is the enemy, so raise execution speed.
principles.quote: The higher your execution speed, the more you’re able to keep up with the flood of ideas.

principles.text: Idea returns follow a power law, so shrink each idea to an MVP and execute fast to avoid missing the big one.
principles.quote: To prevent a diamond idea from being passed over, startups need to compress each idea to an minimum viable product (MVP) as much as possible, and focus on fast execution speed.

principles.text: Hard work consistently beats other factors in building a startup.
principles.quote: Hard work consistently seems to trump other factors.

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on conviction, AI timing, and building when intelligence is abundant
sources.originalTitle: Alexandr Wang: “This is a Once-in-a-Civilization Opportunity”
sources.summary: Wang recounts starting Scale at 19 after a failed medical-agent idea, spotting that data was the missing piece for training models, and holding conviction while investors dismissed it. He argues AI's bottleneck is now adoption, startups can out-compete incumbents with agents, and vision and ambition become the scarce resources.

principles.text: Develop conviction in beliefs nobody else shares; winners toil in obscurity before the idea becomes consensus.
principles.quote: you need to develop conviction in a set of beliefs that nobody else agrees with.

principles.text: Don't follow the herd when making business decisions; build your own compass for what the future looks like.
principles.quote: if you go too much with the herd, you will get immensely confused and you will end up nowhere.

principles.text: Find the gap in your own workflow: Scale started from noticing data was the one input you couldn't just buy online.
principles.quote: for two out of these three things, you could just press a button online and get them. And then for the last one, for data, there was no effective way to get data for training these models.

principles.text: Nobody is good at starting a company at first; the whole game is how fast you improve and learn.
principles.quote: for all entrepreneurs, you start out pretty shity at everything. And the whole game is how do you develop yourself to continuously improve to get better and learn quickly?

principles.text: Bet on the steepest, longest-running exponential, even if it starts out boring.
principles.quote: try to identify what is the exponential in the world that has both the steepest curve and will go the longest.

principles.text: Optimize business feedback loops with agent swarms: pick the right metric and eval, then spend far more on tokens.
principles.quote: if you can develop the right agentic loop and you have the right eval of the right metric for the agents to optimize, you can have a swarm of agents accomplish more than like a team of 100 engineers

sources.title: How Scale's Alexandr Wang approached TAM, customer success, and early pricing
sources.originalTitle: SaaStr Podcast #227: Alexandr Wang, Founder & CEO @ Scale On ...
sources.summary: Alexandr Wang explains why Scale prioritized customer success over sales, let early customers shape the roadmap, and delayed pricing optimization. He argues market growth and ability to dominate matter more than TAM, and that startups die from self-inflicted mistakes rather than competition.

principles.text: Market growth rate and your odds of dominating it matter more than the size of the TAM.
principles.quote: It turns out, what matters actually more than that is that we’ve been able to dominate that TAM and because it’s growing really quickly, our company’s growing really quickly along with it.

principles.text: Ignore competitors and row your own race; startups die from self-inflicted errors like bad hires and wrong focus.
principles.quote: most startups don’t die because of competition but they die by suicide. Another way to put it that I think is good is, startups die of indigestion, not starvation.

principles.text: After your first customers, make your next hire customer success, not sales; happy customers become your acquisition channel.
principles.quote: it’s actually way better for your next hire for example, for there to be a customer success hire versus a sales hire because the reality is the sales piece is important but it’s far more important that you just build this culture of your customers loving you.

principles.text: Hire early customer success people from consulting backgrounds, not big-company CS, because startup CS is chaotic.
principles.quote: I think the profiles that actually are quite good are people with consulting backgrounds, in particular

principles.text: Pick your first customers carefully and let them dictate the roadmap, while digging into the pain to find a better solution.
principles.quote: you should really pick your first couple customers very well because no matter what, these first couple customers are going to define your product roadmap for the next while.

principles.text: Early on, don't optimize deal size; get customers who love the product, then raise prices once there's signal.
principles.quote: The only thing you should be focused on early is get customers who absolutely love you and know that they will pay for it but don’t be worried if they don’t pay too much very early on.

sources.title: How Alexandr Wang built Muse Wonder: talent density, internal evals, and betting before proof
sources.originalTitle: Muse Wonder: Zuckerberg and Wang's $100B AI - Cheeky Pint
sources.summary: Wang and Zuckerberg explain how Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped a frontier model with a tiny, talent-dense team and committed huge compute before knowing it would work. Wang argues AI product decisions live in model training, internal evals beat public benchmarks, and simple consumer UX wins.

principles.text: Frontier AI is entrepreneurship on hard mode: you commit big before proof, so Lean Startup iteration doesn't apply.
principles.quote: it’s like entrepreneurship on hard mode. It’s like the opposite of Lean Startup.

principles.text: A small, talent-dense team keeps motivation high; great people self-drive toward shipping and leaving their mark.
principles.quote: everybody had like a lot of motivation to ship and everybody wanted to sort of like leave their mark, so to speak, on the field.

principles.text: In AI-native products, product decisions are specified through model design: training methods, data, and evals.
principles.quote: how do you specify these product decisions? Well, it’s ultimately in model design decisions, which ultimately boil down to training methods or data or evals

principles.text: Don't outsource product thinking to public benchmarks; build your own evals for what users actually need.
principles.quote: you’re kind of outsourcing all of your product thinking to that PhD student who happened to make a viral benchmark.

principles.text: Obsess over many small user-facing capabilities; each adds little but together they make a product feel magical.
principles.quote: maybe each of them matters like 2% to the user, but in aggregate, that’s the obsession that will ultimately result in these models that feel magical.

principles.text: Keep consumer AI simple: don't push confusing model choices onto non-technical users.
principles.quote: how is somebody who’s not carefully reading API design specs supposed to know what they’re supposed to pick? Like, it’s just far too confusing.

sources.title: Alexandr Wang on Meta's personal agents bet, trust as first principle, and building a talent-dense AI lab
sources.originalTitle: Alexandr Wang: Personal agents are AI's next massive leap and opportunity: Meta's Wang - The Economic Times
sources.summary: In this Economic Times interview, Wang explains why Meta sees 2026 as the year of the personal agent and how its three and a half billion daily users give it a distribution edge. He argues trust is the first principle for intimate AI products, and that talent density, compute and no artificial deadlines make the best research environment. He also says AI tools empower small businesses more than they disrupt jobs.

principles.text: Shift from passive, search-style AI to agents that work for you around the clock and act on your goals.
principles.quote: We're moving away from these AI systems that are passive and are sort of more search-based to ones where they're working for you 24/7. They understand your goals. They're able to take actions on your behalf.

principles.text: Distribution at scale is the edge: reach billions of daily users to make personal agents globally ubiquitous.
principles.quote: At Meta, we have three and a half billion people who use our platforms every single day. And we have an opportunity to really make personal agents globally ubiquitous in a way that we think that very few companies have the opportunity to.

principles.text: For intimate AI products, build trust first. It is the long-term North Star and first principle.
principles.quote: your personal agent that is truly personalised to you will be a technology that is more intimate than any technology has ever been historically.

principles.text: New technology creates new formats and products, so agentic commerce is an opportunity for businesses, not a threat.
principles.quote: consumer technology will continue evolving because new technology enables entirely new formats, entirely new technology, entirely new products for our users.

principles.text: Attract top talent with density, compute and scientific rigor, not artificial deadlines or compensation alone.
principles.quote: Smart people want to be surrounded by other very brilliant people who can help push them and they can learn from and create a very special environment that is frankly not possible in other circumstances.

principles.text: Empowering small businesses and creators with AI tools yields opportunity that outstrips disruption.
principles.quote: when we empower more and more small businesses, more creators with AI tools and AI products and AI platforms, the opportunity vastly outstrips any of the disruption.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how Meta Superintelligence Labs went from a personal-superintelligence vision to shipping Muse, a consumer AI agent, in 7 months with under 200 people. He covers launch-blocking evals, single-point-of-view product building, self-interest marketing, meme-driven growth, and running a flat, talent-dense lab.

chunks.heading: Muse origin: from Personal Super Intelligence to a personal agent
chunks.text:
- Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) launched around Mark Zuckerberg's June 2025 memo "Personal Super Intelligence". Alexandr, Nat Friedman and others worked on it with Mark.
- The idea was to build powerful AI that "lifts the human experience broadly".
- Building a frontier model is a long end-to-end process: build the stack, produce datasets, pre-train, then post-train.
- At the start of 2026, Opus 4.5 and OpenClaw brought agents to the foreground. Nat was the first person in MSL to use OpenClaw. Alexandr calls his experience "somewhere between terrifying and euphoric".
- Alexandr then used OpenClaw deeply himself. Nat's psychoanalysis prompt gave him "the equivalent of like 3 years of therapy" in one sitting.
- In February, Alexandr wrote a memo arguing the super agent is "in many ways the final consumer product". Nat wrote memos titled "blames the clause the law" and "trust is a must", which shaped how the products were built.
- The team built a prototype in one to two weeks and demoed it to the board. Many of the final decisions were already in it, including the Jollybot mascot and an early version of the Muse Charm.
- Muse launched 7 months after that February prototype.

chunks.heading: Why Meta should win consumer AI, not coding agents
chunks.text:
- Early 2026 conventional wisdom said coding agents were the only capability that mattered. Anthropic had a clear lead there, and the industry crowded into that use case.
- Alexandr chose not to compete head-on. He saw personal and consumer AI as where Meta is uniquely positioned.
- His argument: AI will take over the things we "have to do" so people can spend time on the things they "want to do". Meta's products (Instagram, WhatsApp, Facebook) are the things people want to do.
- Meta's heritage is connecting people and helping them discover interests. Its distribution is 3.5 billion people using the apps daily.
- He told Mark early on that Meta would be a special company if AGI or ASI arrives. That idea fed into Personal Super Intelligence.

chunks.heading: Taking an agent from magic demo to reliable product
chunks.text:
- OpenClaw produced magic moments but mostly didn't work reliably. Interest "peaked and then disappeared". Alexandr credits Peter Steinberger as a visionary.
- Muse's edge was "grinding out and sanding out all of the details" of the combined model and product experience.
- The team kept a spreadsheet of more than 100 specific behaviors and capabilities the model needed for an ideal personal agent.
  - They built evals for every row and trained the model on each.
  - They held regular reviews of the rows where the model was weakest.
  - Each row had a launch-blocking threshold and a "good" threshold.
- Some checkpoints were green on 80 of the rows and red on 20. That was not good enough. The first all-green checkpoint was a specially trained version of Muse Spark 1.3.
- Beyond the numbers, they judged readiness by feel: the model was clearly better than anything before it.
- He says the product is very sensitive to model quality: how reliably it completes tasks, communicates about them, and checks back when it needs guidance.
- Other agent products lost users at the start of the year because they were unreliable. If people have unreliable experiences, "they think it's trash".
- The team ran many rounds of user testing with new users downloading from scratch, plus continuous A/B tests across model versions.
- Muse is "not a chatbot", so non-developers need careful onboarding to understand it.
- Alexandr says Meta's culture is to optimize once you know what you're measuring. Pre-AI that meant conversion, referral and onboarding flows. With Muse it meant sanding every detail of the model for the product.

chunks.heading: Small team, single point of view
chunks.text:
- Fewer than 200 people worked on the model and product combined over the 7 months. Everyone knew it would be one of Meta's most important products that year.
- Leadership deliberately kept the team small and focused so it would not balloon across the company.
- He calls Muse "a single work of art". It needed one strong point of view and focus.
- His critique of big-organization products, which he says now plague AI labs: they become a "Frankenstein" amalgamation. Each PM jams in their own idea and it blends into a smoothie users can feel.
- Nat Friedman's taste and sensibilities shaped Muse the way Steve Jobs's shaped Apple.
- Alexandr credits Mark with patience, restraint and trust in the process. Meta kept building publicly through months of Wall Street doubt that it could win in AI.
- Stated user numbers: "millions". He retweeted others' graphs implying Muse is the fastest-growing consumer AI app ever, but gave no figure.

chunks.heading: Marketing Muse: memes, self-interest and screenshots
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says Muse needed to "break through" a torrential stream of AI launches. Meta's distribution alone wasn't enough to make people pay attention. He also wanted to "make Meta cool again".
- At launch he mostly retweeted tens of interesting user use cases. Then some quick, low-effort posts did very well. He remembered that "the internet rewards risk" and surprise, and leaned into unhinged memes, including racy ones.
- The Jolly mascot let him put the character into any situation, for example "MFW I go to work on Monday". He says it likely had a real effect on growth, though it wasn't tracked.
- His critique of AI ads (Anthropic's outdoor campaign, OpenAI's two-people-at-a-desk ad): they are about the company. His principle is "why would someone care?" People are self-interested, so lead with what the product does for them. He has millions of use cases to show.
- Modern consumer product marketing is screenshot-driven. The product must "work on the screenshot", whether shared in group chats, word of mouth or online.
  - A friend's screenshots of Muse retrieving an ID left on a Flexjet spread the product on their own.
  - Having the mascot in the screenshot instantly marks it as a Muse screenshot.
- Alexandr says the wow moment should come as early as possible, since an AI agent can do a lot that surprises first-time users.

chunks.heading: Retention: the trust fall
chunks.text:
- Alexandr describes successful use as a "trust fall". Users give the agent a small task, it works, then a bigger one, and then a bigger one.
- Heavy users go as far as voice-note brain dumps that the AI organizes into plans.
- Retention depends on moving users along this ladder and having the agent work every time.
- His own use: he set up many workflows and treats Muse as a "second brain" during meetings.
- His long-term view: a personal agent is a lasting form factor. It helps people accomplish wants and dream bigger, giving "the adulthood they dreamed of in childhood" and an "escalator of agency" rather than agency that gets crushed over a career.
- He also expects AI to take over more scientific discovery and parts of the economy.

chunks.heading: The Meta–Scale AI deal and how Mark operates
chunks.text:
- Alexandr was introduced to Mark by Alex Schultz around 2021 or 2022. It took about a year to schedule the first meeting. Meta was a scale customer, and they spoke roughly every six months.
- Mark called after Llama 4, which Alexandr describes as a disappointment, asking what Meta should do in AI. From first outreach to announcement took about five to six weeks.
- Alexandr first doubted the deal made sense. Meta's iconic acquisitions (Instagram, WhatsApp) were product-logic deals, and Scale was an enterprise and government business. It became clear Mark wanted talent once numbers were discussed.
- The structure: Meta owns 49% of Scale, Scale continues, and Alexandr and a few people join Meta. He called it a win for Scale shareholders, Scale and Meta.
- It took many weeks of "this is insane" and conversations with Scale staff and investors. He had spent 9 years on Scale and thought of it as his life's work.
- What tipped him: the potential at Meta. AI at Meta looked like "damaged goods", which triggered his entrepreneur side. It also let him build from scratch with the right principles and culture.
- On Mark: he asks for advice constantly, which shows humility. He prioritizes ruthlessly and writes long, rigorous WhatsApp replies fast. Alexandr says he deliberates, then goes all in, and has internalized that "failure doesn't matter", only how big you win. He keeps Meta dynamic rather than slow and bureaucratic.

chunks.heading: Running MSL: talent density, flat structure, coach not auror
chunks.text:
- At Scale, Alexandr believed a founder must be able to do every job. That made the company a product of his point of view but also made him the bottleneck. He says first-time founders should take this approach.
- At Meta he can't do every job. He is not a researcher or product designer. Job number one was to hire brilliant people at the top of their field.
- Founding pitch to recruits: build a lab from scratch with a small team and a clear mission (personal super intelligence). Meta's resources meant no bottleneck on compute, infrastructure or distribution.
- He says the large pay packages were underappreciated: OpenAI and Anthropic stock had run up, so comp was "kind of net neutral" for many hires.
- The design principles: a small, very flat, highly technical team with very high talent density, as Elon has shown.
  - The researchers in TBD report directly to him. He has more than 200 direct reports. He calls this "anti-bureaucracy".
  - Technical leads of pods tie-break technical decisions.
  - The group makes many decisions by debate.
  - "They don't need managers, they need a great environment."
- His role is to set the north star and spot talent. He acts like a coach, and describes himself as a steward of the environment.
- Big companies often have exceptional people who aren't empowered to do their best work, so those people leave.
- He distinguishes two kinds of work. Diamond mining has power-law payoffs: try many ideas and nurture the promising ones, as in VC and AI research. Skyscraper building has linear payoffs and is about operational efficiency, like data annotation or Amazon Prime delivery. He says Scale was skyscraper building and MSL is diamond mining.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains why Muse took off: it brought the agent experience engineers had to everyone else, pitched as saving money and time. He stresses polish, hard security work before launch, and that consumer trust will matter more than raw model intelligence.

chunks.heading: Why Muse took off: bringing agent magic to non-coders
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says that for most of the year agents worked for engineers and nobody else noticed. Coders saw how powerful AI had become, while everyone else still used a chatbot that was "a little bit better than Google."
- The industry focused on making models better at coding. He saw a gap: most people don't code and never will, but they still want AI that takes on end-to-end workflows.
- Muse was built to bring that experience to everyone. His reasoning is that developers tolerate "a lot of jank and a lot of stuff breaking," but a mainstream product has to be smooth and just work.
- The team spent a lot of time polishing small details for that reason.
- He accepts the "mobile phone moment for agents" analogy. Much of it is packaging the capability into a form factor that resonates with people.
- Launch result he cites: 5 million downloads in 22 days. He says the team didn't expect such a hit.
- The Muse character in the product is the same as in the very first prototype. The team debated whether it was too playful or not serious enough, then kept it.

chunks.heading: How Alexandr pitches Muse and what people use it for
chunks.text:
- His one-line pitch to someone who knows nothing about it: "Muse can help save you money and save you time." Everyone wants both, and the meaning varies by lifestyle.
- Money examples:
  - Cancelling subscriptions people shouldn't pay for.
  - Cutting expensive cable and insurance bills.
  - Finding unspent gift cards.
- He calls this "Musenhood" (a Muse Robin Hood). Many things, like cancelling subscriptions, are designed to be hard, and Muse lets people get through them easily.
- Time examples:
  - Dealing with the DMV. The team tested Muse against the DMV website because it was "the pinnacle" of frustrating experiences.
  - Health care and medical claims.
  - Running a small business or social media.
- Muse can make phone calls. It opens by identifying itself as the user's assistant and saying the call is being recorded. Users see the transcript.
- Some users ask Muse to "make me $10,000." The team wants Muse to at least build a plan for vague, ambitious tasks, though the user still has to do their part.
- Known weakness: agent memory is "not like that of a human" and is still one of the more unsolved problems.
- Muse is meant to be a separate entity from the user. That is why it's a cute character: it's socially weird to think you're texting a friend and get their Muse. The team wants to keep making that distinction clearer.

chunks.heading: Vision and business model
chunks.text:
- Long-term vision: Muse as a "general manager" that helps you accomplish what you want out of life, from big goals (start a company, cure a disease) to small ones (eat healthier, spend more time with family). The goal is to reach all 8 billion people.
- Many people lose their big dreams because of the barriers and burdens in the way. He wants AI to help people keep dreaming bigger. Small wants get fulfilled, then people dream a little bigger.
- He says "personal super intelligence" helps with what each individual wants most, which matters more to them than abstract goals like curing cancer.
- Current monetization: Muse is free, with subscription tiers.
- He prefers models aligned with the user. Example: taking a small fee on transactions where Muse saves or makes the user money.
- He says they aren't spending much time on ads now. He doesn't think ad models must consume users' time. His example is Google, where he wants to "get in and get out" and Google doesn't try to stop him.
- If Muse really helps people accomplish their goals, he expects there will be many sustainable ways to make money.

chunks.heading: Privacy and security architecture
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says privacy and security were going to be among the most important factors for consumer adoption. The team delayed the Muse launch "for many months" to get safety and security right.
- Muse Secure VM:
  - A sandboxed virtual machine, like a mini computer that is Muse's "home."
  - User information is stored there and nowhere else.
- Sentinel agent:
  - A separate agent that watches the main agent whenever it wants to send information outside the VM (filling out a website, sending a message, making a call).
  - He compares it to a traffic cop. It blocks things like credit card or social security numbers from leaving.
- Human-in-the-loop checks: Muse asks the user before contacting or sending information to a new website. Some users find this annoying. He accepts that so people know exactly what Muse interacts with.
- Confidential VM (coming soon):
  - Even more encrypted and private.
  - Designed by Moxie Marlinspike, who built WhatsApp encryption.
  - Goal: the same guarantees as WhatsApp, so Meta couldn't hand over data even if a government asked.
  - It was not in the launch because of technical challenges and trade-offs. It may be slower.
- Launch logic: ship a great experience on the Secure VM first, then add Confidential.

chunks.heading: Alignment, discretion, and trust as the product edge
chunks.text:
- Users shouldn't have to list everything an agent must not do (don't bribe or blackmail a doctor, don't email 100 times). Internally the team calls this "discretion and alignment."
- Alexandr's approach to alignment:
  - Vet the data and techniques at every stage of training.
  - Measure alignment by running models through thousands of scenarios.
  - Red team: ask smart people to "do your worst" to get the agent to misbehave, over many rounds before deploying any model.
  - Take user reports of crazy behavior very seriously and investigate them after launch.
- The problem gets harder as models get smarter. He compares it to kids who learn new ways to cheat on tests, so you have to be more explicit about what to watch for.
- He thinks it's one of the most open scientific questions in AI and that nobody knows the solution. He names three ideas:
  - Scalable oversight: use other AIs to watch smarter AIs. The Sentinel is a version of this.
  - Use recursive self-improvement for alignment: point AI research agents at making AI more aligned, measured with agreed red-teaming setups.
  - Go back to basics: find algorithms that are inherently safer and more generalizable.
- His strategy bet: have one agent serving the user and a separate agent whose goal is to make sure nothing bad happens. He likens it to human society's accountability systems, with a microcosm for every user's Muse.
- He agrees that at some point trust matters more than capability for consumers: "if I think about who are my best friends... I trust them." He says the best models for billions of consumers will prioritize trust over raw intelligence.
- His biggest fear is deploying agents worldwide that misbehave without anyone noticing. He cites the OpenAI/Hugging Face agent incident as a sign that pushing capability alone has real risk.

chunks.heading: Industry coordination, regulation, and China
chunks.text:
- Alexandr declines to say exactly how AI should be regulated. He says he has enough humility and sees his role as facilitating dialogue, not pushing his own opinion.
- Why leaders' words and actions seem to diverge:
  - AI moves faster than government and the public can react. A year ago most people coded by hand; now they mostly talk to agents.
  - Distrust among leaders: each says "I'm responsible, those guys aren't," so no one can slow down.
- He calls for something like diplomacy: get leaders who don't trust each other to agree on a common foundation, then set up a process to re-evaluate together as models get more powerful.
- He says personal animosities among leaders shape how they develop the technology, which he finds insane. He wants people to "put our differences aside."
- Current state: no private room of talks that he knows of. The White House-facilitated accord is a real step. It has these parts:
  - Each company sets out internal controls and principles.
  - Verification by internal teams, external auditors and board-level committees.
  - He values it mainly for transparency. The industry has "a lot of trust building to do."
- China: he has changed his view. He once worried more about China, but now thinks it has shared interests such as stability, not losing control of the technology and avoiding catastrophic risk. He believes international cooperation is possible.
- He argues that having everyone experience agents firsthand gives the public perspective on both the risk and the benefit. He also says builders shouldn't talk down to people about AI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang and Mark Zuckerberg describe how Meta rebooted its AI effort into a small, elite lab and shipped the Muse agent and the Muse Wonder model. Wang covers making huge compute bets with no feedback loop, treating the model as the product, why internal evals beat public benchmarks, and why leaders must stay technical.

chunks.heading: Meta's AI bet: build the frontier lab first, pay for it later
chunks.text:
Alexandr describes Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) as "entrepreneurship on hard mode" and "the opposite of lean startup."

- Frontier model decisions have to be made years before any proof point exists. Planning for Muse Wonder started around August of the prior year, and the data centers date back to 2023-2024 plans.
- In his words, you can't "see if you get something working and then double down." If you wait for proof, you are "radically behind."
- By late the prior year, the exec team was deciding whether to spend roughly $100-200 billion on compute before seeing the models. The CFO told them that if the model didn't work, "it's going to be very very bad in financial terms."
- Alexandr argues the ante to start a frontier lab is now extremely high.
- The cost figures he cites:
  - Operating a 1 gigawatt cluster for a year is on the order of $15 billion.
  - Building that capex up front is roughly $50-60 billion.
  - Research costs roughly as much again, because every change is tested on the ladder of smaller runs.
  - Serving the model costs more on top.
  - A frontier model costs "tens of billions of dollars" in total.
