- Meta's clusters are Prometheus in Ohio (scaling past 1 GW) and Hyperion in Louisiana (scaling to 5 GW).
- The risk is bounded. If AI works, other buyers want the compute. For the bet to fail, "AI overall has to fail."
- A launch that needs a few iterations to find product-market fit is "not the end of the world." Muse was a home run at launch, and Alexandr says they could have grown it faster had growth tooling been ready.

chunks.heading: Talent density and a flat, technical org
chunks.text:
Alexandr's first advice to Zuckerberg was that you don't need many people; you need each person to be as good as possible.

- **Team size:** The research team is under 200 people, closer to 100 plus infra staff. Each stage of training has tens of people, not hundreds.
- **Compute per researcher:** He bets on key people and gives them a lot of compute each. Meta is "not peanut buttering across a lot of competing efforts."
- **Reboot:** MSL was framed as starting again from scratch, which made recruiting more compelling. It still pulled in good people from the Llama and FAIR efforts.
- **Flat structure:** Leads have very many direct reports (a joke about "almost 200"). The point is the absence of non-technical managers.
- **Staying technical:** Researchers who move into management lose technical depth faster than they realize. People should use agents and write code.
- **No deadlines:** Meta told the lab there were no deadlines. Alexandr says this worked because a dense group of high achievers is self-motivated to ship.
- **Pessimism check:** He calls the team "insecure overachievers." He records their pessimistic forecasts, then shows them the results three months later.
- **Ownership:** He prefers people who push for what they believe in and argue over things to people "blindly executing." He says "people need to feel ownership."
- **Leader profile:** He wants leaders who are clear thinkers and can update dynamically like an entrepreneur, not experts in the latest technique.
- **A telling moment:** In an early meeting, a lead said consumers didn't need a reasoning model. That convinced him leadership had to be much more "AI-pilled."

chunks.heading: Training a frontier model: pre-train, RL, and why quality beats quantity
chunks.text:
Alexandr gives a high-level recipe.

- **Pre-training:**
  - Public internet, books, and as much data as possible, across modalities (images, audio, video).
  - Domain data (finance, legal, health) goes in early rather than only via RL.
  - It is the highest-stakes stage, with few samples to learn from.
- **Ladder approach:** Train models around four or five times bigger at each step. Muse Spark came from the December pre-train. Muse Wonder is a significantly bigger class. Internal code names were Avocado and Watermelon.
- **Post-training:** Supervised fine-tuning initializes behaviors, which may only fire about 10% of the time. RL then raises how often they appear.
- **Scale everything:** His broad statement is "scale everything." You can scale one dimension, but you get much better results scaling many together.
- **Point releases:** Muse Spark 1 to 1.3 used the same pre-train with more RL, and felt "night and day" different.
- **RL data:** "Less is more." Environments must be curated carefully, because RL magnifies whatever behavior is needed to succeed, including misaligned behavior.
- **Alignment:** He defines it as instruction and values alignment with the person served. Users want reliability and no "moralizing lecture." Truly catastrophic requests should be declined gracefully.
- **Expected speedup:** He expects the time between successive model classes to compress.

chunks.heading: Evals, "big model smell," and building for a specific user
chunks.text:
Alexandr argues public benchmarks are a starting point, not a destination.

- Benchmarks saturate quickly. Early on, external ones confirm you're on track. Each release shifts more weight to internal evals.
- Outsourcing evaluation to public benchmarks means "outsourcing all of your product thinking" to whichever PhD student made a viral benchmark. Much of the team's effort goes into crafting evals.
- Internal evals come from a detailed spreadsheet of small product capabilities. Each might matter about 2% to the user, but together they are "the obsession that will ultimately result in these models that feel magical."
- **Big model smell:** He quantifies it as the gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance (tasks like the RL training versus unlike it). Wonder shows a large improvement over Spark on this measure.
- **Differentiated targets:** Meta targets personal and professional agents. That makes some things matter more:
  - Personality.
  - Discretion: sharing as little personal information as needed while getting a task done.
  - Multimodal perception.
  - Memory.
  - Coding where users may never see the code.
- Memory is built into the model ("active memory"), including how it compacts, not just a harness. Persistence over long tasks is a second focus.
- **Muse Wonder:** He claims it is state of the art on personal and professional agent evals, plus legal and finance evals, and on coding benchmarks. These are his claims, based on Meta's own measurements.

chunks.heading: The model is the product: product principles for AI agents
chunks.text:
Alexandr disagrees that AI product space collapses to a few obvious shapes.

- "The model is the product." Products are getting thinner, and personality, capabilities and behavior are trained into the model. Post-training choices often matter more than UI.
- Traditional product specs aren't the right axes for AI-native products. Dimensions that matter:
  - How proactive the agent is.
  - When it is proactive.
  - How it talks to you.
  - Reliability on tasks.
- The spec of intended behavior in all situations would be an extremely long document. Calling it "just an agent" hides real differences, as "just an app" did in early mobile.
- Meta's agent runs on a dedicated VM. Alexandr says this matters for feeling confident about security and privacy. Much of the conventional product work is privacy and security for connected data.
- Muse has no model selector or effort selector. He criticizes the industry for confusing naming, such as numbers going backwards, and says an average person can't be expected to pick.
- **Embodiment:** Muse feels like a little guy working on your behalf because persistent memory, action-taking and personality come together.
- **Voice:** Voice input is high bandwidth, but consuming information by voice is inefficient. The ideal interface is multimodal.
- **Pricing approach:** Free for everyone on Muse Spark, with a large amount of free tokens. The bigger Wonder model starts on paid subscriptions only. He hopes to later get Wonder-level quality in the cheaper form factor.
- **Distribution:** Wonder is also offered through the Meta model API, OpenRouter, and to Muse Code users. Wonder Full goes to Muse Code subscribers.

chunks.heading: Agentic commerce and how Meta plans to make money
chunks.text:
Alexandr sees agents as a discontinuous change in how commerce works.

- **Browser use:** Meta trained strong browser use into the model so no business has to integrate with Muse. The long-term aim is direct API access with top partners, which is faster and cheaper for both sides.
- **Business agents:** Every business will eventually have agents, like websites and email today, and Muse agents will work especially well with Meta's.
- **Demand shift:** Agentic demand will grow as a share of the pie while other channels persist. He thinks businesses that block agents will probably find that the wrong strategy.
- **Delegated purchasing:** Muse is one of the first products where people fully delegate purchases. Value for the user:
  - Less friction.
  - Criteria applied automatically (for example, "need it by Wednesday").
  - Personalization from a holistic view of your life, not siloed recommendations.
- **Market expansion:** He argues the total addressable market of commerce grows because agents effectively get accounts. His example is creating an Instacart account for Muse, and now using it once or twice a week when previously it was about twice a year.
- **Revenue streams he lists:**
  - Subscriptions, which he expects to be a big business.
  - A small cut of what Muse saves or makes people in commerce.
  - A "business in a box" for small businesses.
  - A model API and a new Meta enterprise platform.
- **Funding:** Meta's core business is "hundreds of billions of dollars" and still growing fast, so it underwrites the buildout. He also notes Meta owns its data centers, so costs are capitalized and depreciated, and older GPUs stay valuable while compute is constrained.
- **Playbook:** Build something, get it to a billion people, then scale revenue while the existing business keeps growing.

chunks.heading: Why no single winner, and why Meta builds the stack
chunks.text:
Alexandr expects multiple frontier labs rather than one winner.

- **Execution evens out:** Every lab has strong and weak periods.
- **Distillation:** It is an "anti-hegemonic force." It packs strong capability into small, cheap models, and today's small models beat the biggest models of a year or two ago.
- **Mission:** Many people and companies want a future where technology reaches billions, which pulls toward a more equal outcome.
- **Differentiation:** He welcomes labs focusing on different things, "the point of capitalism to some extent." He sees value in routers like OpenRouter that help developers understand the subtle differences between models.
- **Safety through diversity:** He thinks a few models in a few hands is the riskier configuration.
- **Why own the stack:** In each technology era, the companies with core technology serve people best. He expects a small handful of companies to build frontier superintelligence and drive the agenda for consumer, enterprise and hardware experiences. Wanting to invent new things that matter means owning the stack end to end.
- **Open lane:** He sees personal and consumer agents as underserved because others focus on automating knowledge work. He believes "the highest use of super intelligence is invention and creation, not automation."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how Meta Superintelligence Labs was structured after Llama 4 fell behind: small, talent-dense teams, high compute per researcher, and a clean rebuilt stack designed for predictable scaling. He also covers recruiting, why compute splits tech companies into two classes, and why AI sentiment stays low until it empowers ordinary people.

chunks.heading: Mission and how MSL is organized
chunks.text:
- Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) is the umbrella unit Alexandr oversees. He has a hands-on role in TBD Lab, and the rest report up into the structure.
- TBD is the large-model research lab where the leading researchers and infrastructure engineers sit. They report to him.
- PAR (Product and Applied Research), led by Nat Friedman, builds products and deploys models to the world.
- FAIR does exploratory research. Alexandr names brain modeling and a universal model for atoms ("UMA") as examples.
- Daniel Gross leads Meta Compute, which plans the long-term GPU and data center infrastructure.
- He frames the goal as "personal superintelligence": the technology should empower people, be as democratized as possible, and reach billions of users and hundreds of millions of small businesses on Meta's platforms.

chunks.heading: Why he joined Meta: model builders and compute
chunks.text:
- He had known Mark Zuckerberg for years and took advice from him while running Scale. Talks about working more closely began about a year before this interview.
- His reasoning: those who build the frontier models earn "greater and greater rights," both economic and product, to build around them. Research pace is fast enough that model-building labs are the most exciting place in the ecosystem.
- He argues the next phase of tech boils down to compute. Companies with lots of compute can make big bets and ship products that companies without it cannot, so he says to think about the two groups very differently.
- Meta had the compute and a founder fully committed to AI, which made it the right place to build at scale.

chunks.heading: The three levers for catching up to the frontier
chunks.text:
When he arrived, Llama 4 was off the needed trajectory. He designed TBD around three ways to get very fast velocity:
- **Higher compute per researcher.** Big labs have lots of compute but spread it across many efforts, which slows any one researcher. A smaller team with more compute each moves faster.
- **Talent density.** "The very small team where everyone is cracked is always going to move faster than the very large organization where responsibility is more distributed."
- **Very ambitious research bets.** Beyond building competitive frontier models, he allocates a large share of compute to big, risky bets that could shift paradigms if they work.

His stated principles for the effort: take superintelligence seriously, technical voices are loudest, scientific rigor, focus on basics, make big bets.

chunks.heading: Organizing a lab around a belief, and the culture he's building
chunks.text:
- A main problem he found: leading labs build the whole organization around the premise that superintelligence is close, then rebuild every other assumption around it. Many people at large companies don't hold that conviction.
- On recruiting, he says the team had to be hired "yesterday," so the blitz was fast and individualized. People needed to see Meta was serious, so it took direct conversations explaining what they were building and why.
- He pushes back on the "mercenary" narrative. He says researchers joined for compute, talent density and freedom to make bold bets, and that most had very strong financial prospects where they were.
- Visitors from other labs say the vibe reminds them of early OpenAI or early Anthropic.
- His management philosophy, citing Steve Jobs: "most companies hire people and tell them what to do, but we hire people for them to tell us what to do." He says he is not trying to boss anyone around, but to create the best environment for researchers.

chunks.heading: What Muse Spark is and the "clean stack" thesis
chunks.text:
- Over roughly 9 months the team rebuilt the pre-training stack, the RL stack, much of the science, and the data work. He calls Muse Spark "the appetizer," an early data point on a scaling ladder.
- The program is built around predictable scaling: pre-training, RL, test-time, and multi-agent scaling. He says larger models are coming in "coming months."
- He says Muse Spark is a very good consumer model but not yet competitive on agentic coding, which the next models target.
- He credits strong results to a very clean stack built from scratch "the right way" by experts, and says it landed better than the team expected.
- On token efficiency (he cites Artificial Analysis), Muse Spark reached similar results with many fewer tokens. His speculation: other models may need more tokens because of inefficiencies elsewhere in the stack that get patched by longer thinking.
- Capabilities like visual coding (websites, games) emerged from combining strong agentic and multimodal ability.

chunks.heading: Product strategy: agents for consumers and businesses
chunks.text:
- Sequence: build great models and products first, then tightly integrate AI across the family of apps and business products. He says that integration push is starting now.
- He says AI sentiment is low because AI hasn't yet given ordinary people what Claude Code gave developers: a tool that visibly increases personal agency. Meta wants to build that for consumers and small businesses.
- His bigger idea: agents for both consumers and small businesses, with a mechanism for them to work together. "Dario always talks about a country of geniuses in a data center. I think we're excited about building an economy of agents in a data center," changing how supply and demand are mediated.
- He sees the market as very early and dynamic. In one year the perceived consumer winner shifted, and he expects each new capability level to unlock new product form factors, each potentially bigger than the last.
- Glasses (Ray-Ban Meta) and other devices are meant to see what you see and hear what you hear, supplying context for proactive agent help.
- He pairs this with the need for social permission: Meta must show it cares about how products are deployed.

chunks.heading: Safety, open source, and where he places Meta
chunks.text:
- Muse Spark triggered some safety checks (bio, chem, cyber, loss of control) in testing under Meta's advanced AI scaling framework, so it is not suitable for open sourcing in its current form. A fuller preparedness report was published.
- He says Meta will keep open sourcing models and is working on open-sourceable versions, but the most powerful models must be judged for safety first.
- Robotics: if you take superintelligence seriously, physical intelligence follows digital intelligence on the roadmap. Meta acquired a robotics AI startup (Assured Robot Intelligence) that builds AI, not hardware.
- He says superintelligence research is "fundamentally a research activity," like experiments in a fog of war, which is why he stresses sequencing and research over rushing straight to downstream bets.
- He names critical-path technologies as superintelligence, robotics and brain-computer interfaces, and, scaling to infinity, energy, compute and robots.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang recounts how Scale AI started after a failed medical-agent idea, and why early conviction in unpopular beliefs matters. He argues AI makes startups "Goliath vs Goliath," that vision and ambition become the scarce resources, and that agentic feedback loops with the right metric are the biggest near-term opportunity.

chunks.heading: Why Alexandr started Scale from a first-principles gap, not a hot market
chunks.text:
- At MIT, Alexandr noticed that training a model needed three things: a cloud compute account, training code, and data. Two of the three could be had by "pressing a button" online. Data could not.
- From that he concluded there would be a way to press a button and get data. That became Scale, which he started at 19 after one year at MIT, via YC.
- Scale's first market was self-driving cars and computer vision. This was before large language models had arrived.
- His first idea at YC was an AI agent to help people get medical care. Jared Friedman pulled the team aside after a month or two and said it probably would not go anywhere. Alexandr says the idea was right but the timing was wrong, and that "that's exactly what we need to hear."
- Alexandr says you cannot start a company by reading the Wall Street Journal for what is hot. You start from simple statements about the world that you know to be true.
- For years, data was "very unsexy." Investors kept asking whether it was durable, even with strong revenue, because none of them had trained a model. The same investors now write think pieces calling data one of the biggest opportunities in AI.

chunks.heading: Build conviction in beliefs nobody else shares
chunks.text:
- Alexandr argues the most successful companies started long before their core idea became popular. They "toil in obscurity for years" before it turns consensus.
- Success depends on identifying truths about the world early, before everyone else.
- Scale worked on AI for a decade. He says you can't base business decisions on what the people around you are saying: "If you go too much with the herd, you will get immensely confused and you will end up nowhere."
- You have to develop your own compass for what the future looks like, because everyone else will confuse you.
- His advice to his 18-year-old self: develop your own internal compass and hold strong conviction in it. Noise is heavy, especially when you're young and have little experience. Scale needed deep conviction to weather years of chaos in the market, the industry and the people around them.

chunks.heading: Nobody starts out good at being a founder
chunks.text:
- Early investors told him he "grew so quickly and changed so quickly" that they did not see it at the time. He thinks that is true of every founder.
- His view: "nobody is good at something they've never done before." Founders start out pretty bad at everything.
- The whole game is how fast you develop yourself, continuously improve and learn.
- His own path: a gap-year job at Quora at 19, then MIT at 18 (as stated in the talk), where he trained his first models and played with TensorFlow, which had just come out.
- He rates working at a real company as highly valuable. From outside, you have no idea how companies are built, how things get iterated on, or how groups make decisions.
- He values YC for being supportive but also honest. It "tells you when you're being a dumbass."

chunks.heading: Pick the steepest, longest exponential
chunks.text:
- Alexandr's advice: find the exponential in the world that has both the steepest curve and will run the longest.
- Decades ago that was Moore's law. Right now he says it is AI progress, but more steep curves will come.
- The starting point can look boring. When he started Scale, the state of the art was "cat detectors in YouTube videos," which was hard to pitch as the most important technology of the era.
- His observation on waves: each wave of AI has been about 10x bigger than the last. Self-driving was the first wave, chatbots were roughly 10x larger, and coding agents roughly 10x larger again. He expects new modalities and form factors that each dwarf the previous one.
- He says the best AI products have not been built yet.

chunks.heading: Startups can now compete Goliath versus Goliath
chunks.text:
- Ten years ago, starting a company meant David versus Goliath. You needed a clever angle and had to compete with far fewer resources.
- He now thinks that with agents, it is closer to Goliath versus Goliath. A startup can be a "mecha Goliath" vastly enhanced by agents and AI.
- If you embrace agents and use their strengths in ambitious ways, you can "easily outcompete incumbents."
- The bottleneck is no longer model progress but diffusing the technology through the world. Even if models stopped improving, he expects decades of upheaval in the economy.
- He calls it a "once in a civilization opportunity" for dreamers with vision and ambition.
- On the future of scarcity: intelligence and agency will become abundant. The scarce resources will be vision and ambition, meaning a clear view of how the world should look in 5 to 10 years and the drive to push through the hard parts to get there.
- Because agents make execution maybe 10x to 100x easier, he says you can now dream bigger.

chunks.heading: Agentic loops are the biggest near-term opportunity
chunks.text:
- Alexandr describes companies as large feedback loops where humans operate each edge: get customers, make them happier, they spend more, you hire more people, get more customers.
- Inside that are micro feedback loops. He sees huge alpha in building agentic systems that operate and optimize them.
- The goal is to spend 1,000x to 1,000,000x more on tokens to drive an outcome in a continuous feedback loop.
- At Meta, with the right agentic loop and the right eval or metric for the agents to optimize, a swarm of agents can accomplish more than a team of 100 engineers "very easily."
- The mechanics, in his words, are mundane: figure out the metric, then skills, markdown files, cron jobs and a goal.
- He thinks agentic coordination problems are among the most interesting problems today, and that real innovation will happen above the harness, in orchestrating loops and ecosystems of agents.

chunks.heading: Running a frontier lab: talent density and an operating model for exponentials
chunks.text:
- About a year into Meta, he says the company did a zero-based build of a frontier lab rather than patching what existed.
- Timeline he cites: Muse Spark 1 launched within nine months, then Muse Image and Muse Spark 1.1 two months later.
- Talent density was the core bet. It compounds, because the more talented people you have, the more of the most talented people want to join.
- Frontier AI work is research and science, which needs a different mindset and operating model than internet products: more experimentation and scaling.
- He frames the lab as an organism that must grow with simultaneous exponentials in capability, compute, and adoption and usage.
- Product direction: keep models cheap so they are not rationed to the wealthiest developers. He says Spark is about 8x cheaper than Opus. Open-source models and a Meta-built agent harness (focused on speed, reliability and extensibility) are on the way.
- Strategy: a decentralized AI ecosystem, with personal superintelligence for billions of people and an explosion of entrepreneurship. He cites 200 million businesses on Meta platforms today and says that number should grow to billions.

chunks.heading: Skills to build as the abstraction layer keeps rising
chunks.text:
- Abstraction has moved from writing code to orchestrating agents, and next to orchestrating armies of them (a million, then a trillion).
- He argues systems thinking never goes out of style, and that going all-in on "wordcell" is a mistake. You still need to be a "shape rotator."
- The scarce skill beyond that is a deeper compass and philosophical view of how the world should develop. He expects humanity to change more in the next decade than in the last 100 years.
- He says builders have a responsibility to help prepare the world, including enterprises, governments, biosecurity and cybersecurity.
- On the AI debate: arguing over exactly when superintelligence arrives is "a bit of a waste of time." In hindsight, he expects it to be obvious that intelligence and agency became abundant.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang recounts how Scale started at YC as an API for human labor, won by focusing on self-driving data, then repeatedly built ahead of AI waves (OpenAI, defense, enterprise agents). He explains when to move from narrow markets to infinite ones, why specialized data and models will be a company's IP, and why caring deeply is the trait he hires for.

chunks.heading: Starting Scale: from chatbots for doctors to an API for human labor
chunks.text:
- Alexandr worked at Quora as a software engineer in 2014-2015, then went to MIT at 18. He applied to YC when he got "antsy".
- The first idea was chatbots for doctors, during the 2016 chatbot boom. He admits they knew nothing about doctors. His read on young founders: first ideas are memetic (dating apps, social apps), and young people have a poor sense of their own "alpha", meaning what they are uniquely positioned to do.
- Mid-batch, while roommates with another YC company, they noticed chatbots needed lots of language data and human "elbow grease". The pivot: do the human data for the chatbot companies. The framing became an "API for human tasks" / API for human labor.
- He found scaleapi.com available one night, bought it, and launched on Product Hunt about a week later. The landing page took about 3 days to build.
- Launch brought inbound from engineers with varied use cases, which was enough to raise money and get going.
- Mechanical Turk was the incumbent. His rule: when people mention a thing in your space but it "sucks", that is a good sign.

chunks.heading: Narrowing to self-driving cars, and why it was right and wrong
chunks.text:
- About 6 months after YC, another YC company, Cruise, reached out via the website and quickly became the largest customer. The contact was an ex-YC founder working there.
- Alexandr decided to focus entirely on self-driving data. His lead investor objected that it was "obviously way too small a market".
- His counter: self-driving companies were getting huge funding and automakers had big programs, so focusing would let them build the business faster.
- Looking back, he says both are true: the focus got Scale to scale quickly, and it was not a big enough market to sustain a gigantic business.
- The company was fully focused on self-driving for about the first 3 years.
- His startup market rule: early on, go for the narrowest markets you can and build momentum. If you want a $100B+ company, you must later switch gears and find "infinite markets".

chunks.heading: Building ahead of each AI wave
chunks.text:
- Scaling laws were not a thing in self-driving, because algorithms must run on the car's limited compute. Scale started working with OpenAI in 2019 (GPT-2 era).
- GPT-3 (2020) made scaling laws feel real to him. Instruct GPT work with OpenAI in 2022 was the "aha" moment for the company. GPT-4 made it clear that the need for data would "grow to consume all available information and knowledge that humans have".
- Because AI needs data to work in any vertical, demand for Scale's data precedes AI's arrival in each industry. Examples:
  - OpenAI on language models: 2019.
  - DoD on defense AI: 2020, long before the drone-fueled AI craze.
  - Enterprises: long before the recent enterprise AI wave.
- He compares this to Nvidia, where Jensen is always ahead of the trends because the company has to get there before the trend can happen.
- Late 2021 / early 2022, Scale began building AI applications, now increasingly agentic workflows, for enterprises and governments.

chunks.heading: Adding a second business: the AWS lesson and the applications push
chunks.text:
- The core data business is highly operational: a "data foundry" with many humans and experts plus quality control systems. That success created momentum to build an applications business.
- Before starting, he studied companies that successfully added very different businesses. The standout is Amazon building AWS. Analysts hated it when it launched in 2006 and Amazon stock fell.
- Two lessons he took from AWS:
  - Conviction that the underlying market is effectively infinite and growing exponentially (compute demand).
  - Sufficient cost advantages from economies of scale.
- His reasoning for Scale: every business and organization must reformat itself around AI, and now agent-driven technology, and that will "swallow the entire economy".
- Strategy: focus on a small number of customers and be selective. Scale works with the number one pharma company, telco, bank and healthcare provider in the world, plus the US government (DoD and other agencies).
- He says the applications business is multi-hundred-million in size, and that investors tell him it is one of the largest AI application businesses. It is growing much faster than the data business.
- Differentiation comes from the data business: help each enterprise generate or harness its most strategic data to build specialized AI.
- Versus Palantir: Palantir focuses on data ontologies and solving the messy data integration problem. Scale focuses on which strategic data enables AI differentiation. In practice Scale is more partnered with Palantir than competitive. He sees the market as too big to be winner-takes-all, like cloud.

chunks.heading: Specialized models as company IP, and the future of work
chunks.text:
- His blueprint: one version of the future is that every firm's core IP is its specialized, fine-tuned model, the way a codebase is IP today.
- Companies add data and environments specific to their day-to-day business problems, which nobody else has. Model providers' base models, plus your data and environments, give a fine-tuned model ("Lego blocks"). Evals matter in this stack.
- He believes the economy stays specialized rather than becoming one "Borg". Alpha will go to those who can encapsulate their business problems into datasets and environments.
- On a model lab asking YC companies for their evals: companies should not hand them over. His view is that the industry will learn the "bright lines", like not giving away your codebase or database. In an AI economy those lines will include evals, data and environments.
- Coding is the case study for work. It moved from assistant, to synchronous agent mode (Cursor-style), to a swarm of agents (Codex-style) that you manage.
- His belief: humans manage agents is the terminal state, since the economy is driven by human demand and vision.
- Management is mostly putting out fires. Coordinating agents and debugging them will be hard. Self-driving showed that getting to 90% is easy and 99% is very hard, and he expects the last 10% of agent accuracy to take a lot of work.
- Self-driving still needs human teleoperators, at roughly 3 to 5 cars per operator by his estimate (companies do not publish the ratio).
- On jobs: people have insatiable demand, so as the economy gets more efficient humans will want more. He frames agents as giving every trade the leverage programmers have had ("the closest thing to alchemy").

chunks.heading: Running Scale on agents internally
chunks.text:
- Because Scale produced the datasets that trained agents with reinforcement learning, it saw how effective RL is for agent deployment.
- Core method: turn existing human workflows into environments and data for RL, where some fault tolerance is acceptable, and convert them into agentic workflows.
- Agents are used in hiring, quality control, data analyses and sales reporting, "embedded at every major org of the company".
- Mindset: identify very repetitive human workflows, then turn them into datasets that let you build automation.
- Concrete example: distilling a candidate's full packet into a brief for a broader committee. He says deep-research-style tasks, which involve clicking around, pulling information, blending it and producing analysis, are the lowest-hanging fruit.
- The data needed is the task, the full dataset needed to do it, and a rubric for doing it well.
- Prompting vs RL: prompting works well most of the time and gets better as models improve. RL goes beyond what prompting reaches.
- Startup advice: have a strategy to "walk up the complexity curve", so the product benefits from rising model capability.

chunks.heading: Hard evals as a lever on the AI industry
chunks.text:
- Scale built Humanity's Last Exam with the Center for AI Safety. Professors and researchers each wrote new problems from their recent research. The problems appear in no textbook and cannot be searched.
- At launch (earlier in 2025) the best models scored about 7-8%. Now the best score is north of 20%. A lab asked to raise the thinking-time limit from 15 or 30 minutes to a day.
- His point: the industry lacks very hard evals. An eval that becomes popular becomes the northstar researchers optimize for, and model providers report on it.
- He expects it to saturate eventually. The next evals will be fuzzier real-world tasks.
- He thinks genuine scientific breakthroughs from reasoning models are plausible, biology most clearly.

chunks.heading: Defense, China, and competing on data
chunks.text:
- Thunder Forge: built with Indo-Pacific Command, the flagship DoD program for AI in military planning and operations. It takes the doctrinal human planning workflow and converts it into a series of cooperating agents. He says it turns decision cycles from 72 hours to 10 minutes.
- He expects warfare to shift toward small, nimble, attritable assets (drones, embodied robots, cyber) and toward agentic decision-making.
- On China: the best open-source models now come from China. His simplest explanation is espionage of training secrets (hyperparameters, tricks, intuitions) leaving US labs. He says Chinese models are about a half step behind.
- US energy grid production looks flat, while China's has roughly doubled over a decade, mostly coal. He expects the US to come out ahead on compute because of chips.
- China's data advantages, per Alexandr:
  - Ignoring copyright and privacy rules.
  - Government data labeling programs, including 7 data labeling centers, subsidies and vouchers for AI companies, and college programs, since employment is a national priority.
  - Factories full of robots collecting data. He says even some US companies rely on Chinese data for robotics foundation models.
- His rough odds: 60/40 or 70/30 that the US keeps an advantage. Manufacturing cost is a big problem for robotics hardware.

chunks.heading: Hiring people who care, and "quality is fractal"
chunks.text:
- His main advice: "you just have to really really really care." He wrote a post years ago called "hire people who give a [damn]".
- In interviews he looks for people who hang on to their work versus people who phone it in. For him the biggest predictor of enjoying working with someone, and of their success at Scale, was how much of their soul is invested in the work.
- He approves or rejects every single hire at Scale.
- Caring means feeling the business more deeply, which lets the company change course, learn and adapt faster.
- He personally hand-reviewed the data sent to partner companies as final quality control, even when Scale was large, because unhappy customers are personally painful.
- Scale value: "quality is fractal". High standards trickle down; standards rarely increase as you go lower in an org, and if a manager does not care, their reports stop caring.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how Meta Superintelligence Labs spent a year rebuilding its model stack around "predictable scaling" after Llama 4 fell short, shipping Muse Spark as an early data point. He covers why risk testing pushed Meta away from open-sourcing it, his view of agents as deeply personal tools, and why AI is also creating more small businesses.

chunks.heading: Meta's AI position a year after Alexandr joined
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says Meta released Llama 4 a little more than a year before this talk. He calls it exciting but "not quite on the trajectory that Meta needed" to keep building its products and experiences.
- Since he joined and started Meta Superintelligence Labs, the team has been building a new scaling ladder for its models, new infrastructure and new research to power a new family of models.
- In April, Meta released the first results of that work: the Muse Spark models and an update to Meta AI.
  - The reception was "even better than frankly we'd expected internally".
  - Meta AI usage rose sharply and the app reached the top of many app stores.
- He is candid that Muse Spark "is not at the tier of the leading frontier models". He calls it "a very exciting data point on the trajectory" and expects the upcoming models to be "quite competitive with the leading models in the world".
- Larger models are in training. He says the early results are "very exciting and promising", and that the next releases will sit higher on the same scaling curves.

chunks.heading: Predictable scaling as the research strategy
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says Meta built its whole research effort around predictable scaling. The central belief behind the modern AI boom is that scaling models gives "predictable levels of increased capability".
- Muse Spark was an early point on Meta's scaling ladder. Later models are meant to be greater points on the same curve.
- What it takes to reach the frontier, as he lists it:
  - Keep scaling data and compute.
  - Keep driving underlying research breakthroughs.
  - Build the infrastructure to support all of it.
- He describes this as a year when all the labs are "dramatically scaling up" their models. He thinks Meta is on a faster trajectory because it spent the past year on this groundwork.
- He treats resources as secondary. The work is to build the infrastructure, scale the data and compute, train the large models and show them.

chunks.heading: Open source versus closed release decision
chunks.text:
- Meta used to open source everything. Muse Spark is not open source.
- Meta updated its "advanced AI scaling framework", its view of the risks in very powerful models and how to handle them in early testing. It published what it saw while training Muse Spark in a preparedness report.
- Muse Spark triggered some high-risk areas in early training, particularly bio risk, and a number of other risks were elevated. He notes the whole industry has seen this as models have improved.
- His reasoning on release format:
  - In a product, Meta has many ways to mitigate risks and launch safely.
  - With an open source model, people can use it "in all sorts of contexts that we may not have full understanding of", so mitigation is much harder.
- Meta is now developing models it believes are "fit and safe to be open source" while keeping as much performance as possible. So open source continues, but he says Llama is not necessarily the brand. He gave nothing on branding.

chunks.heading: Where the next models will be strong
chunks.text:
- Muse Spark already stood out in three areas, even as a much smaller model than Meta intends to train:
  - Multimodality (images, video, audio), which he calls critical for Meta's business.
  - Health, which he sees as critical as models reach billions of people.
  - Early "vibe code" results, such as creating small games or artifacts.
- Meta is doubling down on these and investing in agentic capabilities. Upcoming models should be very capable agents combined with those strengths.
- His stated goal is to build "the best personal agents for everybody around the world".

chunks.heading: Agent vision and how he uses agents
chunks.text:
- Meta just announced a business agent, which advertisers can use to interact with customers. A consumer agent is also in development, and he says it is being "actively cooked".
- His view of how people will use agents:
  - One, maybe two, or a small handful of agents.
  - A personal agent for health, personal relationships and being a better parent, friend and family member.
  - The same agent may carry into work, especially for entrepreneurs, small businesses and smaller organizations.
  - Inside larger enterprises, work and personal agents may split, much like email.
  - Agents become "deeply personal", and people rely on them for more of their personal and work lives over time.
- Trust and privacy: he calls this one of the most important societal questions for agents. He says Meta has built technology on agentic safety so agents respect privacy and boundaries, and that it is an industry-wide problem, not only Meta's.
- His own use:
  - As a leader, agents help him understand what is happening across the company and support his team.
  - The most exciting uses are personal: an agent to help him be healthier and one to help him keep in touch with friends. Both were historically hard for him to stay on top of, and he calls the change "pretty transformational".

chunks.heading: US leadership, AI and jobs, regulation
chunks.text:
- On China: he says it is "incredibly important" for the US to lead on AI technology and its economic benefits, and that Meta focuses on contributing to that. He thinks the US is ahead now, but says it should always track progress in other countries, especially China, and understand the reasons behind it.
- The main thing he wants to protect the lead is continued pace of scaling. He calls research progress today "nearly miraculous".
- On layoffs at Meta at the end of the previous month: he says saying goodbye to teammates is "incredibly difficult" and that Meta does not take it lightly.
- On AI and jobs:
  - It deserves close attention and tracking.
  - He says AI is enabling more new businesses than ever, which Meta sees in its data. He expects more entrepreneurs and small businesses as the tools improve, and says Meta wants to support small businesses worldwide.
- On the Trump executive order for pre-release model review: he welcomes the administration's involvement in responsible deployment. He says regulation is "notoriously difficult to get right", so it is a balance, but models are becoming dramatically more capable, so deployment should be thoughtful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how he designed Meta Superintelligence Labs from a blank slate: research-led, high talent density, no artificial deadlines. He describes a flywheel of models, products and infrastructure, and reflects on trading youthful impatience for long-term foundations.

chunks.heading: Meta Superintelligence Labs: mission and org design
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says he joined Meta about 7 months before this interview. He calls the next 5 years "some of the most monumental discoveries" human civilization has made.
- Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) is dedicated to building the organization that can deliver the scientific breakthroughs for superintelligence. It also builds the products that deploy this technology to billions of people.
- Meta's advantage, in his view, is reach. About 3.5 billion people use its platforms every day.
- He got to design the org and team "from a blank slate". His priorities were:
  - the best scientific foundations
  - the highest talent density
  - an environment for breakthrough research
  - removing artificial deadlines, so the technology is built at the best pace
- He says the first 7 months went to building foundations. He expects "incredible velocity" over the coming months and through the year.

chunks.heading: Research-led flywheel linking models, products and infrastructure
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says Meta must be research-led, because this is a special moment for frontier AI.
- Internally he treats it as one flywheel:
  1. Frontier models are the "base material" for consumer products.
  2. Products that gain scale justify a larger infrastructure footprint, among the largest in the world.
  3. That infrastructure enables better models and more research.
- He sees models, products and infrastructure as a continuous discipline that advances in tandem.
- He argues research and product can no longer be a handoff, where research works in a corner and product deploys the result.
  - He cites ChatGPT and Claude Code as breakthroughs that came from researchers thinking about product and product people thinking about research, working hand in hand.

chunks.heading: Strategy: personal agents deployed globally, plus new hardware
chunks.text:
- Alexandr describes Meta's AI identity as personal agents deployed globally. He argues the reach of roughly half the world using Meta products daily lets it deploy agents to whole communities and countries, which he says is hard for other labs to match.
- He cites Manus, which released agents that work 24/7 on a user's behalf toward their goals. He calls it the first of a series of personal-agent products. He thinks it may be seen in a decade as a big breakthrough in AI productization.
- On hardware, he says Meta has invested for many years in wearables and next form factors. His view is that personal agents make that vision "never more real".
- His picture is a constellation of devices beyond the phone. The agent is always on, "see[s] what you see, hear[s] what you hear", and helps more deeply than today's devices.

chunks.heading: Building durable organizations: patience over impatience
chunks.text:
- Alexandr contrasts his younger self with today. He started Scale AI right after dropping out of college.
  - Impatience is "both a great strength and a great weakness". It makes things happen faster than people expect, but it doesn't set up long-term advantages.
- From studying great businesses, he argues the ones with staying power built a foundation that is very hard to replicate. He compares it to a seed that grows over decades.
- He applies this to MSL and to team building. The goal is durability and a differentiated point of view "all the way down to the organization".
- In his words: "you can't let your impatience drive you too far", and you should always ask what foundations you are building and what the long-term story looks like.
- He says MSL was set up for the long term, not to "cut a corner" for a short-term outcome and "mortgage the long-term opportunity".

chunks.heading: Why he joined Meta and the Scale AI deal
chunks.text:
- Alexandr calls the deal "incredibly non-standard" and says it took Mark Zuckerberg's boldness and vision to come together.
- He frames it as a milestone for Scale. It gave back to investors, employees and supporters while setting Scale up for the future.
- He says Scale continues to execute for enterprises and governments under its team.
- He says he saw an "astronomical" opportunity at Meta. In the middle of the AI race, he argues, people lost sight of the fact that Meta had every ingredient:
  - distribution
  - billions of users
  - scale
  - a business model
  - talent
  - infrastructure
- The opportunity was to "lock everything in" so Meta could succeed long term.

chunks.heading: Responsibility, trust and model behavior
chunks.text:
- Alexandr's view that some peers may not share is that technology must be developed with "extreme responsibility". That covers traditional AI safety and new risks from billions of people using it daily.
- He ties this to the product vision. A personal agent that holds your goals, hopes and fears requires a huge amount of trust from users, the public, governments and every other stakeholder.
- He says some in the industry have moved away from safety commitments, while Meta takes them very seriously.
- On model behavior, Meta works with philosophers and psychologists to shape how the model behaves, so it helps and empowers users.
- He wants a mutual relationship between humans and agents, where each wants the other to succeed. He says engineering and designing that is very important.

chunks.heading: Working with Mark Zuckerberg
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says much of what is said about Zuckerberg is unfair. He describes him as "a very regular guy" and a family man.
- As a leader, he calls him "incredibly bold and ambitious".
- The trait that stands out is how quickly Zuckerberg sees the future. He takes a technological advance and plays it forward to the effect on users, consumers, businesses and the ecosystem. Then he works with the team to make it happen fast.
- He says Zuckerberg lets him and the team "dream bigger than we would otherwise".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang tells how AlphaGo's 2016 win pushed him to drop out of MIT and found Scale AI. He frames AI as chips, data and algorithms, with data quality as the real bottleneck. He argues AI will create jobs, turn workers into managers of agents, and should stay a helpful tool rather than an ad platform.

chunks.heading: How Alexandr describes AI: three ingredients and the race between them
chunks.text:
- AI is "programming computers to be able to start thinking like humans." Traditional programming is "barebones"; AI replicates what brains do.
- Modern AI started with computer vision (ImageNet, AlexNet). A milestone was YouTube's algorithm that could spot cats in videos around 2011-2012. Self-driving cars were the first major use case and "all the rage" when he started Scale in 2016.
- Every AI system has three ingredients:
  - **Chips (compute):** GPUs/TPUs in huge data centers, such as Elon's Colossus.
  - **Data:** where the algorithms learn patterns. "Data is the new oil." Anything an AI knows or says comes from its data.
  - **Algorithms:** the math run on the chips, learned from the data.
- He uses a "body of water" analogy for data. The job is to keep the water as clean as possible and fill it with information about everything.
- Companies and countries compete on all three dimensions. Chips decide who has the most advanced hardware, data decides whose water is cleaner and bigger, and algorithms decide who has the cleverest tricks.
- His US vs China rack-and-stack, as of early 2025:
  - Chips: the US is ahead.
  - Data: China is probably ahead, because it has invested in data for a long time.
  - Algorithms: roughly neck and neck.
- He calls it a tight race and points to DeepSeek's rise as evidence.

chunks.heading: Scale AI's model: the "Uber for AI" data marketplace
chunks.text:
- Alexandr frames Scale as "almost like the Uber of AI." The algorithms that need data are one side of the market. A network of people who produce that data are the other.
- Scale runs this through a platform called Outlier. People, called "contributors," log on and get paid to improve models.
- Contributors earned about $500 million total on Outlier last year, across 9,000 different towns in the US.
- Example of the work: a nurse sees an AI tell someone with stomach pain to wait it out. The nurse corrects it ("you might have appendicitis"), and the correction feeds back into the model.
- He wants experts in everything, in any subject.
- Quality control works in two ways:
  - People check other people's work.
  - Automated systems check for spam.
- Contributors get a short orientation on what to do and what expertise to bring.
- He says models are much better in English, especially American English, than in other languages. Scale hires people worldwide to improve them in other languages.
- Scale sits "under the hood" of the major models. It helps power ChatGPT/OpenAI, Google's AI and Meta's AI, mostly on the data side.
- It also works with large companies and the government:
  - Time Magazine
  - Toyota (cars)
  - Pharma companies
  - Hospitals
- The government is "not our biggest" customer but "an important one."

chunks.heading: Why he says AI creates jobs
chunks.text:
- He argues the jobs story "is not told enough" and that the AI industry is partly to blame for making AI sound sci-fi and scary.
- He expects "jobs from AI" to be "the fastest growing jobs in the world for the years to come."
- Categories of new work:
  - Contributing data and expertise to models. This keeps growing because the world keeps changing, and AI can only partly generate its own data.
  - Building AI into applications and helping companies use it.
  - Managing, improving and watching AI systems so they don't misbehave, for example by spamming a million people.
- Everyone gets "promoted to being a manager." A laptop worker might manage "a little pod of 10 AI agents" and check their work and mistakes.
- He expects the economy to grow so much that the limit becomes "how many AIs can you have," which is capped by how many managers you have.
- He compares this to history. Farming got more efficient, so people moved into entertainment and finance.
- Blue-collar trades (plumbers, electricians) still need physical work.
- Education gap: he says no real training programs exist yet. He would like to help build them with colleges and "teach everybody in America how to best contribute to the AIs."
- Every company will need to figure out AI the way every company had to figure out the internet. He says to start early and find a unique twist so you stand out.

chunks.heading: AI as a tool to turn ideas into reality
chunks.text:
- His pitch: people have thousands of ideas and time for a few. AI should help ideas become real, giving humans "more agency" and "more sovereignty."
- Movie example: ask an AI to draft a script, find funders, suggest cast within a budget, find locations and list talent agencies. Over time it does the legwork, reaching out to people, handling logistics and booking.
- Other uses: starting businesses more easily, planning events, and directors producing more of their ideas.
- He calls this the "agents" idea. Humans stay in control and tell the AI what they want.
- On sameness (everyone getting the same movie): human creativity still matters. You need an angle and "your own spice." The key human job is "what is my fresh take."
- He expects AI to speed up biology and medicine:
  - AI "understands molecules and biology better than humans" in some respects.
  - Work that took a PhD biologist about 5 years can take it minutes.
  - He thinks cancer and heart disease could be cured in our lifetimes, and lifespans lengthened "pretty dramatically."
- How to learn: use ChatGPT for small things. Ask how AI works, your town's history or your last name's origin. Using it shows what it's good and bad at, and that makes it less scary.
- Today's AI is "still really bad at a lot of things." It knows more facts than any person (like Google), but it is not smarter than humanity. He calls it a "very different kind of intelligence."

chunks.heading: Why the US vs China AI race matters
chunks.text:
He gives three reasons the winner matters:

- **Cultural:** AI reflects the values of the country that builds it. US AI supports free speech. Chinese AI is censored, and he says Chinese ideologies would be exported if it won.
  - Example: Chinese models won't answer questions about Xi or Tiananmen. DeepSeek deflected "is Xi a good guy" with "let's talk about something else."
  - He also cites the Uyghurs, which he says a Chinese AI wouldn't discuss honestly.
- **Economic:** the winning country's economy grows faster.
- **Military:** AI is military technology. He cites cyber warfare:
  - Salt Typhoon, a hack of US telecom companies.
  - The earlier hack of the US security clearance database.
  - AI already beating top human hackers, so the contest becomes whose AI defends and attacks better.
  - Information warfare (propaganda), including mass hiring of people to seed stories on chat groups.
- Taiwan:
  - TSMC makes nearly 100% of the advanced AI chips.
  - Its fabs use machines costing hundreds of millions of dollars and are built to withstand seismic movement.
  - He says Xi ordered the military to be ready to move on Taiwan by 2027, and China could see capturing the chips as a way to win AI.
- Chip export controls: he calls them a hot topic in DC. There are good arguments on both sides (free market and bolstering US industry vs. not giving rivals an advantage). His stance: "let's make sure America wins and let's start from there."
- He sees no US government risk of curtailing free speech through AI right now, but says values must be upheld.

chunks.heading: AI safety and his red lines
chunks.text:
- His biggest worry is deception and persuasion. He doesn't want AIs "specifically programmed to make me think a certain thing" or that nudge him to do things he shouldn't.
- How Scale keeps AI "clean":
  - Clean data, with filters and checks on what goes in.
  - Constant testing of models for harm. For example, models must refuse to help make a bomb or a "COVID 2.0."
- Self-improving AI: he says it's a hot industry topic and he's wary. Humans should "always have the steering wheel" and not let AI iterate and improve itself unchecked.
- Advertising: he hopes the AI industry avoids advertising as much as possible. His reasoning: AI should be a tool that "helps people first and foremost," like a thought partner or assistant. People shouldn't feel "used by the AIs."
- Fear of AI comes from not understanding it. His view: "it is a cool technology but it's not that magical." It is data, crunched into algorithms. Explaining it and its opportunities removes the "boogeyman."

chunks.heading: Origin story: from math competitions to founding Scale at 19
chunks.text:
- He grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, where both parents were physicists (his mother studied plasma). Most kids' parents worked at the national lab, so "anything was possible."
- Competitive math drove him:
  - In 6th grade, a state math contest offered an all-expenses-paid Disney World trip for the top four. He placed fourth.
  - He became a nationally ranked "mathlete" in middle and high school.
  - He took the USAMO (a 9-hour, 6-problem exam over two days) first in 8th grade, and attended math camps.
- Competitive math scores helped him get into MIT, where he took the AI classes.
- Triggers for AI:
  - A class side project: a camera in his fridge to catch roommates stealing his food. One step "was too easy" and just worked.
  - AlphaGo beating Lee Sedol in March 2016.
- He dropped out of MIT after one year because he was "feeling really impatient." In May 2016, two months after the AlphaGo match, he flew from Boston to San Francisco and started Scale AI.
- Back then AI was a niche topic. He says he always knew it would get bigger but "could have never predicted" the scale.
- His parents (and two older brothers, all with PhDs) were worried at first. He told them he'd go back and finish school. They're now proud.
- Networking example: in 2018, when Scale was a "baby company," he "kind of YOLO invited" Jensen Huang to a dinner in Silicon Valley, and Jensen said yes.
- He credits his parents for his math skills and says he owes them everything.
- He grew up "solidly middle class."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang spends most of this Shawn Ryan interview on AI, national security and China, but the founder lessons are clear. He found data as the ignored bottleneck in AI, focused on a few big customers, outworked peers, and traded perfectionism for speed. He also shares how he got early hires and traction with no credibility.

chunks.heading: Scale AI's founding insight: data was the neglected third pillar of AI
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says AI comes down to three inputs: algorithms, compute (data centers, power, chips) and data. He used to write algorithms himself.
- At MIT he took the hardest machine learning courses. He then tried to build a camera in his fridge to catch roommates stealing food.
- The project failed because he had nowhere near enough data. It kept producing false positives and false negatives.
- His conclusion was that he'd need "a million times more data," and that every AI thing anyone builds would be blocked on data.
- He saw many people working on algorithms and chips and nobody working on data. Being 19 and impatient, he thought: "if nobody's going to do it, I might as well do it."
- He dropped out and flew straight from Boston to San Francisco.
- He compares data to oil. It is the raw material fed into algorithms and chips.

chunks.heading: Early days: Y Combinator, a tiny team and a launch that went "micro-viral"
chunks.text:
- Scale went through Y Combinator, which he calls "the Hunger Games for startups." About 100 startups grind for a summer and end with a demo day where you either get investment or you don't.
- Scale got investment from YC and from Accel, an early Facebook investor. Those investors helped him build the team.
- At 19 he had no team and no credibility. Experienced San Francisco engineers he met for coffee politely declined.
- He recruited mostly people he knew from school, because they trusted him. Some dropped out and some joined after graduating.
- He coded the first product himself and launched it on one of the sites for launching startups. It went "micro-viral" among people on Twitter looking for startup ideas.
- After that he spent his time coding and occasionally posting. He begged friends to upvote and like it to get "some ounce of traction."
- The first name was Scale API, because that domain was available. It became Scale AI about a year and a half later.
- About a year in he hired someone with the title "head of business."

chunks.heading: Finding a wedge: from odd early customers to autonomous vehicles to defense
chunks.text:
- Early use cases were small. One customer was a custom t-shirt company that needed illegal or gory designs detected. Another was a furniture marketplace that wanted better search.
- About three months in, Scale started working with autonomous vehicle companies. This became the core of the company for roughly the first 3-4 years.
- Customers included General Motors, Toyota and Waymo. The specialty was sensor fusion: combining many sensors into one output, such as "that's one person, that's one car."
- Alexandr says there were tens of competitors, but he doesn't mind competition because of his math-competition background. Scale focused on the best possible data sets.
- Headcount grew slowly at first:
  - Year one: 1-3 people.
  - Year two: about 15.
  - Year three: about 100.
  - Then roughly 200, then 500, and now thousands.
- About 3 years in, Scale moved into defense and began working with the DoD.
- He says the youngest-billionaire outcome came about five years after founding and "did not feel obvious."

chunks.heading: Customer strategy: go deep with the number one player in each industry
chunks.text:
- Scale focuses on a small number of customers where it can have a very large impact. Alexandr says the company is "pretty picky" because building these systems and data sets takes a lot of resources.
- The aim is to work with the best in each category: the number one bank, pharma company, healthcare system, telco and country.
- The pitch is to take how an organization operates today and use AI to transform its workflows and operations. For a large health system, that means better logistics, diagnosis and patient outcomes.
- Scale has two parts to its business:
  - Data foundry: large-scale data production that fuels the major AI models.
  - Enterprise and government work: deploying full AI systems on a customer's own data.
- One of the first defense jobs was solving the DoD's own data problem for satellite and overhead imagery. Scale built:
  - A data foundry that generated data synthetically, with humans validating the output.
  - A facility in St. Louis next to the NGA, staffed by imagery analysts to check AI outputs.
- Scale later moved into larger deployments such as Thunderforge, which uses AI for military operational planning. The goal is to plan in hours instead of days.
- Alexandr says Scale and Palantir target different parts of the problem and ultimately work together well.
- For international customers, his preference is to start with low-stakes uses, such as education, healthcare and permitting. He wants as much of the world as possible to run on an American AI stack rather than a CCP one.

chunks.heading: Founder operating principles: focus, overdoing it, and trading perfectionism for speed
chunks.text:
- He doesn't think he's fundamentally smarter than many others. His advantage was hyperfocus: on math as a kid, physics, then programming.
- His belief: "if you overdo things... you go the extra mile, you go the extra 10 miles... you will improve faster than anybody else by many times." He says others meander or don't put in the extra effort.
- He was a perfectionist early on, partly from practicing violin. He now says "we don't have the luxury to be perfectionists" and is much more pragmatic.
- The shift came when he internalized 80/20: "do 20% of the effort that's 80% as good," and do that over and over.
- He now thinks that for most things speed is the objective, not perfection. A few things still deserve perfectionism.
- He cites an Elon Musk framing for crises. Imagine a bomb strapped to your body that goes off if you don't solve the problem. In startups there are many such life-and-death moments where you have to act and do the best available thing.
- This is what he says "remolded" his brain toward operating quickly.

chunks.heading: Why he dropped out, and how he thinks about credibility and learning speed
chunks.text:
- He left high school a year early to work at Quora on machine learning for ranking and engagement algorithms.
- He went to MIT to learn AI fast by going deep. He took every AI course available.
- He talked his way into the hardest machine learning course as a freshman despite his adviser's doubts. He got one of the top marks on the first test, after which the professor "let me do whatever I wanted."
- He left MIT after one year because he saw a bottleneck nobody was working on and didn't want to wait.
- On credibility, he says early on he had none outside his school network. Investors with strong brands (YC, Accel) helped close that gap.

chunks.heading: Competitive and strategic framing: compounding, numbers games and strategic surprise
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says AI differs from oil because it compounds. Smarter AI creates more economic power, which funds smarter AI, so it doesn't run out.
- He thinks the competition between AI labs is largely about who secures power and real estate for data centers five to six years out. The question that matters is how many copies of an AI you can run.
- On AI-versus-AI conflict, he argues it becomes a numbers game. A side with more AI copies can put half its copies on offense (hacking the other side's AI) while the other half does planning. The smaller side can't both defend and plan.
- He argues the keys to an edge are:
  - Strategic surprise: an AI that reasons differently, or new platforms the adversary's simulations have never seen.
  - Ambiguity about how many resources you really have.
- He thinks the transition is from humans in the loop to humans on the loop. AI agents do most of the work and humans check and decide.
- He believes this raises the consequence of each remaining human decision.
- He says Scale's long-term mission centers on "human sovereignty," meaning:
  - Data that makes models aligned with humans.
  - Oversight so humans supervise AI actions.
  - Not ceding control of critical systems.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains why data is the building block of the AI era and how Scale positioned itself as infrastructure, taking cues from Stripe and Amazon. He also covers hiring for internal locus of control, a merit-based culture, anchoring on big problems, and holding a strong point of view.

chunks.heading: Why Alexandr says data is the new code, not the new oil
chunks.text:
- He agrees with the "data is the new oil" analogy on one point: data will be the main lever of economic power over the coming decades.
- He rejects the commodity framing. Data is not a scarce, uniform commodity. Coding, language and legal data are very different from each other.
- The strategy is therefore not to drill data wells and resell them. Companies need a deliberate plan to connect qualitatively different, useful data sources.
- His preferred line is "data is the new code." For 50 years code was the building block of technology. In the AI era, models and algorithms run the applications, so data becomes the building block.
- His formative experience was at MIT when Google released TensorFlow. He used the exact same algorithm to detect facial expressions and to detect whether food was missing from his fridge. Only the data changed.
- If data is the oil, he says scale is the refinery. Scale turns huge amounts of raw data into high-quality data that can power algorithms.

chunks.heading: How Scale started: autonomous vehicles, infrastructure and the "data engine"
chunks.text:
- Scale began in 2016 with autonomous vehicles. Cars collected huge amounts of video, lidar, radar and other sensor data, but none of it was labeled as "person," "pedestrian," "cyclist" or "car." The algorithm had nothing to learn from.
- Scale's role was moving from raw data to labeled, high-quality data for machine learning.
- His core insight: if AI grows, the need for data grows enormously. He had no idea of the timing or scale, but he was convinced neural networks would spread. The appetite for data has far exceeded what he imagined.
- He drew inspiration from Stripe and Amazon as large-scale infrastructure companies. They saw that every company in the sector faces the same problems. They built easy developer experiences with enough simplicity and economies of scale to become the default.
- He sees three components of AI: compute (dominated by Nvidia), talent (cannot be outsourced, and companies spend billions on it), and data. Each is a large piece of the AI tree, so a company that solves one at high quality becomes required infrastructure.
- Build vs. buy: most companies build a few things in-house to differentiate. But they will do those things less efficiently than the industry standard, because infrastructure providers have economies of scale and network effects.
- Scale now builds a "data engine," a refinery for raw data that feeds every leading large language model company today. The key technique is reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
- Scale first worked on RLHF with OpenAI in 2019.

chunks.heading: How RLHF works and where the bottleneck moves
chunks.text:
- Human experts show the model what good work looks like. An expert says one response is better than another and explains why.
- The model learns an internal sense of good vs. bad, called a reward model. It then uses reinforcement learning to improve its own responses against that sense.
- Models can surpass humans this way. His analogy: anyone can be a movie critic, but none of us can make a film. If humans can teach the model what "better" looks like, it can keep improving far past human ability.
- Bottlenecks today: compute is limited by manufacturing. He says 100% of high-performance GPUs are made in Taiwan, and TSMC has spent tens to hundreds of billions in capex. Exponential growth needs exponential supply chain growth, which isn't economically possible right now.
- Data is also constrained. Text is an extremely compressed form of knowledge, and video is much less compressed. If pre-training data runs short, the compensation is RLHF and post-training data.
- He expects the number and quality of human experts feeding RLHF to become "GPUs in themselves," another supply chain bottleneck for the industry.
- He thinks the frontier labs will find solutions, since this is likely the greatest engineering project humans have undertaken.
- Why models do knowledge work better than physical tasks: it comes down to data availability. Decades of internet use created the largest dataset of human behavior ever, but almost no data exists on picking things up, throwing a ball or making things.

chunks.heading: Advice for companies adopting AI: use your private data
chunks.text:
- Public frontier models are trained mostly on the open internet. He estimates that 99.9% of usable data is private or proprietary (messages, emails, journals).
- Most companies, whether they know it or not, sit on far more data than what is on the public internet.
- The big opportunity is to take strong foundation models and blend, refine and customize them on the company's own data, business and customers. That produces unique, proprietary outputs.
- Scale built a platform, EGP, so companies can fine-tune GPT-3.5, Llama 2 or other foundation models on their data. It supports use cases like customer service, legal applications and developer tooling. Scale partnered with Meta on Llama 2.
- For a non-AI founder or executive, his steps:
  1. Inventory and classify your unique data assets.
  2. Run a thought experiment: imagine a superpowered person who can read all of it faster than anyone. What could they do better than anyone in the world?
  3. Decide where to cut costs (customer service is the obvious example) or play offense.
  4. Build with AI partners such as Scale, OpenAI or Anthropic.
- He expects it to become obvious which companies adopted AI and which didn't, through consumer experience and financial results.

chunks.heading: Why he thinks AI is a bigger economic opportunity than software
chunks.text:
- US GDP is about $27 trillion. Software and IT services are about $2 trillion, which is not even 10%.
- About $16 trillion, more than half, is services. The biggest sector is healthcare, followed by financial services. He sees the real potential of AI as disrupting this $16 trillion of services output.
- The key belief required: models keep improving quickly. He sees no slowdown soon.
- Scaling evidence: in 2019 GPT-2 couldn't count to 10. GPT-4 is arguably more persuasive and eloquent than most humans. That took about four years and roughly a 1,000x increase in model size, from about 2 billion parameters to roughly 1 to 2 trillion, depending on the source.
- Companies have announced plans to scale another 100x, taking spending from hundreds of millions to tens of billions of dollars. He expects costs to reach hundreds of billions, making these projects comparable to particle colliders.
- Don't bet against the technology. At each stage people dismissed it (GPT-2 couldn't count, GPT-3 failed simple math, GPT-4 hallucinates), and each time it improved. Many people, even in the AI industry, don't truly believe models will keep improving.
- The "Turing Trap" (from Erik Brynjolfsson's paper): framing AI as a replacement for humans is a trap. Most value will come from hybrid human-AI systems. He expects AI to create a different mix of jobs and likely a net increase in demand for human labor.
- Democratization: scaling makes the frontier undemocratic, like particle accelerators. The counterforce is open-source models arriving a few years behind and getting cheaper. Models around 10 billion parameters or smaller are reaching GPT-3.5 level.

chunks.heading: Building a company that keeps reinventing itself
chunks.text:
- Investors think they bet on the next few years of a company. In the best companies, he says, they are really betting on continual reinvention.
- Amazon example: online bookstore, then everything store, then Prime, then the largest data center provider. AWS was the unpredicted move, and most analysts attribute most of Amazon's value to it.
- Nvidia example: a GPU company selling gaming and graphics chips for decades. About 15 years ago it saw people using its chips to train AI and invested heavily in R&D long before it showed in financials. It is now a trillion-dollar company almost entirely because of AI.
- Amazon lessons he applies at Scale:
  - Operational excellence is a huge engine of technical value. Jeff Wilke, who ran Amazon's consumer operations, is a close mentor.
  - Embrace operational complexity and marry technology with operations.
  - Take a very practical approach to business decisions.
  - Engineer problems to have as few interdependencies as possible. That lets you run many independent bets in parallel and double down on the winners.
- Culture tactics for reinvention at Scale:
  - Pure meritocracy. People at junior levels with good ideas get full responsibility to execute them. At most companies a manager or VP takes the idea and turns it into a career step.
  - Impact ceiling is unlimited, depending on how hard you work and how good and original your ideas are.
  - Anchor on solving big problems in the industry, the way Amazon anchors on the customer. Scale started with autonomous vehicles, then moved to US government and defense work, then to ensuring AI progress. Each larger problem opened bigger opportunities than the original one.
  - Keep pushing the ambition of the core vision.

chunks.heading: Hiring: the four traits and how he screens for them
chunks.text:
- His favorite interview question: "What is the hardest thing you've worked on?"
- It tests for an internal vs. external locus of control. Internal means you believe your life outcomes come from your actions. External means you feel like a ball in a pinball machine. He only wants to work with internal-locus people.
- A way to measure it: how hard people work on things they care about, and how deeply they obsess over details.
- Scale's early hiring document had four traits:
  1. Internal locus of control.
  2. Problem solving: finds creative ways around obstacles, even when a problem can't be solved head-on.
  3. Impressive: people you genuinely admire, who raise the organization's level. If you admire someone, you are excited to come to work to learn from them.
  4. Collaborative: some people are impressive and driven but bad to work with.
- Test for real passion by asking why candidates want to interview at Scale. A good answer is odd and specific. A weak answer is "AI is the next big thing."
