A strong answer: they spent five hours checking data with a friend while training a model, one small data error broke the whole model, and they found that problem fascinating. He cites Paul Graham on people caring for an irrational reason.
- Warning sign: "If your hiring department looks like a college admissions office, you should be worried." Big-tech brand prestige selects for people who overvalue brand and status over impact. Big companies also give most people a tiny piece of a tiny piece of a problem. He wants people who care about impact, not status.
- Scale is not a "cool" company, because it is infrastructure. He doesn't want people who just want to be cool and work on exciting new technologies. He wants people willing to do unglamorous but important work. People who join know what they are signing up for.
- Non-consensus view: hard-working, high-capability people who are not highly experienced are very valuable. Most startups are "a buzzing hive" of such people building amazing things through trial and error. Much of the ecosystem over-focuses on hiring experienced people who have done it before.
- He also values weird people. Statistically, if you're normal you are inside the bell curve, and it's hard to do great things from there. A normal person's conversation is easy to simulate and has low information content. Surrounding yourself with weird people gives you a richer sea of ideas.

chunks.heading: Taste, strong opinions, and how he runs his day
chunks.text:
- Strong point of view: the older advice was to have a neutral brand to appeal to everyone. He argues we are entering an era where it is right to have and voice a strong view. It attracts aligned talent, builds culture, and matters to customers who want to work with people who share their philosophy. Many enterprise software companies lose their identity and become just another tool in the toolbox.
- Taste: much of a company's product is the output of its taste. That covers taste in people, aesthetics, product and how to organize. Apple is the best example. He credits his violin training for developing taste and comfort with intuition. Business means working in gray areas where you can't be sure decisions are right, and most important things are hard to measure.
- Office space: he spends on a nice office because space affects thinking quality. Natural light is one of the best things for his thinking, and seating arrangements and small differences in space quality matter.
- Daily routine: he sets clear goals at the start of the day, asking "what are the most important things I need to get done today?" Start small, then raise the goals as you learn your limits. He attends many meetings and keeps checking progress against those goals.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang recounts Scale's year of "wandering" after YC, then explains how he thinks about competition, enterprise sales, culture, and AI startups. Core themes: blustery self-belief, treating unglamorous problems with respect, optimizing for net economic impact, thinking independently of trends, and focusing instead of out-spending giants.

chunks.heading: Startup ideation and the "wandering" phase
chunks.text:
- Alexandr describes the first half of his YC batch as a "squiggle" of existential angst, with Google Docs full of startup ideas. He felt "behind the eightball" because everyone around him already seemed to be working on something.
- He found Paul Graham's essay on coming up with startup ideas to be a good focusing framework: live in the future, work out what exists there, and build backwards.
- Scale's original idea followed that framework. In the future, human computation would be orchestrated as easily as compute, through an API, and that API didn't exist yet.
- After the idea, he spent a night searching for a domain. scale ai.com was available, and he calls buying it "unusually good decision".
- Scale launched on Product Hunt and got enough traction from it. After that came about 4 to 6 months of "wandering mode": a few customers, trying to get more.
- He personally talked to anyone who clicked the Intercom chat bubble on scale ai.com.
- About 6 months later, one client who wanted to be really big appeared and the idea "started come into its own". He calls roughly a year of wandering "on the low end honestly of most startups".
- What got him through was high conviction that the thing would exist in the future and didn't yet. That gave him "enough of a gradient" to trust a path from point A to point B.
- He is an anxious person and channeled the uncertainty into "anxiously doing things", so he felt he was making progress in a direction.
- His scariest idea was the YC Hunger Games: about 90% of companies die, but "you could already be dead but you might only find out in three years".

chunks.heading: Competition: blustery confidence and perception in enterprise sales
chunks.text:
- Mechanical Turk and others already existed when Scale started. His answer to competition is "blustery confidence": "you need some kind of irrational self-belief" that you can compete.
- He says you have to believe you will recruit better, make better product decisions and go the extra mile. Over the long term those things accumulate into the self-belief you started with.
- He drew confidence from competitive programming and math competitions: "bring it, we're just going to build the better thing".
- He cites an 18-year-old YC founder who answered a question about competition with "just be better".
- As an example, he describes a Palantir executive telling a government customer, in front of him, that they would regret not picking Palantir. He calls it a "ridiculously aggressive talk track". He sees Palantir's deep belief that its software is the best as a self-reinforcing loop and part of its success.
- For large customers, "perception is more real than reality". The reality is usually too ugly for people to confront, so they live in perceptions.
- In enterprise sales or products, the job is as much to shape the perception as to improve the reality. He calls this one of Palantir's superpowers. Palantir gave new hires an acting book for a long time.
- He adds a caveat: "you also should produce value". Perception-shaping sits on top of building a good product.

chunks.heading: Winning by respecting unsexy problems and optimizing for economic impact
chunks.text:
- Alexandr names Scale's edge as creative problem solving on the least sexy problems. Scale coordinates hundreds of thousands of contributors worldwide to produce high-quality data for models.
- The team treats that operational problem with the same respect as a math Olympiad problem. They ask for the most creative ways to solve it, break it down and apply the scientific method.
- Scale holds "no elevated sense of purpose" about only solving certain problems. They pair that with working "like hell".
- He sees two common failure patterns:
  - Brilliant teams that work on useless, intellectually interesting problems.
  - Scrappy teams that take any problem but fail to solve it in a scalable way or abstract it.
- Culturally, he wants employees to think about net economic impact more than technical difficulty. School teaches that mastery comes from harder technical problems, but he says technical difficulty and economic value are poorly correlated.
- He says many valuable problems are not technically hard, they just have "a lot of hair" you must sift through. He says that is where most good startup opportunities are. Climb the ladder of economic impact relative to technical difficulty.

chunks.heading: Enterprise vs. SMB as a startup customer
chunks.text:
- On enterprise, he says you often can't believe what large organizations tell you. Many contacts have nothing to do with the company's success and just own a job. He calls it a "rats nest" you must learn to navigate.
- If it works, enterprise can work "incredibly well". He says the largest companies in the world are either enterprise or consumer companies, while SMB eventually taps out.
- His rule of thumb: going enterprise means spending roughly 30% of your time navigating bureaucracy.
- SMBs "don't even have time to lie to you", so you can take what they say at face value. He calls this a great benefit for startups.
- His general advice is to focus on SMBs to get liftoff. But if 99% of the startup ecosystem is chasing SMBs, there may be less opportunity there.
- He describes a startup cycle: many founders copy the currently hot companies and end up in "perfect competition", getting no traction. A company working on some fringe idea with no competition then works and becomes the next hot company, and everyone copies that.
- His conclusion: "you never want to be exactly where all the other companies are focused". Do something a little fringe to avoid perfect competition.

chunks.heading: Thinking independently in a hype-driven AI market
chunks.text:
- He estimates that "80 to 90%" of what's out in AI is nonsense, and that nobody truly knows what is going on. Many people are confident and wrong.
- Investors, product leaders and others are "paid to have a thesis", so many beliefs are not grounded in reality.
- Anecdote: in early 2018, Scale's Series A deck had a slide saying data is the lifeblood of AI systems. A senior Sequoia partner loudly said that wasn't true and that AI no longer needed more data. The partner then stopped paying attention, and Sequoia passed. He uses it as an example of confident people being wrong in early industries.
- He says founders can raise $50M or $100M Series A rounds by following a trend, and the idea can still turn out to be stupid.
- His mandate for founders:
  - Work out what you actually believe, then execute against the flow.
  - Keep a mechanism for learning from the ecosystem, so you don't dig in and get "washed out in the tide".
  - Avoid being someone who "get[s] all their ideas off of Twitter and parties".
- Whatever you build will be popular and unpopular at various points, and your job is to weather that. He notes Nvidia has gone between unsexy and sexy.
- Few AI categories have a clear winner yet. Funds raised and usage metrics are weak signals, so he says not to get psyched out by competition.
- A contrarian take on a crowded sub-domain is interesting.

chunks.heading: Capital efficiency and focus in AI
chunks.text:
- He says a business plan that requires raising and spending a lot of money "is in business terms a bad business". The goal should be a profitable company that can keep compounding for a long time.
- Example: self-driving cars. Hundreds of billions were raised and, in his view, close to none of those companies succeeded. Waymo is the one winner, and it has "an infinite bank account".
- Training foundation models means competing with some of the richest entities in history. He says not to compete with an infinite balance sheet.
- His advice: find something genuinely differentiated that you can keep investing in over a long horizon.
- In AI right now, "the premium is actually just picking a certain problem to care about for a really long time".
- OpenAI, Anthropic and Google each have thousands of things to worry about. Focus gives a big premium. Perplexity is his example: it spends far less and its simple search-based LLM output is still better than the others'.
- On owning a workflow (Cursor as the example): it is "pretty hard to fully monopolize a workflow". Developers are fickle, and a company must lay roots to solidify its position.

chunks.heading: Data as the AI bottleneck and agent product opportunity
chunks.text:
- He argues the 12 to 18 month focus on who has the biggest cluster was unnuanced. Even with big clusters, the industry is hitting limits of publicly available data, and he believes the data wall is real.
- Pre-training limits have been hit. Progress now comes from post-training, which is bottlenecked by specialized, high-quality data that doesn't look like internet data.
- On synthetic data: it works and is part of a world-class post-training effort, but it is not a "philosopher's stone". Each trick yields a bit more data, and it doesn't work "to infinity".
- Reasoning-trace data from models didn't pan out for pre-training, since synthetic data loses much of the richness of the real distribution.
- His view of the path to AGI: compute must scale exponentially, and data production needs a similar curve alongside it. New forms of human-generated data will be needed. Scale's role is producing that data.
- He thinks the $1T, $5T and $10T cluster talk is normalizing, but $100B clusters are probably still needed.
- Agents: models do well in a single turn and then "fall off a cliff" over more turns. Models don't know what they don't know. Labs must improve multi-turn reliability.
- He calls product design the biggest blocker for a breakout agent moment. Models are already good enough for a mind-blowing agent product.
- Cursor shows the pattern: it put the model into an engineer's workflow, and most engineers hadn't realized how good the models were.
- He says the opportunity is to break models out of the chat paradigm and bake them into fundamental workflows. He calls finding the right agent modality perhaps the biggest startup opportunity of 2025.

chunks.heading: Inputs, customers and political literacy
chunks.text:
- To form good opinions, Alexandr relies on:
  - Writing on the internet, including Substack, where experts post high-quality detail.
  - Talking to specific experts who "truly do not care about what other people think". He describes them as independent thinkers who seem strange and weird.
- He treats customers as always right: "you have to be super super subservient to your customers".
- He says Silicon Valley is under-investigated politically. Getting the broad political and demographic threads right can reveal 20-year tailwinds and big growth trends. He names populism, nationalism and isolationism, and says greater political literacy in Silicon Valley is underrated.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang argues AI progress has hit a "data wall": compute spend has exploded since GPT-4, but the easy internet data is used up. The next gains need frontier data (reasoning chains, agent traces) produced by human experts working with models. He also covers data as the one durable moat, consumption pricing, going direct instead of traditional PR, and keeping a very high hiring bar.

chunks.heading: Data, not compute, is the bottleneck for foundation models
chunks.text:
- Alexandr notes that GPT-4 has been out since fall 2022 and no model has been "jaw droppingly better" since, despite far more compute spend.
- In the same period, Nvidia data center revenue went from roughly $5 billion a quarter to north of $20 billion a quarter.
- He names three pillars of AI progress: compute, data and algorithms. His view is that the industry scaled compute dramatically without building the other two in tandem.
- He explains the plateau as a "data wall". GPT-4 was trained on nearly all the easy internet data (Common Crawl and similar, plus torrented material).
- In his view, if compute and data were produced in lock step, models would become "astronomically more capable".
- His misconception answer: people think "all that's between us and AI's compute", but "we need data to get there too".

chunks.heading: Frontier data: what agents need that the internet lacks
chunks.text:
- Pre-training made models excellent at emulating the internet. Alexandr says AGI needs systems that do tasks, solve hard problems and collaborate with humans, and the internet cannot teach that.
- Most reasoning that powers the economy is never written down. His example is a bank fraud analyst who weighs several data sources to decide whether a transaction is fraudulent, without documenting each step.
- He defines "Frontier data" as complex reasoning chains, agent chains (look up data, reason, look up more, self-correct), tool use, advanced code, and advanced physics, biology and chemistry data.
- He wants a shift from data scarcity to data abundance of Frontier data.
- Models reason well in scenarios where they have seen a lot of data. They lack the human ability to drop into a new setting and cope.
- So either a general reasoning breakthrough happens, or it is a data problem: "overwhelm them with data in all those scenarios".

chunks.heading: Mining existing data and producing new data
chunks.text:
Alexandr describes two directions:

- **Mining existing data.** Enterprises hold huge proprietary data. He cites JP Morgan's internal data set at 150 petabytes against GPT-4's internet training set of under one petabyte. He sees this as a one-time benefit, and expects only the most sophisticated companies to do it within 5 years.
- **Forward data production.** He argues the world thinks about expanding chip production (bigger fabs, smaller nanometers) but not "the means of production" of data. He calls for a similar build-out.
- He describes production as a hybrid human and synthetic process. Algorithms do the heavy lifting, and human experts step in when the model gets stuck, makes factuality errors or hits something new. He compares this to safety drivers in autonomous vehicles who disengage and take over.
- Longitudinal collection helps but will not push the frontier. Examples are enterprise process mining (apps used, copy-paste flows) and consumer wearables like Limitless or Meta Ray-Ban. Frontier data needs experts collaborating with models.
- He calls contributing expert data to AI one of the highest-leverage jobs. A mathematician who makes GPT-4 slightly better at math multiplies that gain across every student, company and developer who uses it.

chunks.heading: Data as the durable moat for model labs and enterprises
chunks.text:
- Of the three pillars, Alexandr says data is the one where a long-term competitive advantage can form. Algorithms are IP that the industry eventually learns, and compute can be bought by spending more.
- Early signs are OpenAI's deals with the Financial Times and Axel Springer. He expects labs to start building data strategies to differentiate.
- Content owners will not give exclusives to one lab, so each lab needs its own method to produce unique data. He suggests Anthropic could lean into Enterprise use cases and OpenAI into its large user base.
- He predicts labs will brag about data access and data production the way they brag about GPU counts today.
- Enterprises realize their data may be their only competitive differentiator in an AI world. They fear "mortgaging away their entire future" by sharing it with a model developer.
- That creates a large unmet need for open or on-prem models (Llama, Mistral) that enterprises customize on their own data without it going back to a model developer or cloud.

chunks.heading: Where AI value accrues, software, and pricing
chunks.text:
- Alexandr cites Andy Grove's *High Output Management*: Intel kept discovering value capture was moving to a different part of the stack. He sees the same in AI.
- He doubts much value accrues at the model layer because competition is intense. He is confident about value below the model (Nvidia, the third most valuable company in the world) and above it (apps and services).
- He discusses Chris Pike's "end of software" article, which compares software today to media before social media. He agrees with the provocative claim only in part: enterprises will demand more customization and personalization.
- He sees Palantir as an early version of this: go into enterprises, understand their problems and build the perfect application on top of their data. It was derided as a consulting company.
- As software creation costs fall, more enterprise software will be custom built for exact problems.
- Engineers will spend less time on routine work. The valuable part is turning customer problems into scoped engineering tickets an AI engineer can solve.
- He argues per-seat pricing stops making sense when AI agents do more of the work. Software providers want to capture the value agents produce, so he expects a shift toward consumption-based pricing.

chunks.heading: Policy, China and closed versus open models
chunks.text:
- Alexandr argues that permissive data regulation fits with a liberal democracy. He says the US protects chip production but does not take a pro-data regulatory stance.
- He proposes pooling data where it gives no proprietary advantage to one player. His examples are aerospace safety data, and fraud and compliance data in financial services.
- He says rules like HIPAA and PII regulations effectively block patient data from training models. He wants clear anonymization provisions so existing patient data can improve health outcomes.
- On China, he says it was far behind two years ago. Now 01.AI's Yi-Large sits just behind GPT-4o, Gemini and Claude 3 Opus, so capability is close to neck and neck.
- He argues the CCP is strong at aggressive centralized industrial policy, citing solar and EVs, and is "better at turning the crank" once an industry is established.
- He calls AI potentially "one of the greatest military assets" in history, possibly more than nukes. He worries that a totalitarian state with AGI could use it to conquer.
- He wants the most advanced systems kept closed, with open versions of less advanced models still allowed. He says Llama 3 is not a military asset yet.
- He expects the cost of training models to rise from billions to possibly tens or hundreds of billions. Foundation model efforts will then coalesce around nations or hyperscalers. He is unsure how the OpenAI-Microsoft and Anthropic-Amazon partnerships play out.

chunks.heading: Company building: PR, personal brand, hiring and hypergrowth
chunks.text:
- **PR.** Alexandr says traditional press is click-oriented: it builds you up and tears you down for clicks. He says he got fairer treatment testifying to Congress about military AI than from media.
- He tells founders to skip traditional PR and own direct channels (podcasts and similar) where their message is not altered. He notes people follow personalities, not companies.
- **Hiring.** He wants hires who "give a" and care about quality, detail and impact, 10 to 100 times more than average employees at big companies. His aim is "Navy Seals".
- At about 800 people, he still approves every hire, by interviewing or reading feedback. He overrides the team's recommendation roughly 25 to 30% of the time, usually for new hiring managers who need calibrating or for edge cases. He draws on having seen who succeeds and fails at scale.
- **Hypergrowth mistake.** In 2020-2021 he assumed company hypergrowth meant team hypergrowth. Headcount went from about 150 in 2020 to over 700 by end of 2022. The bar slipped subtly, and problems the org used to solve calcified.
- The team has since stayed around 800 while revenue grew dramatically. He now separates team growth from company growth and invests in quality.
- He relays Patrick Collison's point that the best Stripe hires would have joined even if Stripe weren't the hottest company. He wants a self-preserving talent ecosystem that keeps a high bar whether the brand is hot or not. He cites Airbnb's Brian Chesky shrinking the team and raising talent density.
- **AI hype.** From autonomous vehicles he learned that bold promises divorced from technical reality cause a painful trough. He fears generative AI may repeat it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains why data is the next bottleneck for AI after compute and algorithms, and why renting out models is a weaker business than the layers above and below it. He also shares hiring lessons: keep high-performing teams small, onboard outside executives slowly, and stay in the key decisions as founder-CEO.

chunks.heading: Scale AI's three pillars and the data wall
chunks.text:
Alexandr says AI progress rests on three pillars: compute, data and algorithms. Compute is powered by folks like Nvidia, algorithms by the large labs like OpenAI, and data is "fueled by Scale". Scale's goal is to produce the frontier data needed for frontier advances, in partnership with the large labs. It also helps every enterprise and government use its own proprietary data to build frontier AI.

- He describes Scale as "the data Foundry for AI".
- He calls producing frontier data "one of the great human projects of our time". The only model for the intelligence being built is humanity, so data production is a marriage of human experts with technical and algorithmic techniques.
- Publicly available data is largely exhausted ("Common Crawl is all done"), so the industry is hitting a "data wall".
- He expects data production to be a hallmark of the next phase of AI.

chunks.heading: Three things data needs to do next
chunks.text:
Alexandr names three requirements for getting past the data wall.

- **Complexity (frontier data):** Many desired capabilities are blocked by a lack of data. Agents are the example: "there's just no agent data on the internet", and no agent really works well.
- **Tool composition:** Scale has work coming out showing that all the frontier models are very bad at chaining multiple tools in a row. An example is looking something up, writing a Python script, then charting the result. Humans do this naturally, but the reasoning and agentic chains are not captured anywhere.
- **Abundance:** Capture more of what humans do in the field of work, and invest in synthetic and hybrid data, where synthetic data is generated with humans in the loop. He compares this to chips: "we need to have effectively data foundries" to produce huge amounts of data, the way chip foundries produce chips.
- **Measurement:** This is the "often underrated" last leg. The industry used to add data and check how good the model was. Now it must get scientific about what the model cannot do, and so exactly which data to add.

chunks.heading: Phases of language model development
chunks.text:
Alexandr splits the field into phases.

- **Phase one:** Early, small-scale research, from the original Transformer paper up to roughly GPT-3.
- **Phase two:** Scaling, from GPT-3 until now. OpenAI scaled to GPT-4 and beyond, then Google, Anthropic, Meta and xAI joined. He says it was mostly engineering and execution: making large training runs work, avoiding bugs, and setting up bigger clusters.
- **Next phase:** Research matters more again. He expects more divergence between labs over which research directions break through.

On big tech's data advantage, he sees regulatory limits on using existing corpora, especially in Europe. His example is Meta's research training image recognition on public Instagram photos with their hashtags, which caused regulatory problems in Europe. The labs' bigger edge is profitable businesses that supply near-infinite capital.

chunks.heading: Why big tech keeps spending on AI
chunks.text:
Alexandr lays out why the large companies' capex risk is lopsided.

- If they nail AI, they could add about a trillion dollars of market cap. If they under-invest and miss it, there is existential risk, since their businesses are all potentially disruptable.
- The extra spend, which he puts at roughly 20 or 30 billion of capex per year, can be recouped even in the worst case. Facebook and Google can improve their advertising systems, and Apple can drive an upgrade cycle.
- The spending benefits the industry. The cloud providers rent out compute, and open-source models like Llama 3.1 make the fruits of that investment broadly accessible.

chunks.heading: Model-layer economics and where the good businesses are
chunks.text:
Alexandr says inference pricing has fallen by two orders of magnitude over about two years. "Intelligence might be a commodity."

- Renting out pure models is "likely to be a relatively mediocre long-term business", unless a lab has a durable breakthrough.
- Two things cap value at the model layer: Meta continuing to open source, and several labs reaching similar performance.
- The better businesses are above and below the model. Below are Nvidia and the clouds. Clouds have good margins because it is logistically hard to set up large GPU clusters.
- Above are applications. ChatGPT is a great business, and startup apps that nail early product-market fit can be too, because the value they create for customers far exceeds inference cost.
- He expects labs to push into deeper product integrations, citing Anthropic's Artifacts in Claude. "Boring chatbots" are not the end product.
- Product innovation is hard to predict. OpenAI was itself surprised by how popular ChatGPT was. OpenAI and Anthropic each hired a Chief Product Officer within about two months of each other.

chunks.heading: How enterprises should approach AI
chunks.text:
Alexandr describes an enterprise frenzy of proofs of concept (POCs). Many companies bought AI tools to try every low-hanging idea, and far fewer POCs reached production than the industry expected. The results so far are marginal efficiency gains, such as support and some creative tasks.

- He pushes customers to ask which AI efforts could meaningfully move their stock price. He says nearly every enterprise has latent potential to do that.
- Today the gains come mostly as cost savings. Better customer experiences follow, especially where there is a lot of manual customer interaction, and those can eventually win market share.
- It is a multi-year investment cycle: CEOs may not see gains next quarter, but those who pull through will see massive transformation.
- He views small-use-case experimentation as fine, but "that's not what we're all here to do".
- On enterprise data, big data only brought better analytics. AI could change how products work. Much of an enterprise's data is not relevant, but some is hyper-valuable, such as a bank's historical customer interactions for wealth management, where little in-distribution data exists on the internet.
- Enterprises struggle to use their data. It is poorly organized, and consulting firms get paid tens or hundreds of millions for data migrations with no change in results. He frames it as a race: enterprises against startups that find a way to build a different product from a small subset of data.

chunks.heading: Headcount, executives and founder fantasies
chunks.text:
Over the past few years Scale kept headcount basically flat, growing it only very slightly, while the business grew 5x to 6x.

- His lesson from the 2020-2021 hiring boom: more people feels like better results, but a high-performing team is "like this very intricate sculpture". Adding even great people disrupts it, and you regress to the mean.
- Large sales teams can still work financially if operationalized to sit slightly above the mean. He says sales is different from product.
- Startups work because of very high-performing teams, so keep them intact as long as possible.
- A common failure mode: things scale but the team is junior, investors say to hire executives, the searches are "soul crushing" and work about half the time. Then the executive says to hire a massive team, the founder gives them a lot of rope, and this "almost always results in ruin".
- Outside executives can work if they first get steeped in how the company works and why the working things work. They should make small suggestions, with trust and verify, and earn sweeping changes through a track record of small beneficial steps.
- The "exec fantasy" is coming in to fix everything and make it professional. In reality you are recruiting a teammate with good judgment over time, not "some magic wand" or "magical bag of goods". Scale has made this mistake.
- The "founder fantasy" is hiring pros who do everything the founder doesn't want to do. A founder is good because of repeated good decisions, and pulling yourself out of those loops is "kind of crazy".
- Founder-led startups carry an innovation premium, and investors believe they will out-innovate the market. So the founder must stay in the strategic decisions.

chunks.heading: MEI hiring and the AGI definition
chunks.text:
Scale rolled out MEI: Merit, Excellence and Intelligence.

- In every role it hires the best possible person regardless of demographics, with no quota-based optimization of the workforce.
- It still wants diverse pipelines and a diverse top of funnel.
- Alexandr says most people at Scale saw it as implicitly true already. Codifying it gives everyone confidence that it won't change as the company changes. Scale operates in a competitive industry and needs "incredibly smart people".

His AGI definition is that AI can do 80% or more of the jobs people can do purely at a computer. He puts it at "four plus years" out, possibly sooner depending on algorithmic innovation cycles.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang explains why he started Scale AI around the data pillar of AI, how the company moved through self-driving, government and generative AI, and why frontier data, hybrid human-AI synthetic data and rigorous evals are the bottlenecks to better models. He also argues AGI will come by solving many small problems, each with its own data flywheel.

chunks.heading: Founding insight: AI rests on three pillars, and data was the neglected one
chunks.text:
- Alexandr studied AI and machine learning at MIT in 2016, the year of AlphaGo and TensorFlow's release. He saw that models are "very much so just a product of their data."
- He frames AI as three pillars: algorithms, compute, and data.
  - Research labs such as OpenAI and Google were working on algorithms.
  - Nvidia was already the clear compute leader.
  - Nobody was focused on data, and he judged data would only get more important over the long arc of the technology.
- He dropped out of MIT, did YC in 2016, and started Scale to solve the data pillar. He calls Scale the "data Foundry" for AI.
- The mission was to solve the hard problems of producing enough data to fuel the whole AI ecosystem.

chunks.heading: How Scale's business evolved by following where AI applications emerged
chunks.text:
- **Infrastructure rule:** As an infrastructure provider, Scale has to guess where breakthrough AI use cases will appear and "lay down the tracks before the freight train of AI comes rolling through."
- **2016-2018, autonomous vehicles:**
  - He followed the early-startup advice to focus. Scale built the first data engine for sensor-fused data, meaning 2D camera data plus 3D lidar data.
  - It became an industry standard. Customers included General Motors, Toyota and Stantec.
  - For the first few years the company did only autonomous driving and a few robotics use cases.
- **2019-2020, government:**
  - The future of AI applications was unclear, so Scale moved to government, where applicability was high.
  - It built data engines for geospatial, satellite and overhead imagery. This fueled the first AI program of record for the US DoD.
  - He says that technology proved critical years later in the Ukraine conflict.
- **2019 onward, generative AI:**
  - Scale partnered with OpenAI on the first RLHF experiments on top of GPT-2. The models were rudimentary, and "it did not seem like anything to us."
  - The reasoning was simply that OpenAI had smart people and Scale should work with them.
  - Scale worked on InstructGPT, the precursor to ChatGPT.
  - After DALL-E 2 and ChatGPT in 2022, Scale redirected much of the company toward being the data foundry for generative AI.
- **Today:** Scale's data fuels nearly every major LLM effort, including OpenAI, Meta and Microsoft. The ambitions of those labs have exploded, covering agents, complex reasoning, multimodality and multilinguality, and the infrastructure has had to grow to match.

chunks.heading: Data abundance versus scarcity, and what "frontier data" means
chunks.text:
- **Scarcity as a choice:** On "are we going to run out of tokens," he says the industry can choose data abundance or data scarcity. He sees Scale's job as building abundance.
- **The scaling bottleneck:** The key to scaling language models is scaling data. He calls it a fundamental bottleneck on the path from GPT-4 to GPT-10.
- **Easy data is gone:** The easy data (the internet) is largely exhausted. What is needed now is forward data production with high supervisory signal. He calls it frontier data.
- **Quality bar:** Models can no longer learn much from Reddit comments. Frontier data includes:
  - reasoning chains and chain-of-thought from experts (mathematicians, physicists, biologists, chemists, lawyers, doctors)
  - agent workflow data, from enterprise, consumer and coding agents
  - multilingual data across the world's languages
  - multimodal data (video, audio) and the esoteric data types inside enterprises and industry
- **Sources of new tokens:**
  1. The best and brightest minds contributing expertise. He argues improving a model slightly, integrated over all its future uses, is "near infinite impact." Contributors are motivated by money and by fueling AI progress.
  2. Proprietary enterprise and government data. His example: JP Morgan's proprietary data set is 150 petabytes, while GPT-4 was trained on less than one petabyte.
  3. Synthetic data, specifically "hybrid human AI synthetic data": AI does the heavy lifting and human experts contribute reasoning and insight to keep quality and fidelity high.
- **Data production as spice:** He compares data production to spice in Dune, "the lifeblood" of future AI systems.
- **Data capture gap:** Digitization did not capture the data AI needs. Most incumbent vendors never captured the information needed to teach a model.

chunks.heading: Humans plus models: why expert input stays additive
chunks.text:
- **Hybrid framing:** The question is not whether a model beats an unassisted human. It is whether human plus model beats the model alone. He expects that to hold "for a very very very long time."
- **Evidence for complementarity:** Models show odd failures (ROT-13 works but ROT-8 does not, the reversal curse). He reads these as a sign model intelligence differs from biological intelligence.
- **In practice:** Humans critique model outputs, flag factuality and reasoning errors, and guide models through long reasoning chains.
- **Model beating a physician:** Asked whether experts stop adding value once a model beats a doctor on Med-PaLM-style tests, he says never.
- **Why never:**
  - Biological intelligence optimizes over very long time horizons (lifetimes, reproduction) and keeps adjusting long-term goals.
  - Current models are trained on small "nuggets" of intelligence, "a shot glass full of human intelligence," and are bad at sustaining it over long horizons.
  - That quality has to be transferred through data. We lack environments to train models on amorphous long-horizon goals, so he calls it a fundamental limitation.
  - Architectural breakthroughs will help performance dramatically, but he does not expect them to remove it.

chunks.heading: Evals: why measurement is hard and what Scale is building
chunks.text:
- **Role in the loop:** The AI lifecycle is data, then train, then evaluate, then repeat. Evaluation is also how governments, enterprises and labs build trust and confidence.
- **Why it is hard:** Evals are essentially IQ tests for models, which is a fraught philosophical problem, and the practical problems are real too. Academic benchmarks are "fraught with issues," and many models are overfit because the benchmarks leak into training data.
- **GSM1K:** Scale published a held-out math eval, GSM1K, built so it could not appear in training data. Some models performed well, but others did much worse than their reported performance.
- **Answer:** Use human experts and the best minds for expert evaluations to find where models are strong and weak and what the risks are.
- **Transparency:** He wants public leaderboards and rigorous public evaluations. He also wants platforms for governments, enterprises and labs to run constant evaluation.
- **Launch:** Scale is releasing private held-out evals with leaderboards for leading LLMs, rerun every few months.
  - Starting domains are math, coding, instruction following and adversarial capabilities, with more over time.
  - He describes it as "an Olympics for LLMs" but every few months instead of every four years.

chunks.heading: Enterprise and application strategy: self-improvement via data flywheels
chunks.text:
- **GPT-4 timing:** After GPT-4 launched there was an application frenzy (agents and more). He thinks GPT-4 was "a few generations too early" for the thousand flowers to bloom. He expects a trough of disillusionment, then stronger models that enable agents.
- **Flywheel thesis:** The large labs improve through data flywheels: constantly collect new data that improves the model, and constantly evaluate to find weaknesses. He argues every enterprise, government and startup will need that self-improvement loop in its applications, and that it is hard to build.
- **Scale's product:** Scale's GenAI platform is the groundwork for building these loops. For enterprises Scale works at the platform level, not by building the applications.
- **Enterprise data problem:**
  - Not all data is equal. Frontier data can be "10,000 times more valuable" than run-of-the-mill data.
  - The work is compressing a mountain of scattered data into the high-quality subset that can fine-tune or train models for differentiated performance.
- **Government (Donovan):**
  - Scale is launching agentic features in Donovan, an "AI staff officer" application that plugs into whichever model the customer prefers.
  - He says valuable government agent use cases are often boring: writing reports, filling out forms, moving information between places.

chunks.heading: The raise and ecosystem positioning
chunks.text:
- Strategic investors named include AMD, Cisco, Intel and Meta.
- Reasoning:
  - Scale is infrastructure and aims to serve the entire AI ecosystem.
  - The strategics span infrastructure providers (Intel, AMD), industry players (Meta, Cisco) and the stack layers of infrastructure, technology and application.
  - The goal is a broader industry view of what future data needs are.
  - Tens of billions, maybe hundreds of billions, are going into compute. Real investment is needed in data production too.

chunks.heading: Contrarian views: AGI as curing cancer, and staying nimble
chunks.text:
- **AGI path:** He believes the path to AGI looks more like curing cancer than developing one vaccine. It means solving many small problems with little leverage from one to the next, and building separate data flywheels for each capability.
- **Limited generalization:** He sees little positive transfer between capabilities. As he understands it, training on lots of video does not help text problems much, and vice versa. So each capability area needs its own flywheel.
- **World-model claims:** He calls Nvidia's world-model story a "great narrative" without strong scientific evidence yet.
- **Societal read:** He says this is a bullish case for society adapting, because progress will be consistent and slow for a long time.
- **Multimodal launches:** On the OpenAI and Google multimodal releases, he notes the labs converged on similar demos. He also notes multimodal data is scarce for personal agents. He was disappointed because the industry mainly needs smarter models, a GPT-5-class jump, to unlock more applications.
- **CEO mindset:** The market looks crowded, but the technology is at "one 100th or one 1,000th" of its future capability. What he thinks about most is nimbleness, so Scale keeps adapting as the technology develops.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how Scale became the data infrastructure layer for AI by focusing on a base primitive (data) that must scale as the industry scales. He gives founder advice: start before a trend is cool, avoid crowded categories, don't build ahead of the technology, and ignore small-TAM objections. He also shares his outlook on multimodality, proprietary data and enterprise AI.

chunks.heading: Starting scale: the data bottleneck and the infrastructure thesis
chunks.text:
- Alexandr grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, with two parents who were weapons physicists at Los Alamos National Lab.
- At MIT, around when AlphaGo and TensorFlow launched, he built side projects: a facial-emotion detector and a fridge camera that told him when roommates took his food.
- His insight: models are "sponges for data." The facial-recognition model and the fridge camera were the exact same algorithm, fed different data.
- He concluded the bottleneck for AI was not the algorithm. It was data and its availability.
- Starting thesis for Scale: AI needed an infrastructure platform "like an AWS or Stripe," focused specifically on data.
- Seven years in, Scale had been at the forefront of each major AI wave:
  - Autonomous vehicles (General Motors, Toyota, many startups).
  - The first major US government AI programs of record.
  - Large language models (working with OpenAI since 2019, plus Meta, Microsoft, Character and others).
- He says the industry has progressed much faster than he predicted a decade ago.

chunks.heading: What makes a company infrastructure: boil it down to primitives
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says the key trait of an infrastructure company is deep focus on primitives.
- His example is AWS. A "stroke of genius" was boiling cloud computing down to the core APIs: EC2 (compute on demand) and S3 (storage on demand).
- He sees four primitives behind every advanced AI model:
  - Compute: high-end GPUs and accelerators.
  - Data: what models train on and learn concepts from.
  - Talent: very scarce, high-end AI talent.
  - Algorithms: now broadly open-sourced (Transformers), so least differentiated.
- Test for a great infrastructure opportunity:
  - It is a base primitive with no way around it ("you can't build AI without data fundamentally").
  - It has to scale exponentially as the whole field scales.
- Scaling laws (found by OpenAI around 2018-2019): every 10x increase in model size gives a predictable performance increase.
  - GPT-2 was about 2 billion parameters.
  - GPT-4 is reported at roughly 1.5 to 2 trillion (sparse), almost a thousand times larger.
  - Companies are on record seeking roughly another 100x in compute.
- He calls this a rare ~100,000x scale-up of anything in human history.

chunks.heading: Advice for founders starting AI companies
chunks.text:
- Most successful companies start long before a trend becomes cool, so the head start is what lets them win when it does.
- Crowded AI categories are hard. He cites AI-powered sales, with "probably literally 50 if not more" companies, where even a great team ends up marginally better than competitors.
- He references Peter Thiel's Zero to One: the best capitalists skate away from competition. His advice: pick unpopular areas where AI can have a large impact.
- Don't build ahead of what the technology can do. Models still hallucinate, are weak at reasoning, and tool use doesn't work well.
- "I wouldn't start a company assuming these problems will go away." They might, but that is a lot to risk the whole company on.

chunks.heading: Naivety, small TAMs and irrational conviction
chunks.text:
- Alexandr believes there is "a huge premium to naivety." Approaching an industry with a blank slate, without knowing what makes it hard, lets you do what entrenched players can't. He cites AI labs and Elon Musk's companies.
- Founders should not be dogmatic about the "HBS business case" framework.
- Scale's early fundraising got a lot of "nos." Investors said it wasn't important or big enough, or the TAM was small.
- The counterpoint he took on: the TAM was small, as it was for every important company at the start. What mattered was that the market was growing super fast.
- The case for investing in Scale rested on believing the AI industry would grow many-fold. Founders need that kind of early conviction.
- Midjourney example: it looked weird and unlike a business at first, and is now bigger than most SaaS businesses despite an unusual user experience.
- He says the rules are being rewritten. No business-school graduate would have advised OpenAI to spend hundreds of millions to a billion dollars training GPT-4 speculatively with no business plan.

chunks.heading: Predictions: multimodality, proprietary data and enterprise AI
chunks.text:
- Multimodality will keep improving: images, audio, and especially video. Models will see and understand what humans see, enabling an always-present AI assistant.
- Models will go deeper into proprietary data:
  - Today's models train mostly on internet data.
  - He says 99.99% of data is private and proprietary. Example: how few of your phone photos end up on the public internet.
  - Enterprises and governments will customize models through training, fine-tuning or RAG on their own data.
- Enterprise opportunity, top down:
  - Roughly $27 trillion of US GDP, of which about $15-16 trillion is services.
  - Healthcare is the biggest bucket, financial services second.
- Healthcare example: care is reactive because of a shortage of medical talent. His vision is a healthcare AI buddy that constantly monitors you and catches problems early.
- Labor: this is one of the first technologies to pressure knowledge work. The shift is from being "the computer" to being a user of computers who orchestrates AI systems.

chunks.heading: Open questions: misuse and the global AI race
chunks.text:
- He says the field has high uncertainty on several fronts.
- Misuse: he subscribes less to the AI-doom view and more to the view that bad people will use AI to do bad things, with real risk in bioweapons and cyber attacks.
- Global race: ChatGPT was the "firing gun" of something like a modern space race.
  - Mistral (France) has produced top open-source models.
  - The UAE and Saudi Arabia have been aggressive, announcing large compute clusters. The UAE has trained multiple LLMs, including large Arabic ones.
  - China has bought roughly $5 billion worth of high-end Nvidia GPUs.
- He says he doesn't know how this plays out long term.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how Scale AI grew from solving AI's data bottleneck into a 700-person company. He covers keeping startup energy while growing, hiring people who care, and why ambition shapes outcomes. He also argues AI should be applied through concrete, near-term use cases.

chunks.heading: Building a company that makes AI useful: the data bottleneck and foot-by-foot progress
chunks.text:
- Alexandr's founding insight came from trying to apply AI to a small, concrete problem. In 2016 he tried to build a camera inside his refrigerator to detect roommates stealing his food, and after weeks of effort found it nearly impossible because there was no way to get the data to build it.
- He concluded that data was the fundamental bottleneck for AI. Most of the community was fixated on far-out outcomes ("all powerful AI systems"), while few focused on the step-by-step work needed for AI to have real impact.
- He positions scale as the company doing that unglamorous work: turning raw data into something useful so ambitious organizations can use AI to solve important problems.
- He argues you don't need to "squint" to see near-term uses of AI: more efficient energy use against climate change, and scaling medical care beyond the limited number of doctors.

chunks.heading: Customer use cases that show the range of the product
chunks.text:
Alexandr walks through three examples to show the technology applies across fields, none of them a "big bad AI":

- **Ukraine:** scale ran AI algorithms on satellite imagery to map major cities (Kyiv, Dnipro, Mariupol) and track damage building by building, day by day. The goal was to redirect humanitarian aid, medical attention and infrastructure projects to wherever damage occurred. They worked with both the US and Ukrainian governments and open-sourced much of the data. He was told this granularity had not existed before.
- **E-commerce:** Instacart is a customer. Scale helps retailers build an "encyclopedic understanding" of their products and the data to feed it, so recommendation algorithms act like a "digital salesperson" who knows the products in and out and guides the buyer from limited information.
- **Medical:** with MIT Media Lab and Stanford, scale analyzed dermatological data to automatically identify skin conditions. He cites roughly a 10x global shortage of doctors, which medical schools cannot close.

chunks.heading: Intelligence machines vs. learning machines
chunks.text:
- He argues modern AI systems are "intelligence machines, not learning machines." They reach impressive capability but hit a cap, and they learn slowly, needing the biggest data centers and huge energy.
- A child by contrast is a learning machine, many orders of magnitude more efficient, who starts knowing nothing and quickly reasons about almost anything.
- He compares today's AI to industrial-revolution machines: purpose-specific tools that beat people at one task, while people can do everything else. The question is how to harness them to raise human creativity.
- Example: movies. Low-budget films still cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars and big Marvel films cost hundreds of millions, so studio executives decide what gets made. AI automating visual effects, editing and special effects could deliver comparable visuals for a small fraction of the cost, letting almost anyone make movies.
- On Marvel: only Marvel could afford to weave a 20-movie story arc. At one hundredth of the cost, many people could become "Kevin Feige-like" architects of broad story arcs.
- Waste example (raised by the host, which he affirms): any business selling physical goods faces the problem of knowing who will buy what and where. Amazon solved it with accurate forecasting so products sit close to the doorstep for two-hour delivery. He says this needs to be rolled out across the whole economy.

chunks.heading: Getting big without getting bad: hire missionaries, not mercenaries
chunks.text:
- Scale was about 700 people at the time. Alexandr cites the original iPod, which took roughly six months to release, as a sign of how fast small focused teams move.
- He describes early-startup energy as "reaching into a nuclear reactor": otherworldly, powerful, hard to define, and something to keep as the company grows.
- His number one rule is to "hire people who give a [damn]." In a small company, only people who deeply care will join. As a company gets successful, recruiting turns into "a college admissions office," selecting the most impressive and diverse applicants rather than those who "live and die for the mission."
- His framing: bring on "missionaries versus mercenaries." The company is made of the people you bring in, so fervent, caring people are the foundation.
- He wants a high density of people who are both passionate and competent. He cites Apple, where very small teams built products that shaped the future.

chunks.heading: Optimism and ambition shape reality
chunks.text:
- Scale's belief, in two phrasings: "optimism shapes reality" and "ambition shapes reality."
- Evidence he gives: a histogram of marathon finishing times is jagged, not a smooth curve, with clusters just under each hour or half-hour mark, because people accomplish what they set their mind to. After the four-minute mile was broken, many others broke it.
- Application: create a culture where people dream big. "Thinking small is a self-fulfilling prophecy," so you may achieve small things but never big ones.

chunks.heading: Keeping innovation alive as the company grows
chunks.text:
- Maintenance trap: once a company has a successful core business, there is "massive temptation" to only maintain or incrementally improve it. Startups have no choice but to build from nothing; larger companies must deliberately keep a building mindset and consider other ideas, not dismiss them as "small little things" next to the core.
- Idea rooms: some people and small groups create resonance, where one idea builds on another "like a snowball rolling down a hill." This needs the right preconditions: people feel safe and excited. His advice: keep trying to find those rooms, and when you find one "never let go of it."
- Tip for people inside non-innovative companies: "there's nothing more seductive than the invitation to think bigger." Give people a roadmap to a bigger framing. Example: with an agriculture company, frame the problem as the coming global food shortage and ask how satellite data, robotics and better technology could meet it, and you will be surprised by the ingenuity that follows.

chunks.heading: Career advice and long-term vision
chunks.text:
- He says people think about careers backwards, optimizing a resume (companies, tenure, promotions). The better question: what did you actually build, and what products would not exist without you in the trenches driving the vision and execution?
- He echoes the Steve Jobs biography idea of the opportunity to do your "life's work," and notes most people never leave a dent in the universe, partly because they don't think in those terms.
- His 5 to 10 year outlook: not Terminator-like AI taking jobs, but meaningful progress on the world's biggest problems: the food crisis, climate change and sustainability, scaled medical care, geopolitical stability, and simpler tasks like finding things on the internet. He calls himself "a big optimist" that AI gives humanity a real chance against these problems.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang explains how he spotted data as the missing pillar of AI after seeing AWS and Stripe become platforms for their eras. He shares lessons on ambition, hiring and people, acting under uncertainty, and a costly early mistake of neglecting a key customer.

chunks.heading: Why data decides AI quality ("data is the new code")
chunks.text:
Alexandr's core thesis for Scale AI is that "better data results in better AI." He argues the performance of machine learning systems will be dictated by the datasets they are trained on far more than by the code written to power them.
- He frames the raw ingredients of ML as compute, data and human insight. Annotated data is produced by mixing raw data with human insight.
- Scale started with data labeling and annotation, first in autonomous vehicles. It then expanded into e-commerce, financial services, government and large tech platforms.
- Over time it added data management and algorithms, such as document automation and e-commerce AI, on top of annotation.
- He says most industries have lots of data that is not "AI ready": not annotated, not cleaned. Old AI use cases like ads, search and social ranking have "natural labels" from user clicks, and most other industries do not.
- Step one at Scale is turning huge pools of unstructured data into well-labeled, unbiased, high-quality datasets.
- Where data is hard to collect (privacy, missing sensors), he points to synthetic data and data augmentation. These combine real-world data with diverse, realistic synthetic data.

chunks.heading: How he spotted the opportunity at 19
chunks.text:
Alexandr was studying AI at MIT in the year TensorFlow and AlphaGo launched. A side project, a camera in his fridge to catch roommates stealing food, made the point viscerally: "the algorithm is only as good as the data that it's trained on." He gave up on it in about two hours because the data needed would have been astronomical.
- He saw few people focused on the data problem.
- His pattern recognition came from platform companies: "what aws has done for the cloud or what stripe has done for payments," there was an opportunity to do for AI.
- He admits he "didn't have all the answers" and did not know the idea would become this big. The fundamentals justified exploring it.
- For the first years the company just focused on data labeling and annotation. Only later did it look up and realize it could expand into many more industries.

chunks.heading: Going full time without a big decision
chunks.text:
Alexandr says he wishes he could claim he was fully convicted, but the reality was less dramatic.
- He put the work on hold for finals and final projects. When summer started he had nothing else to do, so he worked on it in earnest.
- Over the summer the company gained enough momentum that "there's kind of no option but to just keep going."
- His advice: the mental barrier of sacrificing your current life feels huge. Avoid that false dichotomy and put yourself in situations with freedom and flexibility to explore, then see whether you gain momentum.
- He also says that early on it helps to "dare to dream big" even when a big outcome is only a pipe dream.

chunks.heading: Ambition, building and the "ambition shapes reality" value
chunks.text:
He argues that going from an idea in your head to something real is empowering, even when it does not always work. It gives you the sense that you can will things from your mind into reality.
- Scale has an internal value called "ambition shapes reality." His claim: an ambitious project and an unambitious one can take the same amount of work, so dream big and then build.
- He collects examples of limits being broken once someone shows it is possible, such as the four-minute mile.

chunks.heading: Training annotators: AI helping humans, and an internal edtech system
chunks.text:
Alexandr describes two principles for working with human annotators on specialized data (for example cilantro vs parsley stems, or melanoma on skin).
- Give trained people as much leverage as possible. ML systems do as much of the work as they can, and humans spend effort on the edge cases and high-judgment work that give top quality.
- Treat training as an education problem. Scale tracks the nuances and edge cases of each data problem. It monitors which ones each annotator handles well and which trip them up, then proactively serves them materials and examples. He calls it "one of the more interesting edtech systems out there."
- He believes all future AI systems will depend heavily on human insight, at minimum for oversight.

chunks.heading: Bias, responsible AI and data privacy
chunks.text:
He says responsible AI depends on high-quality, representative data: "you are what you eat."
- Example: with the MIT Media Lab on medical imaging, Scale found far more light-skinned than dark-skinned images. It added data for under-represented classes, using real-world data, data augmentation or synthetic data, and significantly de-biased the model outcomes.
- He calls bias a hard problem with no architectural silver bullet. It comes down to the "nitty gritty" of knowing what your dataset looks like, spotting bias ahead of time, fixing it and repeating.
- Customers often sit on huge troves of data but lack tooling to find the "needles in the haystack." Scale's Nucleus product lets them search their own labeled data for more samples of an under-represented class.
- His philosophy is continual improvement of algorithms through continual improvement of data.
- On privacy, he says the community must shift from "however I can get the data, I will use it" to collecting data responsibly. Providers should understand how their data is used, and it should be collected in a de-biased way and in sufficient amounts. He accepts this will make some AI harder to build, and says Scale helps customers do it.

chunks.heading: Where he sees AI opportunity by 2032
chunks.text:
Alexandr says we are in the "golden age of AI." His analogy is "software eats the world": take any industry or problem and ask how machine learning, applied properly, could make it far more efficient.
- Examples he cites: fraud and transaction flows in finance (Brex, PayPal, Square), automating global trade workflows (Flexport), driver-assistance systems, and insurance claims processing ("10x more efficient").
- He highlights four areas for aspiring founders:
  - **Science:** simulating expensive experiments (AlphaFold, fusion simulations) to counter slowing scientific progress.
  - **Metaverse and AR:** needs fine-grained understanding of the world, a very hard ML problem.
  - **Government, defense and intelligence:** warfare is shifting to digital, and he argues democracies need best-in-class technology.
  - **Broad automation:** AI spreading across every industry.
- He thinks human-like AI with real judgment is far off. He points out that OCR and document processing still do not work fully reliably.
- The nearer-term issue is AI shaping how humans think (content ranking, chatbot "friends" for children). He frames political polarization partly as a "data distribution problem" in ML content systems.

chunks.heading: Lessons from running the company
chunks.text:
- **People matter most:** The hardest and most rewarding part has been building the team and getting people to buy into the mission, covering team, investors and customers. If he could tell his earlier self one thing, people matter "10x more" than he thought.
- **Never be paralyzed:** Moments of self-doubt are part of the journey. "It is not okay to be paralyzed." Even the worst action beats no action, because there are no one-way doors and action gives you information to course correct.
- **Customer-centricity:** One of Scale's first large customers took a big bet on a "janky" early product. Scale lost focus on them while chasing other big customers, stopped solving their problem, and they left. It made him question whether Scale had a business. The lesson was to always stay focused on customers and make them ecstatic. He is grateful it happened early.
- **Partner, don't just sell:** On nuanced issues like privacy and bias, he works with customers as partners rather than selling a finished product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang explains Scale AI as a data refinery for machine learning, where machines do the bulk of labeling and humans correct errors. He argues infrastructure providers must be reliable like AWS, that great people differ exponentially from good ones, and that products must improve every day or decay. Much of the episode is AI-future opinion rather than business playbook.

chunks.heading: Why Scale AI exists: data is the bottleneck for machine learning
chunks.text:
- Alexandr describes machine learning as a subset of AI where programs learn tasks that normally need human judgment by being fed lots of data.
- He frames AI as a "once in a generation shift in technology," comparable to the advent of computing, because it is an enabler of things that previously had to be done by humans.
- The idea came while he studied machine learning at MIT. He had product ideas but hit an "elephant in the room" problem: how to get the data to build the models.
- Scale's stated mission is "to accelerate the development of AI applications."
- He left MIT after about a year, bored by the slower pace of school. He had earlier worked at Quora for a couple of years, having been recruited through anonymous online coding competitions in high school.

chunks.heading: What Scale does and how the data pipeline works
chunks.text:
- Scale is a "data refinery." Customers send raw data such as camera images. Scale labels it so models know what they should be doing, for example outlining people, cars and lane markings in a self-driving image.
- Customers named as examples: Waymo and Uber.
- The pipeline is mostly machines, with humans on top:
  - Scale's own classical computer vision and ML models do a first pass (for example drawing and tracking boxes over time).
  - A large team of well-trained humans spots and corrects errors, mainly where the models are uncertain.
  - He says Scale uses "more sophisticated filters" than a simple confidence cutoff.
  - Accurate data goes back to the customer, who retrains their models. He calls it "a wonderful cycle."
- Positioning: Scale is "an infrastructure layer for machine learning globally." It takes the data problem off customers' plates so they can focus on building models.
- Team size at the time: about 150 people, mostly in the San Francisco Bay Area.
- Total raised: over $100 million, with Founders Fund named as an investor.

chunks.heading: Quality as an infrastructure promise
chunks.text:
- Scale takes responsibility for data quality. Customers can audit all the data.
- He compares it to AWS: infrastructure providers must be extremely reliable, because many people build on top of them. Reliability is what lets customers trust the layer beneath them.
- On bias and weird model behavior, he says the cause can usually be traced to the data. The fix is large, diverse, representative datasets that fill gaps and make models more robust over time.
- Example he gives: face unlock failing across similar-looking faces comes down to what was in the training data.

chunks.heading: Why companies keep their data private, and the open-source tradeoff
chunks.text:
- Companies train on separate datasets, and he sees that as reasonable. Data and models are their IP, which preserves the incentive to build novel, valuable things.
- He ties this to free-market logic: many parties running in different directions produce variety, versus a planned economy with efficiency but low variance.
- Open datasets do exist in research. He credits ImageNet (Stanford's Fei-Fei Li and her lab) as the large dataset that kicked off the deep learning wave.
- He says shared infrastructure that a large community builds on is "very valuable."

chunks.heading: Lidar vs cameras: use multiple sensors
chunks.text:
- Scale published a blog post on lidar versus cameras, based on seeing a lot of both kinds of data.
- Lidar strengths: an accurate, reliable 3D map, and it works in the dark because it makes its own light.
- Lidar weakness: snow, fog and smoke reflect its lasers and distort the model.
- Cameras: the best computer vision models are about 99% accurate, which is not enough for driving where rare failures matter.
- His conclusion: use both. Sensors with different strengths and weaknesses can cover each other to reach the extreme reliability needed.
- He says real vehicles from companies like Waymo and Cruise combine them, and many still lean heavily on lidar.

chunks.heading: Where AI goes next, and why automation creates work
chunks.text:
- Self-driving timeline: he would not give a precise year but expects it within roughly ten years. He thinks regulation won't be that hard, citing precedent from airplane autopilot.
- He argues the "AI replaces humans" narrative is far from reality. His example is ATMs: bank teller jobs grew because ATMs expanded banking, brought in new customers, and let tellers move to higher-value work like mortgages and credit.
- Trucking example: long-haul automation targets the boring, arduous stretches in a market short of drivers (median driver age around 50). Current drivers can move to higher-value short trips, such as warehouse-to-meeting-point runs.
- Automation arrives first where there is an acute problem today, then makes existing jobs higher value.
- Near-term "boring" opportunities he names: paper form processing, email reply suggestions, and medical imaging (X-rays, ultrasounds, scans). The World Health Organization reportedly shows roughly a 10x global shortage of doctors, so automating first-pass reads and marking problem zones has huge value.
- He also names adaptive education as an obvious application, and notes the Apple Watch fall detection as an example of useful "boring" ML.
- He is skeptical of near-term general AI. He says "Moore's law is gonna be dead," quantum computing is far away, and it is unclear that infinite compute would produce general AI.

chunks.heading: Principles for building a company
chunks.text:
- On talent, he tweeted that there is a huge "band gap" between good and great people. Great people are "clever, determined, fight hard, more loyal in hardship, and strategic."
- His five-step recipe for building something great:
  1. Build something you care about.
  2. Find users and listen to them.
  3. Improve it every single day (the step he says people leave out).
  4. Find people who inspire you and convince them to work with you.
  5. Repeat.
- On improvement: a product is either getting better or getting worse. If you stop, a competitor improves and your users get used to an average product.
- On startup ideas, he tweeted that watching YC demo days showed many ideas derivative of hot financings, and that "one of the unhip ideas will be the big company." On large YC batch sizes, he thinks a hundred is fine because it is "Black Swan farming," and takes "as many as it takes."
- Long-term thinking: he praised Quora's Adam D'Angelo for thinking extremely long term, calling it a competitive advantage in an ecosystem where most people are short-sighted.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang argues AI depends on humans because algorithms need data and good data needs human judgment and values. He explains how he saw the data bottleneck at MIT and founded Scale AI around it. He frames AI as a tool that automates repetitive work so people can focus on creative problems.

chunks.heading: Why AI depends on humans and will not replace them
chunks.text:
- Alexandr argues AI "has always been and will always be dependent on humans." He says this belief is part of why he started Scale.
- His core setup: algorithms need data, and data needs humans.
- Expert humans are often required to keep data accurate. Only humans understand the context and nuance needed to annotate data correctly before it is fed to algorithms.
- Humans teach algorithms what to do. They make the decisions and guide the system, and the AI learns from that and repeats it.
- He sees AI as a tool, not something to fear. It is a "supercharger" for humanity: where AI is better than humans, it makes humans better.

chunks.heading: Why Scale was started: data is the bottleneck for AI
chunks.text:
- Alexandr studied AI at MIT in 2016 and noticed almost no one outside of coursework was building anything with AI. Mechanical engineers built catapults, electrical engineers built robots, and computer science students built apps.
- He concluded data was the missing piece: "Bad data or lack of data leads to bad AI." Data cannot be treated as an afterthought.
- A personal experiment made it concrete. He put a camera in his fridge to predict grocery restocking. He could not generate enough data alone to make the algorithms succeed (it did reveal his roommate was stealing his food).
- The conclusion was that building large, high-quality datasets to power every AI application would be a central problem for AI. That was the motivation for Scale.
- Scale's premise: high-quality data, which produces reliable AI outcomes, requires human insight and guidance.

chunks.heading: Teaching AI human values and intentions
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says AI needs humans to teach it individual values, push it toward thoughtful outcomes, and keep human intent and values aligned with the AI.
- "Machines make mistakes." Humans have to teach them and push them toward telling the truth.
- Teaching intentions and values is how AI ends up with fair, ethical outcomes in line with human values.
- Continuous alignment with human intent will always require humans, and human ideas and creativity can matter more with AI power behind them.
- Real-world problems have a long tail and there are always "unknown unknowns," so humans can never be fully removed from the AI development lifecycle.

chunks.heading: Human-in-the-loop example: chatbots in 2016
chunks.text:
- When chatbots took off in 2016, just as Scale was starting, Alexandr says people assumed a fully automated system was impossible. Conversations can take many paths, and it is hard to build AI that handles all of them.
- Chatbots work because humans behind them make a decision once, and the bot repeats it again and again.
- His takeaway: it is impossible for AI to improve or change without human involvement.

chunks.heading: What AI automates first
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says the first things AI automates are not what people expect. It is not the tasks humans consider simplest, but the areas "where we have the most data."
- His example is weather. Forecasting is hard because tiny factors can have huge effects (the butterfly effect) and there is far more data than any person can understand. AI can analyze those vast oceans of data and already gives very accurate short-term predictions, including for critical storms and floods.
- He says the brightest minds in AI are focused on positive use cases, not on building replacements for humans. They build tools that save human time and energy so people can focus on what humans uniquely solve.

chunks.heading: Healthcare and drug discovery
chunks.text:
- Alexandr cites the Association of American Medical Colleges: the US could face a shortage of between 38,000 and 124,000 physicians by 2034.
- Healthcare is full of repetitive tasks suited to AI. Patients generate blood tests, lab results, X-rays and more, and doctors analyze all of it to make decisions.
- AI can proactively analyze that data and cross-reference it against past cases. It can flag that something is wrong long before a doctor would and alert the doctor if it needs attention.
- Doctors stay integral, but diagnosis takes less time. This lets them serve more patients.
- In drug discovery, AI processes trial data, patient data and protein simulations to guide a more efficient process for finding new drugs and compounds. He says recent advances have sped up the scientific process by letting teams process more data than ever.

chunks.heading: Scale's Ukraine satellite imagery work
chunks.text:
- Alexandr points to the Russia-Ukraine war as a real-world example. AI can assess satellite imagery quickly and accurately so Ukrainian forces can respond faster.
- Scale used its platform for damage assessment in key war-affected areas. It analyzed more than 2,000 square kilometers of Ukraine and identified more than 370,000 buildings, including thousands not available in other datasets.
- The focus was Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipro. Scale provided some data directly to the government and users, and made data publicly available to the wider AI community.
- Uses he describes: change detection (algorithms monitor imagery continuously and alert a human when they see movement or change), resource allocation, and tracking farmland and agricultural damage in real time, since Ukraine is a major food supplier.

chunks.heading: Human-led AI and creativity
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says AI will automate repetitive tasks that do not require continuous human decision or creativity. That frees time to explore new ideas.
- He believes it lets people be more creative and idea-focused, embracing "the generative aspects of human nature" so they can move faster with ideas and build better solutions to the biggest problems.
- His conclusion: "human-led AI is the way forward."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang explains that after interviewing every Scale offer, he screens for two things: caring about the company's mission and caring about work in general. He warns against becoming a credential brand, argues recruiting should feel like courtship, and shares his interview questions for spotting obsession.

chunks.heading: Hiring for "giving a shit" over credentials
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says that when he interviews, he mainly screens for one thing: "giving a shit." At the time of writing, Scale had hired more than 200 people, and for a long time he personally interviewed everyone who got an offer.
- He wrote the memo to the company before the team grew from roughly 75 to 150.
