- He splits the screen into two parts: the candidate gives a shit about Scale (its mission, product and problem), and gives a shit about their work in general.
- His reasoning: giving a shit does not guarantee great work, but without it good work is guaranteed not to happen.

chunks.heading: Why caring about the company's mission is critical
chunks.text:
- Alexandr argues there is "no future" if you hire people who do not identify with the mission, product and problem. The company becomes "an undifferentiated crowd of uninspired people" with no shot at a generational company.
- He says this criterion will only become more important as the company grows.
- Early on, nobody joins a startup for credentials because nobody knows it. As the company grows, more people interview for the brand rather than the substance.

chunks.heading: Avoiding becoming a credential instead of a cult
chunks.text:
- A scary outcome for him is Scale becoming "a credential rather than a cult," like Harvard or MIT, where people attend to signal that they are smart or prestigious.
- Growing companies often miss this effect. They see far more top-of-funnel and find it easier to recruit raw numbers, but the ROI of each hire drops dramatically.
- The end state resembles a university: constant churn of smart but uninvolved people who stay a few years and never dive deep enough to do meaningful work.
- He says that unless you actively fight it, it will happen.

chunks.heading: Recruiting as courtship, not admissions
chunks.text:
- A recruiting team that looks like a college admissions office is "certain death for a startup." Sifting a swarm of homogeneous candidates only yields a "higher credentialed homogeneous soup."
- Recruiting done right "looks more like courtship": you need a spark, sometimes preceded by months of convincing and pursuit.
- The target is people you would be willing to spend every waking moment with, since there will be many long nights if things go right.

chunks.heading: Screening for obsession in general
chunks.text:
- Fervor for the company can be faked in an interview. Alexandr's check is whether the person has been deeply obsessed with something before. If not, it is a bad bet that the company will be the first.
- His line of questioning:
  - What's the hardest you've ever worked on something?
  - How many hours were you working a week?
  - Why did you work so hard? Why did you care?
  - When were you the most unmotivated in your life?
  - What's the thing you're the most proud of?
  - Do you think it was worth it?
- His test: "For an obsessed person, it's always worth it."

chunks.heading: Culture is the company, not the cosmetics
chunks.text:
- He says most people don't give a shit. His example: the common pattern for engineers at big companies of coming in at 11am and leaving at 4pm. He argues you cannot work 5 hours a day and give a shit, so very little meaningful work gets done there, which he admits is slight hyperbole.
- He calls conflating culture with cosmetics one of the worst trends in Silicon Valley. Flexible hours, open desks, office design, no dress code and perks tell you nothing meaningful beyond how comfortable a company is spending money.
- His conclusion: "The company is the culture."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A short vision essay arguing that most human wants go unexpressed and unrealized because the world is a maze of obstacles. Muse is pitched as a general-manager-like AI that draws out what you want and handles the execution. The thesis is that no one knows what people will want once everyone's agency is switched on.

chunks.heading: Why Alexandr is building Muse: unspoken wants
chunks.text:
- Alexandr's starting premise: "Most people never say what they want." People want "fiercely and constantly" (more time with family, overcoming social anxiety, eating healthier, opening a bakery, building an app, finding calm) but rarely express those wants, and more rarely see them come true.
- His claim: "When we can't name our dreams, we mostly can't reach them."
- He frames every unrealized want as "a quiet tragedy of human potential."

chunks.heading: Why dreams die: friction, not lack of desire
chunks.text:
- Alexandr describes the world as "a maze of forms and gatekeepers and schedules and obstacles."
- Most dreams "die by a thousand paper cuts long before they are said aloud."
- They die in "the not-knowing-where-to-start and in the phone calls never made."
- The bottleneck he identifies is getting started and executing the logistics, not wanting.

chunks.heading: The product vision: a second mind that acts as a general manager
chunks.text:
- He imagines every person having "a second mind beyond their own": a general manager whose whole job is to find out what you want and make sure it happens.
- It hears a half-formed sentence such as "I feel like there's something more I could be doing" and helps fill in the blanks.
- It is not a genie. It says, "This is the thing you've been dreaming of your whole life. Let's go get it. Here's how."
- What it does:
  - Builds a plan.
  - Sends the email.
  - Makes the phone call.
  - Finds the funding.
  - Keeps you on schedule.
  - Clears the way and solves the problems it can.
- The goal is that "the wanting and the dreaming" is all that's left for the human.

chunks.heading: The bet: unlocking everyone's agency
chunks.text:
- Alexandr argues that "we have no idea what people will want."
- Until now the world has been shaped by "the small number of fanatics" who found a way to make their wants real.
- Humanity has never been seen "with every single person's agency fully switched on."
- The premise: eight billion people who "just need to write their dream down in order to get started making it happen."
- The input he wants Muse to require is minimal: write the dream down.

chunks.heading: Muse's mission
chunks.text:
- Stated purpose: "we built Muse to help people build the world they want."
- The product is positioned as an agent that turns stated desires into executed outcomes, serving everyone and not only highly driven people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang reflects on founding Scale in 2016. He argues for taking risks while you are most risk-seeking, minimizing regret, and working extremely hard because learning compounds super-linearly. Since startup idea returns follow a power law, he says to compress ideas to MVPs and move fast.

chunks.heading: Minimizing regret and taking risk while risk-seeking
chunks.text:
- Alexandr frames his career choices as "minimizing my regret," a concept from decision theory and machine learning, rather than a plan to start a startup.
- In December 2015, as an MIT freshman, he interviewed broadly for engineering and ML roles (Deepmind, Snapchat Research, Opendoor, Stripe). He felt aimless because no offer felt irrefusable and none felt like a growth opportunity after working at a few mid-stage startups.
- Opendoor CEO Eric Wu gave him the key framing: people get more risk-averse with age (marriage, house, kids), so "today, you're the most risk-seeking you'll ever be. So, if there's a risk today that you aren't willing to take, then you might never end up taking that risk."
- That conversation convinced him to decline all offers and try to start a company, because he knew he would regret never being an entrepreneur at the perfect time.
- His test for whether you are chasing enough: "if you don't have opportunities you regret not taking, you aren't chasing after enough opportunities." He accepts that some regret is unavoidable given how many opportunities exist and how high-variance outcomes are (he notes Snapchat and Opendoor are doing well).

chunks.heading: Path from side projects to Scale
chunks.text:
- In January 2016, while working at Hudson River Trading (a high-frequency trading firm), he began hacking on side projects.
- He cycled through a couple of ideas over a few months, "consistently learning and iterating," before landing on Scale, which "felt like magic."
- A precursor product, Ava, had an iOS app he built over spring break.
- Scale was started in June 2016. The Product Hunt launch and a TechCrunch article (July 25, 2016) got a very positive response, and growth was rapid afterward.
- Scale is an API for human intelligence; early customers named include Uber, Alphabet, Houzz, and P&G.
- Scale joined Y Combinator over the summer. Alexandr notes YC's pitch for Demo Day as possibly the single best fundraising environment, so summer progress directly makes fundraising easier.

chunks.heading: Hard work compounds super-linearly
chunks.text:
- He concluded before YC that "the amount I learned grew super-linearly with how hard I worked," an economies-of-scale effect on effort.
- Evidence from his own experience: after a few months of 12-hour days at Quora, he went "from a code monkey to a legitimate system architect," despite years of prior coding.
- In early 2016 he juggled 5 graduate CS courses plus side projects, took no breaks, and spent spring break building Ava's iOS app, then flew to SF right after finals.
- He worked 80-100 hour weeks for a full year.
- YC partners told the cohort to always work extremely hard because time in YC is highly leveraged. Paul Buchheit said many consider YC the most productive time of their lives.
- Momentum makes it easier: "if you have a lot of momentum, it's not too difficult to keep grinding even further." He cites Paul Graham's trick for surviving startups: don't stop to think about how tired you are.
- His conclusion: "Hard work consistently seems to trump other factors."

chunks.heading: Idea flood and why speed matters
chunks.text:
- Makers often get ideas faster than they can build them. When the rate of good ideas exceeds build speed, "time becomes the enemy" and you start craving 100-hour weeks.
- Higher execution speed lets you keep up with the flood of ideas.
- Returns on startup ideas follow roughly a power-law distribution, like startup outcomes themselves. A few ideas (examples: Snapchat Stories, Facebook News Feed) overshadow the rest.
- Prioritization tries to find the outsized ideas but cannot be perfect.
- Tactic: compress every idea to an MVP as much as possible and focus on fast execution so a diamond idea isn't passed over.
- At Scale this means a team-wide habit of shipping feature after feature. Examples he cites from 2016: image recognition, audio transcription, a data collection endpoint, and a Python client library.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang recounts starting Scale at 19 after a failed medical-agent idea, spotting that data was the missing piece for training models, and holding conviction while investors dismissed it. He argues AI's bottleneck is now adoption, startups can out-compete incumbents with agents, and vision and ambition become the scarce resources.

chunks.heading: Early path: work at a real company, then explore at school
chunks.text:
- Alexandr grew up in rural Southwest New Mexico, did math and computer science competitions, and knew he wanted to do "really big things" without a clear path.
- A friend into programming pushed him toward the Valley. After high school he took a gap year to work at Cora in Silicon Valley at 19, then went to MIT at 18 (as he states it) and started Scale at 19.
- He calls ages 17 to 19 "drinking from the fire hose."
- Why working at a company mattered: from the outside "you have no idea how companies work," what it looks like to build, iterate, or how groups of people make decisions.
- Why MIT mattered: room to explore what was interesting. He trained his first models there, played with TensorFlow the year it came out, and came up with the idea for Scale.
- He applied to YC after one year at MIT. He values YC for being supportive but also telling founders "when you're being a dumbass."

chunks.heading: Pivoting from a mistimed idea to Scale
chunks.text:
- Alexandr arrived at YC with an AI agent to help people get medical care. He now thinks the idea will ultimately exist (such agents are "very real" today) but that it was the wrong timing.
- After a month or two, Jared Friedman pulled the team aside and said it might not go anywhere. Alexandr calls that "exactly what we need to hear."
- The team went back to the drawing board and thought deeply about where the opportunity was, which led to Scale.
- Lesson: an idea can be right and still be early. Honest outside feedback early saves months.

chunks.heading: Spotting the gap: training data as the missing "button"
chunks.text:
- Training models at MIT required three things: a cloud compute account, code to run, and a dataset.
- Two of the three could be had by "pressing a button" online. For data there was no effective way to get it.
- It felt "incredibly obvious" that the future would be a button you press to get data. That became Scale.
- Method: he found the opportunity by building with the technology and noticing the missing piece, not by following what was hot.
- Investors were skeptical for many years. In the early years data was "very unsexy." Even with great numbers and revenue, VCs asked whether it was a good business and whether it was durable.
- His read: none of those investors had ever trained a model, so they did not get it. The same investors now write think pieces about data being one of AI's biggest business opportunities.

chunks.heading: Conviction and first-principles thinking
chunks.text:
- Successful companies are started "long before the core idea was popular" and "toil in obscurity for years" until the space becomes consensus.
- "You need to develop conviction in a set of beliefs that nobody else agrees with."
- Scale had worked on AI for a decade. He argues you cannot base business decisions on what everyone around you says: "If you go too much with the herd, you will get immensely confused and you will end up nowhere."
- You have to build your own compass for what the future looks like, because everyone else will confuse you.
- He says deep conviction was what let Scale weather "many years of chaos in the market, in the industry, in the people around us."
- Nobody is good at starting a company when they start one. Early investors told him he grew and changed very quickly. "The whole game is how do you develop yourself to continuously improve to get better and learn quickly."

chunks.heading: Why this is the best time to start a company
chunks.text:
- His view: the bottleneck is not model progress but diffusing AI through the world. Even if models never improved, there would be "decades and decades" of upheaval in the economy.
- He calls it "probably a once in a civilization opportunity" for people with vision and ambition.
- Ten years ago, startups were David versus Goliath and had to find a clever angle with far fewer resources. Now, if a startup properly embraces agents and uses their strengths ambitiously, it is more like a "mecha Goliath" against traditional Goliaths and "can easily outcompete."
- Each AI wave has been roughly 10 times bigger than the last: self-driving, then chatbots, then coding agents a few years later. He expects new modalities and form factors that are each dramatically bigger, and thinks the best AI products have not been built yet.
- Advice for picking what to work on: find the exponential with both the steepest curve and the longest runway. Right now he says that is AI progress. The starting point can look boring. When he started Scale, the state of the art was cat detectors in YouTube videos.

chunks.heading: Agentic loops: where he sees the most alpha
chunks.text:
- His view: there is "astronomical opportunity" in agentic looping, meaning building systems that let you spend 1000x or 1 million x more on tokens to drive an outcome in a continuous feedback loop.
- Framing: a company is a set of large-scale feedback loops (get customers, make them happier, they spend more, hire more people, get more customers), with micro-loops inside. Agentic systems can operate and optimize those loops.
- Inside Meta, with the right agentic loop and the right eval or metric for agents to optimize, a swarm of agents can accomplish more than a team of 100 engineers "very, very easily."
- Mechanics: first figure out the metric. Then it comes down to skills, Markdown files, cron jobs, and a goal command. "It's always funny how mundane everything is once you really dig into it."
- Agent coordination is, in his words, one of the most interesting problems today.

chunks.heading: Building a frontier lab and shipping models at Meta
chunks.text:
- After about a year at Meta, he describes a "zero-based build" of a frontier lab after Llama 4 was not on the needed trajectory.
- Timeline he gives: Muse Spark 1 launched within nine months, then two months later came an image product and Muse Spark 1.1 (the transcript renders the name inconsistently as "Meta Spark" and "Moose Spark").
- Talent density was the core bet, because it compounds: the more talented people you have, the more of the most talented people want to join.
- Frontier AI work is research and science, which needs a different mindset and operating model than internet products: more experimentation and scaling. The aim is a lab built like "an organism" that compounds with exponential growth in capabilities, compute, and adoption.
- Product stance: models should not be so expensive that they are rationed to the wealthiest developers. He claims Muse Spark is cheaper than Opus and offered $1,000 in free API credits to the audience.
- Coming from Meta: bigger models, open-source models, and a harness for agentic developers focused on speed, reliability, and extensibility. He expects much innovation above the harness in orchestration and loops.

chunks.heading: Skills, roles, and vision as the scarce resource
chunks.text:
- Systems thinking stays essential because the abstraction layer keeps changing: from writing code, to orchestrating agents, to orchestrating a million and then a trillion agents.
- He calls it a mistake to go all in on "wordcel." Builders need to "shape rotate," plus a deeper philosophical compass on how the world should develop.
- He expects intelligence and agency to become abundant. The scarce resource becomes vision and ambition: a clear view of what the world should look like in five to ten years and the drive to push through "all the crap" to make it happen.
- Agents make that maybe 10x to 100x easier than a decade ago, so builders can dream bigger.
- Builders also have a responsibility to help enterprises and governments adapt and to address biosecurity and cybersecurity risks.
- Debating when superintelligence arrives is "a bit of a waste of time" because powerful models are inevitable.
- Meta's stated view: personal superintelligence for billions of people, and a rise in entrepreneurship from 200 million businesses on Meta's platforms today toward billions, with business agents working alongside personal agents.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alexandr Wang explains why Scale prioritized customer success over sales, let early customers shape the roadmap, and delayed pricing optimization. He argues market growth and ability to dominate matter more than TAM, and that startups die from self-inflicted mistakes rather than competition.

chunks.heading: TAM matters less than growth rate and your odds of dominating it
chunks.text:
- Alexandr argues that TAM "in the traditional sense" barely matters. When Scale raised its Series B, its TAM was not "tens of billions of dollars." It was smaller but growing very quickly.
- What mattered more was that Scale could dominate that market. Because the market was growing fast, the company grew fast along with it.
- A big TAM only means you are playing in an established market. It does not show how likely you are to capture a significant portion of it.
- The two things he looks at: is the market growing quickly, and do you have a real chance to win it.
- TAM estimates are often wrong early:
  - Uber's early pitch deck put its TAM at $4 billion, and the company was about to IPO at $100 billion.
  - Airbnb's TAM at the start was "literally zero," or very small, for home sharing. It is now a $30 billion company.
- Focusing on TAM means you miss the best ideas and ignore the fact that the market you are in is growing and you have a chance to win it.

chunks.heading: Competition: row your own race
chunks.text:
- Alexandr believes in "ignore it and row your own race" over embracing or maniacally monitoring competitors.
- Most startups die by suicide, not competition. His phrasing: "startups die of indigestion, not starvation."
- The real risks are hiring a bunch of the wrong people, which kills culture and productivity, or focusing on the wrong things.
- It is very hard for any business to catch up to a startup with momentum, fast growth and a strong culture. So maximize your own growth rate.
- One caveat: it helps when there is no very threatening incumbent. Competing with Uber and Lyft in ride sharing would be threatening. A "laggier" incumbent is better.

chunks.heading: Invest in customer success before sales
chunks.text:
- Early on, Scale was focused only on growth: get a customer, then go get the next one. Alexandr says he later realized it matters far more in the long run to build a culture where customers are "supremely, supremely happy."
- After the first one or two customers, he argues the next hire should be customer success, not sales.
- Once Scale embedded customer success and customer centricity in its culture, it grew far faster. Happy customers told their friends, and those friends came saying they had heard great things about Scale.
- Customer success becomes a primary acquisition channel through word of mouth. He calls this unintuitive: investing in customer success over sales makes you grow faster, and many of the fastest-growing SaaS companies do it.

chunks.heading: Who to hire for early customer success
chunks.text:
- Early-stage customer success is very hard because everything is breaking, customers have many demands, and the startup moves fast and can look chaotic. The job is to make it seem stable to the customer.
- He would not hire someone from a big company. There, customer success is cookie cutter and sits on a much more stable platform.
- He prefers people with consulting backgrounds (McKinsey, Bain, BCG). They work with Fortune 500 clients who often dislike the consultant and where the service is nebulous.
- They get good at uncertain environments and at building relationships even when seen as the adversary.

chunks.heading: Let early customers drive the roadmap, but dig into the pain
chunks.text:
- Early customers are extremely influential, and Alexandr says you should build a lot of what they ask for.
- The number one startup failure mode he sees is being too "in their head," being principled and philosophical about products and building things nobody wants.
- Pick your first couple of customers very well. They will define the roadmap for a while. Choose ones representative of where the future is going or of a much broader set of customers.
- Question them and understand the pain so you can maybe find a better solution. Still, the roadmap should be dictated more by customers than by anyone else.
- On "customer informed, not customer driven": hear the pain first, dig into it, then reach your own conclusion about the best solution. Focus on pains, not customer-proposed solutions.
- You have only a couple of big, innovative bets (the Henry Ford "faster horse" case). Everything else should be intuitive and "just solves the customer's problem, plain and simple."
- To validate a launched product:
  - Remove onboarding as a risk by teaching customers in person how to use it.
  - Then ask customers directly whether they love it. Usage and revenue metrics can help, but asking is better.
  - A trusting customer success relationship makes customers open with you.

chunks.heading: Don't optimize deal size early; flip to pricing later
chunks.text:
- Early on, the only focus should be customers who "absolutely love you" and will pay, even if not much. Don't over-optimize.
- Scale's path: first deals were "a couple thousand dollars," then hundreds of thousands once it had a sales team, then a couple of million-dollar deals.
- It is hard to predict early how much people will pay. Get in the door, get feedback, get people to use and love it, then optimize pricing, ACVs and revenue.
- He cites Segment: it started as open source, then, once charging, roughly doubled its price on every contract until people said no. He recommends companies do this once they have enough customers to experiment on.
- When Scale flipped the switch:
  - After a handful of happy customers, about three in autonomous vehicles, all innovative companies.
  - After hiring the first sales rep, who was told not to worry about pricing and just land great customers, because Alexandr did not want value extraction before there was enough signal the product was right.
  - Then the rep said they could charge more, and Scale "turned the switch."

chunks.heading: Raising money when early ACVs are small
chunks.text:
- Alexandr says VCs "get it wrong all the time" and miss big winners. He points to Airbnb's YC story and Robinhood's early rounds as examples. Form your own opinion.
- At seed and Series A, what moves a VC most is customers genuinely loving the product, especially in reference calls, more than financials or ACVs.
- You still need a story for the ACV question. Either:
  - Data points showing people will pay much more, or
  - A plan to blanket the market with very low customer acquisition cost.
- Mike Volpi found Scale for its Series B because he heard from customers how much they loved the product.

chunks.heading: Other views: hiring, API companies, ignoring the noise
chunks.text:
- Hardest role to hire: marketing. It moved in a few years from brand and corporate marketing to very technical and metrics-driven, and good marketing is very product-specific, so you need very creative people.
- Admires API companies (Stripe, Twilio, Plaid, Checkr). They grow quickly and become important infrastructure for customers.
- First job advice: join a high-growth startup that is winning. You see what winning looks like, and you get more power and impact, which builds the founder mindset.
- What he wishes he had known: "a lot of people will get it wrong at the start." Nobody knows what you will accomplish, so believe in what you are doing and don't over-rotate on what others tell you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Wang and Zuckerberg explain how Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped a frontier model with a tiny, talent-dense team and committed huge compute before knowing it would work. Wang argues AI product decisions live in model training, internal evals beat public benchmarks, and simple consumer UX wins.

chunks.heading: Talent density over headcount: how Alexandr staffed Meta Superintelligence Labs
chunks.text:
- Two days after a 44-minute first call with Mark Zuckerberg, Alexandr sent a written plan. Its first point: "you don't need a lot of people, and talent density is the thing that matters."
- The research team is under 200 people, closer to 100 by Mark's count, plus infra staff. Each stage of model training (pre-training, post-training) is tens of people at Meta versus hundreds elsewhere.
- Compute is concentrated on a few key people. The lab does not "peanut-butter" it across competing efforts, so each researcher gets a lot of compute.
- A small, talent-dense team is a recruiting pitch in itself: it feels like a startup with a big company's stability and resources.
- Flat structure: nearly 200 direct reports in principle, with team leads in practice. The point is the absence of non-technical managers, not heavy managerial support.
- Staying technical is a rule. People must use the agents and write code, because leaders who move out of the details lose technical understanding faster than they realize.
- Alexandr says the team is full of "insecure overachievers." He records their pessimistic 3-month forecasts, then replays them after a ship to show what they actually delivered.
- He prefers strong-willed people who argue for what they believe, because ownership matters more than blind execution. He recommends hiring people who really care.

chunks.heading: The full reboot after Llama 4
chunks.text:
- Llama 4 launched in April 2025. Zuckerberg began calling people for advice around April 20-21.
- Early on, the group "jammed a bunch of people together" in a Supernova-style push. Neither slept much for the first couple of months, and Mark cleared his calendar for a month or two to meet researchers.
- The reboot was not planned upfront. It emerged during recruiting conversations: to make the effort attractive to the best people, it had to feel like starting from scratch. Strong people from Llama and FAIR were pulled in as well.
- Alexandr says the construct was shaped in real time during early recruiting conversations: when a pitch to a candidate didn't work, they adjusted it.
- A diagnostic moment from his first week: a lead of the old effort said consumers did not need a reasoning model. He took it as a sign that leadership needed to be far more AI-pilled and forward-leaning.
- Once the CEO visibly shifted, long-tenured Meta leaders adapted quickly. His example is Adam Mosseri at Instagram, who built an effective personal vibe-coded mini-app setup.
- A reboot needs the whole company behind it: infrastructure, data centers and other teams had to pivot. Only one thing can be the top priority at a time.
- Alexandr sets no deadlines and tells the team the work will go at "the right pace." With high-talent people this still produced speed, because they were self-motivated.

chunks.heading: Making huge bets before there is proof
chunks.text:
- Alexandr calls frontier AI "entrepreneurship on hard mode" and "the opposite of Lean Startup." You cannot build, check, then double down, because planning runs a year or more ahead.
- Muse Wonder was planned from August of the prior year, with data centers and clusters planned years before that. Muse Spark was a stepping stone to it.
- At the end of the prior year, with no models yet, the exec team (CFO Susan Li included) discussed a roughly $100-200B commitment. Alexandr's evidence was a "vibe report" and some plots. His felt risk: "this is a fuck ton of risk."
- He credits Mark with internalizing power laws: "it's not how much you fail, it's how big the win is when you win."
- Mark's counter-view of the risk: if the models fail, AI overall has to fail for the compute to be worthless, because others would pay for the capacity. He also notes the company believed in the product thesis (a personal consumer version of coding agents).
- Cost figures Mark gave: about $15B a year to operate a 1 GW cluster, about $50-60B CapEx to build one, with research testing at every rung roughly doubling the run cost. Alexandr's estimate for training a frontier model is "tens of billions of dollars."
- Alexandr's view on CEO conviction: once Mark decides something is right, he reshapes everything (calendar, company, spend) to match. Alexandr sees this as rarer than just saying AI is important: "look at what they're actually doing and how consistent are their actions with that belief."

chunks.heading: Product thesis: the model is the product
chunks.text:
- Internal saying at Meta: "the model is the product." Products are getting thinner while the model carries more of the experience.
- Alexandr argues traditional product specs are the wrong axes for AI-native products. Decisions about personality, proactivity, tool use and behavior in each situation are specified through training methods, data and evals.
- The comparison he draws: early mobile, when "it's just an app," hid enormous differences between apps. Today "it's just an agent" hides real differentiation.
- Muse has no model selector or effort selector. Alexandr criticizes AI products built by technical groups with no "randomly sampled American" in mind, where model names are confusing and version numbers sometimes go backwards.
- Mark's examples of where product work remains: the privacy and security model for connected data, and a dedicated VM per agent so users feel their data isn't running on shared compute.
- Muse is built as a personal and professional agent, not a retrieval assistant: delegation, not lookup.
- Alexandr names the pieces that make the product feel right: reliable task handling, proactivity (and in what context), and how it talks to you. Reliability is a big part of the "magic": if everything were slightly less reliable, people would throw the app away.
- Multimodal was an early priority from Alexandr, against an industry consensus that "coding was all that mattered." His reasoning: most consumers experience the world through voice, video and images.
- He says personal agents are best framed as "a team of experts in your corner" (legal, finance, medical). Wonder is state of the art on many finance and legal evals by their measurement.

chunks.heading: Evals and how Alexandr measures a model
chunks.text:
- Early on, public benchmarks are fine for finding "signs of life." As the program matures, a growing share of what the lab watches is internal.
- Alexandr's critique of external benchmarks: someone's PhD project that went viral shouldn't set your product direction. "You're outsourcing all of your product thinking to that PhD student."
- A big part of the work is crafting evals. They keep a rigorous spreadsheet of small capabilities that matter to end users. "Maybe each of them matters like 2% to the user, but in aggregate, that's the obsession" that makes a model feel magical.
- He quantifies "big model smell" as the gap between in-distribution (RL/post-training tasks) and out-of-distribution performance. The gap shrinks sharply from the Spark line to the Wonder line.
- Mark uses his MMA coaching setup as a personal eval: the agent must process video and give feedback within a 1-minute round break, which tests speed and coding ability.
- Alexandr prefers a differentiation lens for models: the models of different labs have different "texture," and flattening them to the same benchmarks hides that.

chunks.heading: How frontier models are built (Alexandr's mental model)
chunks.text:
- Pre-training is the massive-data, massive-compute stage. It's the highest-stakes stage and the most scientific, with very few samples. The team invests a large share of compute in it and goes through "troughs of uncertainty."
- Climbing a ladder: you train models roughly 4-5x bigger in steps rather than jumping straight to your largest cluster. Domain and modality data (health, legal, finance, images, video, audio) should be in pre-training, not RL'd in at the end.
- Post-training has two parts. SFT (supervised fine-tuning) initializes behaviors and personality; they may appear only about 10% of the time. RL then drives those behaviors up reliably.
- RL: environment and task design is a place of intentionality, and "less is more" for data there, which he calls flipped from pre-training. Large RL runs can magnify misaligned behavior if the only way to succeed in an environment is something unsafe, so environments are curated.
- Both axes scale: his one-line summary is "scale everything." Muse Spark went from 1 to 1.3 with RL recipe gains only, and feels "night and day" better. Agent harness co-optimization is another axis.
- Alignment view (Mark's): it means instruction and values alignment with the person served, not moralizing lectures.
- Wonder features: active memory (the model is aware of memory as a core system and handles compaction itself, rather than relying on a harness), active focus (persistence over long horizons through setbacks), domain expertise, and frontier coding.

chunks.heading: Why no AI winner-takes-all, and where Muse monetizes
chunks.text:
- Alexandr's reasons AI hasn't become winner-takes-all: execution varies by lab and averages out; distillation packs capability into smaller models and helps open source; and many people and companies want a plural outcome and choose where to work and do business accordingly.
- Muse Wonder and Muse Spark focus on personal and professional agents, which he thinks is a real differentiation from other labs. "There should be differentiation in the economy."
- Distribution plan: free for everyone on Spark, a paid subscription for Wonder because it's costly to serve, then API access (Meta Model API, OpenRouter) and Muse Code. Mark hopes to get Wonder-level quality in the cheaper Spark form factor soon.
- Agentic commerce: Alexandr says Muse is among the first products where people fully delegate purchases. He sees value in reduced friction, hard criteria applied automatically ("need it by Wednesday"), and personalization from holistic context versus siloed recommendation systems.
- Alexandr says he told Patrick Collison in 2023 that agentic commerce was coming ("directionally correct, but like 3 years early").
- Mark's framing of the opportunity: agents get accounts, so total commerce demand may grow, not just conversion rates.
- Alexandr on demand shifts: agentic commerce will grow as a share of commerce, like e-commerce next to brick-and-mortar, and businesses must decide whether to participate.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this Economic Times interview, Wang explains why Meta sees 2026 as the year of the personal agent and how its three and a half billion daily users give it a distribution edge. He argues trust is the first principle for intimate AI products, and that talent density, compute and no artificial deadlines make the best research environment. He also says AI tools empower small businesses more than they disrupt jobs.

chunks.heading: Personal agents as the next leap, and where Meta aims to deploy them
chunks.text:
- Alexandr thinks this is "the year of the personal agent." AI is moving from passive, search-style systems to ones that "work for you 24/7."
- Agents should understand your goals, act on your behalf, and constantly look for ways to improve your life and get tasks done.
- He frames the opportunity as distribution: Meta has 3.5 billion people using its platforms every day. That lets it make personal agents "globally ubiquitous in a way that we think that very few companies have the opportunity to."
- Meta released Manus agents on Telegram after acquiring Manus. Meta plans to keep investing in this area through the year.
- The vision comes from Mark Zuckerberg's "personal superintelligence" essay. It asks what the world looks like if AI is deployed to every person, so they can build the businesses they want, explore passions or finish projects.

chunks.heading: Agentic commerce and why it doesn't threaten Meta's ad business
chunks.text:
- Alexandr believes in agents "you would trust enough to ultimately make purchases on your behalf and ultimately coordinate very complex logistics on your behalf." He explicitly endorses agentic commerce.
- Asked whether agent-to-agent transactions would undermine advertising and the social graph, he says he is not very concerned.
- His reasoning is that new technology repeatedly enables new formats and products, and Meta's products have evolved that way through the years.
- If agents enable dramatically more commerce, he sees "a lot more opportunity to help businesses," not less.

chunks.heading: Models vs productisation: open source, frontier research and deployment
chunks.text:
- Meta remains committed to open source and will "probably release a mixture of closed and open source models."
- He is equally committed to the frontier. When he joined about seven months earlier, a priority was setting up research to "deliver the very best models in the world" and to "get back to scientific fundamentals."
- A new series of models was coming "in the coming months."
- Productisation matters just as much. He says models are powerful, but "what we really, really care about is that we can actually deploy this technology to everyone in the world."
- The two-part goal is to build great AI in the lab and deliver it into products in new ways.

chunks.heading: Compute and infrastructure strategy
chunks.text:
- He sees two drivers of spend. The first is "incredible returns" from putting more compute into research, because model improvement is still fast.
- The second is inference. Meta must serve billions of users, so it needs enough capacity to run inference at that scale.
- On chips, he describes a "multi-Silicon strategy": use many silicon providers and avoid reliance on any single one, "and this includes investing into our own Silicon."
- The aim is infrastructure that scales with demand. He declined to comment on talks about buying Google TPUs.

chunks.heading: India as a market and a place to deploy personal agents
chunks.text:
- India is "one of the most important countries for Meta, full stop," with more than half a billion daily active users across WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook.
- He argues India is one of the few countries where a personalised, powerful agent for every user could be made real quickly, because of Meta's platform reach there.
- Meta's India investments include connectivity, support for enterprises, and a joint venture with Reliance Industries on enterprise AI adoption.
- On job disruption, he says that when small businesses and creators get AI tools, "the opportunity vastly outstrips any of the disruption."
- He expects AI coding and knowledge-work tools to be used more by small businesses, entrepreneurs and new businesses.
- He cites a founder at an Indian roundtable who said there are more Indian consumer AI companies than American ones. Backing entrepreneurship and small business is, in his view, "a nearly endless sort of growing sector."

chunks.heading: Trust as the first principle for personal agents
chunks.text:
- A truly personalised agent will be "more intimate than any technology has ever been historically." It will know a lot about you and make many decisions for you.
- Because of that, trust is "incredibly, incredibly important." He says Meta's success depends on building trust with the billions of people on its platforms.
- Decisions about AI and future technology are "rooted in how do we build that level of trust," as a long-term "North Star and first principle."
- This was his answer to questions about OpenAI introducing ads.

chunks.heading: Building and keeping a frontier research team
chunks.text:
- His main lever is the environment. Researchers are inspired by the science, so it is his and Meta's responsibility to build the best place for them to work.
- Talent density is one pillar: smart people want to be surrounded by brilliant people who push them and teach them.
- Compute is another: researchers need ample resources to test scientific ideas.
- A third is a return to basics. He says "we're going to focus on scientific rigour" and "we are not going to have artificial deadlines," approaching the work in a way that is "proper and correct for the long term."
- On compensation, he acknowledges Meta's hiring made headlines but says others were already paying researchers well, and that "more than the compensation, we really focus on creating the best environment."

chunks.heading: Builder's perspective and the definition of superintelligence
chunks.text:
- On criticism of his youth and limited research background, he points to AI's dynamism: Google led, then OpenAI, then Anthropic.
- He argues there are always openings for fresh perspectives that let organisations do things incumbents can't. His role is to bring "more of a builder's perspective" to differentiate Meta in the marketplace.
- He says he started his company at 19, in 2016, inspired by AI's potential. The focus then was autonomous driving, "the holy grail use case."
- He defines superintelligence as "AI that is able to outperform humans on any measurable task."
- He says Superintelligence Labs was named to signal the ambition of the research agenda. He admits the term risks becoming a buzzword but says Meta cares about "the scientific definition of very powerful AI."
- He says he and Zuckerberg are in sync on personal superintelligence, personal agents, global deployment and being at the frontier. He praises Zuckerberg as "always open to feedback."

Today we’ve formalized an important hiring policy at Scale. We hire for MEI: merit, excellence, and intelligence.

This is the email I’ve shared with our @scale_AI team.

———————————————————

MERITOCRACY AT SCALE

In the wake of our fundraise, I’ve been getting a lot of questions about talent. All of our external success—powering breakthroughs in L4 autonomy, partnering with OpenAI on RLHF going back to GPT-2, supporting the DoD and every major AI lab, and the recent $1bn financing transaction—all of it is downstream from us hiring the best people for the job. Talent is our #1 input metric.

Because of this, I spend a lot of my time on recruiting. I either personally interview every hire or sign off on every candidate packet. It’s the thing I spend the plurality of my time on, easily. But everyone can and should contribute to this effort. There are almost a thousand of us now, and it takes a lot to hire quickly while maintaining, and continuing to raise, our bar for quality.

That’s why this is the time to codify a hiring principle that I consider crucial to our success:
Scale is a meritocracy, and we must always remain one.

Hiring on merit will be a permanent policy at Scale.

It’s a big deal whenever we invite someone to join our mission, and those decisions have never been swayed by orthodoxy or virtue signaling or whatever the current thing is. I think of our guiding principle as MEI: merit, excellence, and intelligence.

That means we hire only the best person for the job, we seek out and demand excellence, and we unapologetically prefer people who are very smart.

We treat everyone as an individual. We do not unfairly stereotype, tokenize, or otherwise treat anyone as a member of a demographic group rather than as an individual.

We believe that people should be judged by the content of their character — and, as colleagues, be additionally judged by their talent, skills, and work ethic.

There is a mistaken belief that meritocracy somehow conflicts with diversity. I strongly disagree. No group has a monopoly on excellence. A hiring process based on merit will naturally yield a variety of backgrounds, perspectives, and ideas. Achieving this requires casting a wide net for talent and then objectively selecting the best, without bias in any direction. We will not pick winners and losers based on someone being the “right” or “wrong” race, gender, and so on. It should be needless to say, and yet it needs saying: doing so would be racist and sexist, not to mention illegal.

Upholding meritocracy is good for business and is the right thing to do. This approach not only results in the strongest possible team, but also ensures we’re treating our colleagues with fairness and respect.

As a result, everyone who joins Scale can be confident that they were chosen for their outstanding talent, not any other reasons.

MEI has gotten us to where we are today. And it’s the same thing that’ll get us where we’re going, as we embark on our next chapter focusing on data abundance, frontier data, and reliable measurement to accelerate the development and adoption of AI models.

Alex

At the YC Alumni Reunion, I got lots of questions from new founders about how to build a successful company, but realized that they all had the same answer. And it’s this:

—————————————————

DO TOO MUCH

As a new founder, I’d often look at the CEOs of successful companies and wonder, “How do they do it?”

As Scale grows and as I learn on the job, I’ve come to realize that leaders of great organizations never just do it. They overdo it.

As a leader, you are the upper bound for how much anyone in your company will care. You need to do more, care more, attempt more than would seem reasonable. It will seem like overkill. But too much is the right amount.

This is true in big and small ways.

- What people say is overoptimism is just optimism.
- What people say is overcommunicating is just communicating.
- What people say is overdelivering is just delivering.
- What people say is micromanagement is just management.
- What people say is ruthless prioritization is just prioritization.

Actually living this way will seem crazy, and that’s ok. There is no Apple without Jobs’s “obsessive” attention to detail. There is no SpaceX or Tesla without Elon’s “maniacal” drive for execution. I have never seen ordinary effort lead to extraordinary results.

If we had not done too much, Scale would not be the company it is today.

When AI really started to take off in 2022 and “generative AI” became a thing, within 6 months Scale shifted the vast majority of our team to working on generating data for scaling LLMs.

Most companies would go through quarters of bureaucratic planning cycles and only move after a competitor started eating their lunch. In our case, the change was drastic and abrupt — some might say jarring or extreme.

What people might have reasonably described as overreacting was just reacting. And in hindsight, that reaction to developments in AI was what made Scale’s subsequent path possible, including growing 4X over the last year.

What we’ve accomplished to date represents the compounded results of everybody embracing the culture of overdoing. Scale will do things incumbent companies wouldn’t, because it’s simply too scary or painful, but others not going to the same lengths is a feature not a bug.

Creating something meaningful is a beautiful, and yes, scary and painful thing. And if you’re not overdoing it, you’re underdoing it.

What does DeepSeek R1 & v3 mean for LLM data?

Contrary to some lazy takes I’ve seen, DeepSeek R1 was trained on a shit ton of human-generated data—in fact, the DeepSeek models are setting records for the disclosed amount of post-training data for open-source models:

- 600,000 reasoning data [1]
- 200,000 non-reasoning SFT data [2]
- human preference (RLHF) dataset of undisclosed size [3]
- human-processed synthetic data for cold-start data [4]

According to Chinese AI engineers, DeepSeek actually values data annotation even more than other Chinese labs, with the CEO personally labeling data for the model [5] (This reminds me of @karpathy who used to spend a quarter of his time labeling at Tesla). The DeepSeek-v3 paper even has a dedicated acknowledgement section for Data Annotation [6].
DeepSeek-V3, which was distilled from DeepSeek-R1, was also trained on an instruction-tuning dataset of 1.5M samples. [7]

These SFT datasets are even larger than other open-source models:

- Qwen-2.5 was trained on 1M SFT samples [8]
- the last time Meta disclosed was for Llama 2, which was trained on only 30k SFT samples and 3M RLHF samples [9]
- Kimi k1.5 was trained on roughly 1M SFT, 1M multi-modal SFT, 800k samples for classic reward modeling, and another 800k CoT labeled examples for reasoning [10] 

It’s interesting that the size of the RLHF dataset was undisclosed, while they disclosed the size of the SFT and reasoning datasets. This could be because it is much larger than one would expect, or it reveals some interesting technical detail they don’t care to share. Human preference datasets are often much larger than SFT datasets in most models, so a reasonable estimate would be that DeepSeek’s models are probably trained on at least 3-5M samples, which is quite a large preference dataset!

The main technical breakthrough of DeepSeek-R1 is that for reasoning, you can forgo SFT data in favor of reasoning data—but reasoning data is still human data of difficult problems&answers in a variety of domains. 

The reasoning dataset is actually quite large—600k reasoning samples is a LOT. This is in line with a broader trend we’ve seen from SFT data towards other data types like human preference/RLHF data and reasoning data. This is for technical reasons—SFT caps the performance of the model at a certain level, whereas RLHF or other methods enable the models to continue improving without bound beyond the limits of the dataset.

DeepSeek R1 is a very exciting model, and it’s great to see o1 reasoning capabilities replicated in the wild. In terms of training data, however, the DeepSeek models are actually setting open-source records in terms of the amount of human data used.
